articles.title: Concerns mount over integrity of Israel’s upcoming October elections
articles.excerpt: Concerns are being raised about the integrity of Israel’s upcoming general election with politicians, civil society groups and even President Isaac Herzog warning of potential political interference i...
articles.body_text:
Concerns are being raised about the integrity of Israel’s upcoming general election with politicians, civil society groups and even President Isaac Herzog warning of potential political interference in the vote.

Israelis will ultimately decide the country’s next government and prime minister when they vote in legislative elections on October 27, which will see Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu attempt to win another term in office.

But there are mounting concerns over the future of Israeli democracy amid apparent attempts by Netanyahu’s government to entrench its power.

A poll by the Israel Democracy Institute found that almost three-quarters of Jewish Israelis were concerned about the integrity of the 2026 election, while 43 percent said they were optimistic about the future of democratic rule in Israel.

Opposition leader Yair Lapid, former Prime Minister Ehud Olmert and President Herzog have all raised concerns about the vote.

In a televised speech in mid-July, Herzog raised concerns about interference in the election and the threat of violence following a meeting with the heads of the electoral commission and internal security service, Shin Bet.

Using biblical stories as examples of the dangers of internecine infighting, Herzog pleaded with the public not to “cross red lines” during the campaign season.

“I turn to elected representatives, activists and all candidates from all parties, and demand that you do not cross red lines. Do not turn rivals into enemies,” Herzog continued. “I call on the people of Israel, in a clear voice: Remember that elections are not a civil war.”

The governing coalition will continue its campaign, begun in 2021, to free itself of judicial oversight, an issue that has bitterly divided the nation. Netanyahu – himself on trial for corruption – is also seeking to defer an independent inquiry into the Hamas-led incursions of October 2023, which led to criticism of his handling of security issues.

Growing international criticism of Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza and settler violence across the occupied West Bank, as well as Israel’s multi-front war against neighbours in Lebanon, Yemen, Syria and Iran, will also be hot topics in the election.

Israeli Member of the Knesset (MK) Ofer Cassif, who had a no confidence motion in June, told Al Jazeera that violence has become a part of the Israeli political landscape, particularly in the occupied West Bank.

“There’s no need to speculate about the potential for violence, it’s already happening,” he told Al Jazeera. “We’re seeing anti-government activists, and not just Palestinians, but Israelis being arrested and even judges harassed by far-right pro-government militias.”

Ofer said that “problematic” candidates, such as members of his left-wing Hadash Party, were preparing for government attempts to bar them from the election. He also warned of growing unrest in the run-up to election day itself, which could see attempts to suppress voting in areas with large Palestinian citizen of Israel populations, he said.

“Then there’s after the election itself, suppose – purely for analytical purposes – we say it goes against the government. What then? What if they refuse to leave their offices? Who’s going to remove them, Ben-Gvir’s police or Netanyahu’s Shin Bet?” he asked. “They’re already conquered… This is a very dangerous time we’re approaching.“

There has even been criticism from members of Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud Party, some of whom are against the appointment of Dean Livne as acting head of the Central Elections Committee. MK Avichay Buaron called him “clearly politically biased”, while Diaspora Affairs Minister, Amichai Chikli, said his appointment casts “a heavy shadow” over the election’s integrity.

The coalition has cut the committee’s budget by 50 million New Israeli Shekels (NIS) or (roughly $15m), even though there have been multiple warnings of foreign interference and the risks posed by artificial intelligence in the vote.

The government has been accused of resisting efforts to expand access to voting to care homes. Accusations have also been levelled at the office of Transportation Minister, Miri Regev, of limiting flights into Ben Gurion Airport before election day, which could hinder left-leaning overseas voters from flying into Israel and casting votes against Netanyahu.

“There’s always a tension between whatever governing party is in power and a fair election,” said Therese Pearce Laanela of the intergovernmental electoral monitoring agency, International IDEA. “In the main, their responsibilities are twofold: to ensure the legislation is in place to hold the election and to make the resources available to ensure they’re carried out fairly. What they mustn’t do, is undermine the electoral authority or criticise it in public… There can be a disconnect between perception and reality.”

Political analyst Ori Goldberg said that many Israelis now see Netanyahu as a constant in political life. Some attribute the powers of a “wizard” to him, able to conjure a fresh tactic, or way out of any situation during every Israeli election.

“People always expect Netanyahu to do whatever it takes to stay in power, whatever the cost,” Goldberg said. “Every Israeli election is portrayed as somehow seismic, but this one might actually be. If this coalition is returned to power, it’s Israel telling the world that it’s OK with multiple wars, with enforced starvation – and it’s OK with genocide.”

articles.title: What now as Israel rejects Trump’s 15-point plan for Gaza?
articles.excerpt:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected United States President Donald Trump’s 15-point plan for Gaza, saying that Israeli forces will not withdraw until Hamas is “genuinely disarmed”.
...
articles.body_text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected United States President Donald Trump’s 15-point plan for Gaza, saying that Israeli forces will not withdraw until Hamas is “genuinely disarmed”.

“Israel rejects the 15-point document,” he said at a cabinet meeting, stressing that Hamas must give up all of its weapons before any pull-back.

Trump late last month announced a breakthrough in the US-led ceasefire framework, saying that Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza had accepted a phased plan under which they would surrender their weapons to a new Palestinian governing body, and Israel would begin pulling out troops in tandem with disarmament.

Netanyahu, under pressure from his right-wing base ahead of elections, has seemingly hardened his stance after days of mounting criticism of the plan.

So, what is Trump’s 15-point plan, and why has Israel rejected it?

On July 30, the US-led Board of Peace proposed a 15-point roadmap for Gaza, detailing a phased, conditional framework for disarmament and reconstruction in the war-torn coastal enclave.

The plan mandates that Hamas disarm in exchange for a full Israeli military withdrawal and the transition of governance to an independent Palestinian National Committee, supported by an international security force.

The Board of Peace, created by Trump in October with him serving as its lifetime chair, is led by the US government. United Nations Security Council (UNSC) Resolution 2803 designates it the body responsible for overseeing the Gaza peace plan.

Trump said the agreement would be implemented in stages, with Israeli forces withdrawing as the disarmament process advances.

Despite the framework, significant challenges remain, as Hamas hinges its compliance on an end to Israel’s genocidal actions.

A member of Hamas’s negotiating delegation last month told Al Jazeera that the group’s implementation of the agreement will be dependent on Israel fulfilling its commitments.

However, the Board of Peace earlier this week said an Israeli withdrawal from Gaza will only take place after the disarmament of Hamas is complete.

Israel has killed more than 73,300 Palestinians in Gaza since its genocidal war began in October 2023. And since agreeing to a US-mediated “ceasefire” with Hamas in ⁠⁠October 2025, it has continued ⁠⁠to carry out strikes on Gaza, killing more than 1,200 Palestinians, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.

The Israeli army “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens”, the Israeli prime minister said.

Netanyahu added that Israel was engaging with Washington over its concerns about the plan.

“They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us, and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters,” he said.

The Israeli leader, who is expected to face a tough national election in October this year, with successive surveys showing he is on course to lose, said that Hamas must give up all of its weapons.

“We are talking about real disarmament, not fictitious disarmament,” Netanyahu said.

Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from the occupied West Bank, said discussions around the 15-point plan, including Hamas’s disarmament and Israel’s potential withdrawal, “are extremely controversial for the [Netanyahu-led] right-wing government”.

“It seems that Netanyahu, so close to elections, has hit the reset button, saying that none of that will happen under his watch,” she said.

“This is extremely problematic for the Board of Peace and the mediators who have been working for months now to try to find a way to carry out the disarmament of Hamas and have Israel commit to a phased withdrawal from Gaza.”

Al Jazeera’s Hani Mahmoud, reporting from Gaza City, said most people in the war-battered coastal enclave “expected” Israel to reject the proposal.

“The only concern that people have right now is that this is translating into greater uncertainty,” he reported, adding that the plan “was meant to provide more structure and a framework”.

“There are important elements that were part of the plan in terms of security: Israeli withdrawal from the area that it has been occupying over the past years across Gaza known as the ‘Yellow Line’, the disarmament of Hamas, as well as the entry of international stabilisation forces. Now, the full rejection here puts the sequencing and the steps to complete that into serious question. It translates into no clear end to hostilities and wars.”

Political analyst and former adviser to the Palestinian negotiations team Xavier Abu Eid says the Board of Peace and UNSC Resolution 2803 were accepted late last year because it was argued at that time that they were the only way to end the Israeli genocide in Gaza.

“But it was very clear from the very beginning that the 20-point plan of President Trump and the 15-point disarmament and implementation plan that followed were more about meeting Israeli interests than the Palestinian right to self-determination,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Justice for Palestinians is something that nobody talks about. So, certainly, this remains a position,” he said, adding that Trump is unlikely to be happy with Netanyahu’s rejection.

“But at the same time, Trump has never even pretended to push any sort of accountability measures for Netanyahu violating even their own agreements,” the analyst said.

Israeli analyst Dan Perry said Netanyahu’s move against the proposed Gaza plan is “misaligned with what the people in Israel would generally want, if they understood correctly what’s going on”.

“I have no naivety about Hamas. But even if there is an idea that there is a declarative agreement to disarm, it is something that should be welcomed so clearly,” Perry, the former chief of The Associated Press news agency in Europe, Africa and the Middle East, told Al Jazeera.

“I keep hearing about a trade-off between Israeli security demands and the obvious needs of the Palestinian people, the need to alleviate and fix the humanitarian disaster in Gaza, but these are not at loggerheads.”

Much of Israeli society has backed the genocidal war on Gaza following the October 7 attack on southern Israel, as well as the war on Lebanon and Iran.

Alon Pinkas, a former Israeli diplomat, says Netanyahu needs “a forever war”.

“This Israeli rejection of the Gaza plan … should be viewed entirely in the context of the upcoming Israeli election on October 27,” he told Al Jazeera.

Pinkas said Netanyahu made a “calculation that this is risk free”, “that he can supposedly defy Trump because Trump doesn’t care enough, because of the sequence, because Hamas hasn’t disarmed yet, because he can get away with it”.

“And this is all about the forever war and the election,” he concluded.

articles.title: The Mecca pact is not just another regional alliance
articles.excerpt:
Executive Director of the Middle East Council on Global Affairs.

The joint defence agreement signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, and Pakistan in Mecca on Friday is not another entry in a region already ...
articles.body_text:
Executive Director of the Middle East Council on Global Affairs.

The joint defence agreement signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, and Pakistan in Mecca on Friday is not another entry in a region already crowded with alliances and communiques. Its significance lies less in its provisions than in what it signals: a shift in how the Gulf states conceive of their own security.

Riyadh and its neighbours appear increasingly unwilling to tie strategic security to a single guarantor. The alternative is a wider network of partnerships that diversifies options, capabilities, and room for manoeuvre.

Read this way, the pact does not mark the end of the United States-led order. It marks the start of preparation for a more pluralistic one — a system in which regional powers produce security rather than import it. It is, in effect, an insurance policy against a world where the US is less present and less predictable.

The pact has all the potential to jump-start a major transformation of regional security.

Events of the past decade have changed the calculus in the Gulf. The question is no longer the magnitude of American power, but the predictability of its use.

A state can buy tens of billions worth of US weapons, host bases and troops, and cultivate deep ties with Washington — then discover in a crisis that the decision to act is determined by American domestic politics and geopolitical calculations largely unrelated to allied security.

Gulf capitals have now concluded that partnership, however deep, is not an automatic guarantee of protection.

The resulting strategy is straightforward: keep the alliance with Washington, but build options beyond it. This is not a defection from the American camp to the Chinese, Russian, or Turkish one. It is an attempt to move past the logic of camps altogether. It is also a reflection of a region preparing itself for a likely US withdrawal in the future.

The most sensitive dimension of regional security in this scenario concerns the balance of power. If the American role recedes, the danger lies in who may fill the vacuum it leaves behind.

Iran has spent decades building regional influence beyond its borders and continues to direct missiles and drones at Gulf and Arab capitals. Israel has demonstrated military and intelligence superiority that has enabled force projection across the region. At the same time, it continues to pursue occupation and settlement policies and military action against Arab states.

Diminished American weight could leave the region inside an order whose rules are set by two actors alone: Israel and Iran.

The Mecca pact is best understood as an early attempt to build a third pole — a bloc that does not need to fight either power, but one that has enough weight to deny either a monopoly over the region. The objective is not victory. It is the prevention of hegemony.

Iran cannot be written out of the Gulf equation. Turkiye’s ties to Tehran mix cooperation and rivalry; Pakistan shares a long border with Iran and will not open a permanent front. The alliance’s most useful function is therefore deterrence: raising the cost of any attack on a member.

For decades, the Gulf was a security consumer. It bought advanced weapons, hosted foreign forces, and relied on Western-designed intelligence, communications, and protection networks. The model worked in many respects, but carried a structural flaw: final decisions came partly from the outside.

What the Mecca pact could do is accelerate defence localisation. The agreement is meant to go beyond a standard military alliance and build capacity at home.

The pact brings together three regional powers with complementary strengths: Saudi Arabia offers capital, geographic position, political weight, and a substantial defence market; Turkiye contributes an advanced military-industrial base, particularly in drones, missiles, naval platforms, and electronic systems; Pakistan adds a large and experienced military, significant strategic capabilities, and the distinction of being the pact’s only nuclear-armed member.

The pact’s value will be measured in integration: joint air defence, early warning, intelligence, munitions, cyber defence, and a joint command able to function under fire.

Just as important will be defence cooperation that evolves from purchasing Turkish and Pakistani systems to co-producing and co-developing them in Saudi Arabia.

The maritime dimension will also be crucial.

Gulf security no longer begins at the region’s borders. It stretches from the Gulf to the Red Sea and from the Strait of Hormuz to Bab al-Mandeb arteries where the majority of regional energy trade and a significant share of global commerce move.

If the pact matures into organised maritime cooperation, it could underpin arrangements to protect ports, shipping, and energy routes without total dependence on Western fleets. That is precisely the capability the region needs to hedge against future US retrenchment.

The region has never lacked agreements; it has lacked shared political foundations. The Arab coalition in Yemen established in 2015 eventually faltered after divergent views of the war clashed. The Islamic Military Counter Terrorism Coalition, also set up in 2015, assembled an impressive roster of participants but failed to translate numbers into unified capability.

Bringing states together is not the same as aligning their interests.

The Mecca pact could become the first serious building block of a more autonomous regional security order. The outcome will be determined not by defence budgets or membership numbers. It will be determined by the answer to one question: are the signatories genuinely willing to bear the cost of defending one another?

If yes, the region may finally begin building a balance that does not rest entirely on power arriving from across an ocean.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Syria says it reached deal with Moscow on future of Russian bases
articles.excerpt:
Syria says it has reached a deal with Moscow on the future of Russia’s two military bases in the country, which were used to support ousted President Bashar al-Assad during the Syrian war.

Syria’s of...
articles.body_text:
Syria says it has reached a deal with Moscow on the future of Russia’s two military bases in the country, which were used to support ousted President Bashar al-Assad during the Syrian war.

Syria’s official SANA news agency quoted the Foreign Ministry as saying on Sunday that the Hmeimim airbase and Tartus naval base would be turned into “joint training and capacity-building centres” under new arrangements aimed at preserving mutual interests.

The memorandum of understanding, reached after a year and a half of negotiations, sets a deadline of no more than three months to complete the transition, SANA said.

In the meantime, civilian facilities at both bases will be handed over to Damascus.

Russia has yet to officially comment on the agreement.

Both the Hmeimim and Tartus bases had remained operational while talks were ongoing.

While this memorandum of understanding may have come as a surprise to some, Syria’s government is using it to send “a clear message that the central government in Damascus is in control of all assets that belong to Syria and are part of Syrian territory,” said Al Jazeera’s Obaida Hitto, reporting from Damascus.

In short, Damascus is affirming that “its national sovereignty is not up for negotiation,” said Hitto.

Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani visited the sites on Sunday “to inspect the facilities and installations included in the historic memorandum of understanding”, according to SANA.

Russia was a key Assad ally during Syria’s 13-year civil war, helping to keep the former leader in power by providing vital military support.

Assad’s ouster in 2024 dealt a major blow to Moscow’s influence in the region.

President Vladimir Putin has since worked to build relations with his Syrian counterpart Ahmed al-Sharaa to secure the future of Russia’s only two official military bases outside the former Soviet Union.

“Russia has significantly downgraded its military presence from over 100 military bases to just these two positions on the Syrian coast,” said Al Jazeera’s Hitto.

“Now that those positions are going to be augmented in terms that are acceptable to both sides, according to a statement by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, it’s going to become clearer in the coming weeks what kind of military presence Russia will maintain here in Syria.”

Syria has also expressed a willingness to cooperate with Moscow, with Putin receiving Sharaa twice in Moscow since taking power.

During Sharaa’s last visit in January, Putin said “much has been accomplished in terms of restoring our interstate relations”, commending Sharaa for his “efforts to restore Syria’s territorial integrity”.

While Sharaa praised Russia’s “historic role” in Syria and the region, Damascus has repeatedly demanded that it extradite Assad, who has been sheltering in Moscow with his wife since his ouster.

articles.title: Israel rejects Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, Netanyahu says
articles.excerpt:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected US President Donald Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, stating that no military pull-out will happen until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed.

Trump's B...
articles.body_text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected US President Donald Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, stating that no military pull-out will happen until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed.

Trump's Board of Peace said last month it had reached an agreement for the "complete disarmament" of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza.

But Hamas said handing over its heavy weapons was contingent on Israel ending "all forms of aggression" and withdrawing its forces from Gaza.

Israel has continued to carry out strikes on Gaza since agreeing to an initial ceasefire in the territory last October.

"Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting on Sunday.

The Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens", he added.

A Hamas official told the BBC on Sunday the group "reaffirms it commitment" to the agreement and it was ready "to engage seriously and responsibly in implementing" the 15-point plan.

They called on mediators to ensure "that all parties comply with what has been agreed".

Israel's rejection signals another blow for Trump's Gaza peace plan which was announced in September last year.

The plan included the creation of the Board of Peace to oversee the agreement's implementation, as well as the disarmament of Hamas, withdrawal of Israeli troops and reconstruction of Gaza.

Netanyahu's statement does not come as a surprise.

But he has taken some time to make it, perhaps reflecting the difficult position the Israeli leader is in.

He clearly is unhappy with Trump's plan but at the same time he will not want to upset his closest ally.

It's just over a week since Trump announced what he called a "monumental step toward lasting peace and security" - that Hamas for the first time had agreed to disarm, on condition that Israel withdraws its forces from Gaza.

On Sunday, Netanyahu was clear that was not going to happen under his watch. He said Hamas had to disarm first, adding that it couldn't be some "fictitious disarmament" - it had to be real.

The reality is any disarmament and withdrawal of Israeli forces would likely need to be phased.

Netanyahu said he was now in discussion with US officials about how to go forward.

"They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters," he said.

But just months before Israeli elections and under pressure from members of his right-wing coalition to take a tough stance on Gaza, he is unlikely to want to make concessions.

He has faced calls from far-right parts of the coalition to hold a new cabinet vote and end the Gaza plan, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir who dismissed the draft as "not acceptable".

Large crowds turned out in Gaza City on Tuesday for a mass funeral for 112 people, mostly women and children, who were killed in an Israeli strike on a residential block in late 2023

Nickolay Mladenov - a senior diplomat tasked with implementing Donald Trump's peace plan - defended the plan on Sunday and said discussions were ongoing in the hope of a "positive outcome".

The board's high representative for Gaza told Israel's Channel 12 that Israel had been asked "to give the process a chance" and said the plan was "the only way forward" to ensure there was no repeat of the 7 October 2023 attack by Hamas.

Mladenov said the plan was built on a process that was "verifiable, that is reversible, that at each stage can be stopped, and that we have built up with a very clear-eyed understanding of what are the challenges ahead".

He also said that Israel would not be required to withdraw until it could be verified that Hamas was taking steps to disarm.

According to the United Nations, about 1.9 million people - 90% of Gaza's population - have been displaced in the territory since the war in Gaza started.

The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Israel responded to the attack by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.

articles.title: Three Banksy artworks in London cost taxpayers nearly £150,000 in upkeep
articles.excerpt:
Costs of security and removal efforts have reignited debate over whether work is vandalism or valuable public art

Three Banksy artworks have cost taxpayers almost £150,000 in removal efforts, securit...
articles.body_text:
Costs of security and removal efforts have reignited debate over whether work is vandalism or valuable public art

Three Banksy artworks have cost taxpayers almost £150,000 in removal efforts, security and other costs, with the bill expected to rise.

The largest bill relates to a mural painted on the Royal Courts of Justice in London in September 2025, where efforts to remove it and provide security have so far cost more than £85,000, according to the BBC.

The mural depicted a judge in a wig beating a protester with his gavel. Banksy confirmed the work was his by posting an image on his website and Instagram account.

The Ministry of Justice told the BBC, after a freedom of information request, that £50,000 had been spent trying to remove the paint from the wall of the Grade II-listed building on Carey Street. A further £35,000 had been spent on overtime and security.

“The Royal Courts of Justice is a listed building and HMCTS are obliged to maintain its original character,” the HM Courts and Tribunals Service said.

The costs have reignited a debate over whether Banksy’s work constitutes vandalism or valuable public art, particularly when it appears on historic buildings. The artist, who emerged from Bristol’s graffiti scene in the 1990s, is one of the world’s most famous street artists. His work has sold at auction for upwards of £18m.

The shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, said it was “outrageous” that taxpayers’ money was being spent cleaning up after the artist. “Our courts are a national symbol of justice and the rule of law,” he said. “Banksy’s vandalism should be stopped and he should foot the bill for the costs he imposes on others.”

But the art critic Estelle Lovatt defended Banksy’s work and highlighted the benefits for tourism. “Some people visit Buckingham Palace and others visit Banksy’s art,” she told the BBC. “His work brings people together in a way that politics can divide us. He’s like the Pied Piper or a town crier.

“It can be intimidating if a mural appears on your building, in terms of the crowds, but he makes art accessible because there’s no gallery fee.”

Initial attempts to remove the mural were unsuccessful and contractors have since been using laser technology. If Westminster city council considers the result inadequate, another cleaning method will be required. As a final option, the affected stonework could be removed and replaced.

A listed building consent application has also been submitted for railings to be installed across the wall where the mural appeared. The cost of the installation is not yet known.

Another Banksy work has generated almost £60,000 in costs for Westminster city council.

A statue of a man carrying a flag appeared in Waterloo Place in the capital, near Trafalgar Square, in April. Banksy claimed responsibility by posting a video of the overnight installation on Instagram.

The council said it had spent almost £60,000 on safety barriers, administration and a security guard to monitor the statue.

“Ownership of the statue now sits with the council as landowner,” it said. “The council has notified the artist’s agent that it is reviewing options for the short, medium and long term.”

In August 2024, another Banksy work appeared on a City of London police sentry box. The artist painted a shoal of piranha fish over the box, which had been installed in the 1990s as part of security measures against the IRA.

The box was subsequently removed at a cost of £2,200 and was never replaced. It is due to go on display at the London Museum when it reopens in November.

articles.title: Most X accounts posting about Belfast and Southampton unrest were based outside UK
articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: Analysis shows 55% of accounts were located overseas – and seven of 12 most-read posts came from US

More than half the accounts that posted on Elon Musk’s X about the rioting in Belfast an...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: Analysis shows 55% of accounts were located overseas – and seven of 12 most-read posts came from US

More than half the accounts that posted on Elon Musk’s X about the rioting in Belfast and the civil disorder in Southampton in June were based outside the UK, an analysis by the Guardian can reveal.

Of the 8,672 accounts whose combined posts about the events exceeded 1,000 views, just 45.3% were shown as from the UK, according to the social media platform’s own location function.

One in six (16.8%) came from the US, 4.5% from Ireland, and about a quarter from all European countries other than the UK.

Seven of the 12 most-read tweets about Belfast and Southampton came from the US – including one from Musk himself and two other US “alt-right” commentators – while an eighth was linked to North America.

The analysis underlines that US rightwing actors are seeking to influence the UK and boost their position on X in moments of disorder – an exploitation of flashpoint events that has only intermittently attracted political attention in Britain.

The Guardian collected 43,000 tweets mentioning Belfast, Southampton, Henry Nowak or Vickrum Digwa posted on X during the period of the unrest in both cities.

This covered the period from 2 June to the end of 3 June for Southampton and from the evening of 8 June to the end of 9 June for Belfast.

For X accounts whose combined tweets reached more than 1,000 views, we extracted their location and the number of times they have changed their username as shown in the “about this account” tab.

Using a large language model (LLM), the team first classified which posts were directly related to the protests in Belfast and Southampton, and then categorised them as containing explicit or implicit racist language or anti-immigration comments. For those about Belfast, we also classified tweets as containing calls inciting to violence.

A team of three people manually verified more than 5,500 posts, statistically testing the accuracy of the model to be robust and in line with academic standards.

Nearly a third of all 43,000 posts on X relating to the two incidents contained racist or anti-immigration comments. Almost one in 10 relating to Belfast contained calls for violence or paramilitary or vigilante action.

Imran Ahmed, the chief executive of the Centre for Countering Digital Hate, said the data demonstrated that X had become “a weapon of choice” for hostile foreign actors seeking to manipulate shocking and divisive content.

Their goal, he added, was “to amplify local tragedies and crises, intensify racist narratives, and incite violence in communities they have never set foot in and to whom they have no real connection.”

A post from Musk after the life sentencing of the killer of 18-year-old Henry Nowak, who had been falsely accused of racism by police after being stabbed in Southampton, has been viewed more than 28m times.

“Legacy mainstream media, same ones who wrote about George Floyd millions of times, are dead silent about Nowak,” Musk posted shortly before 3pm on 2 June, in effect promoting his own platform at a time of heightened tension and disorder in the Hampshire port.

Eleven police officers were injured on the night of 2 June in Southampton as people claiming to protest over Nowak’s murder marched to the site of his death. This followed a rally, addressed by the far-right activist Tommy Robinson, outside the city’s main police station.

Musk is based in the US and has not visited the UK since November 2023. A Guardian analysis last month found he posted about race and immigration in the UK twice as often as he did about SpaceX in the run-up to the aerospace company’s initial public offering in June.

Security experts including Fiona Hill, a former adviser to the US and UK governments, have warned that the UK is a soft target for online manipulation by overseas actors because it does not take the idea of civil, or “psychological”, defence seriously.

Dr Julia Ebner, a researcher at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue and the University of Oxford, said flashpoint episodes such as in Southampton and Belfast had become “strategic events” for far-right actors seeking to amplify and exploit them.

“They are using the UK as a negative example, smearing the UK to promote their own narratives of western civilisational decay or social collapse,” Ebner said. “But the other purpose is to influence UK politics, and European politics more widely,” using crisis moments to “promote a strong, strengthened far-right wave across the world”.

Four of the top 12 most-seen tweets came from UK accounts: two were by the leader of the Restore Britain party, Rupert Lowe, whom Musk has endorsed; another was from GB News, while the most popular, with 37.6m views, was written by the “anti-woke” rightwing political commentator Konstantin Kisin.

Other accounts located in the US were anonymous, though familiar. @EndWokeness posted a blurry still image of a black man attacking a white man in Belfast on 8 June, saying the full video was “too graphic” to post. It attracted 16.3m views.

The assault, a stabbing in which the victim, Stephen Ogilvie, lost an eye, prompted three nights of racially motivated rioting targeting non-white people in Belfast. An asylum seeker from Sudan was charged with attempted murder and at least 23 people were arrested.

The @EndWokeness account, which has 3.9m followers, was cited by a parliamentary committee after it amplified a false claim that the 2024 attack in Southport, in which three girls were killed, was carried out by a Muslim man.

The account has been linked by an open source analyst to Jack Posobiec, a rightwing influencer who promoted the Pizzagate conspiracy, a false accusation that leading US Democrats were engaged in satanic child abuse at a child-friendly pizza restaurant in Washington DC.

Another leading poster was the US rightwing influencer Benny Johnson, who accused the New York Times of writing nothing about Nowak and thousands of pieces about the murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis in 2020 – though Nowak was murdered in the UK.

The analysis of the most-viewed accounts did not reveal any posts from Russia or China – both countries that have been behind online disinformation campaigns – though it is possible that posters successfully disguised their locations using virtual private networks (VPNs).

X shows location data for most profiles, inferred by the platform from user IP addresses, though government accounts are excluded. Last November, after the feature was introduced, X’s then head of product, Nikita Bier, said it was more than 99% accurate. When it was launched, it revealed that some pro-Scottish-independence accounts were based in Iran.

But there were signs of inauthenticity in popular posts. Two of the top most-seen tweets came from the US-based C3 (@C_3C_3) account, accusing “legacy media” of not reporting about the Nowak case. Its profile picture is a baby wearing a Make America Great Again cap; the username has changed 14 times previously.

One UK account, which tweeted at least six times about the murder of Nowak, with almost 3,800 combined views, had changed its name more than 400 times. NewsSceneUK – subsequently changed to BritifyFooty – wrote in one tweet about the “huge crowd of patriots outside #Southampton Police Station”.

Accounts posting from overseas that changed their usernames more than 20 times included one in Kenya that wrote after the Belfast stabbing: “When the state fails to protect people, the streets find their own language.” Another, from Europe, described the Nowak case as “a globalized, calculated and malicious evil” affecting “every White person and every White nation”.

Close to a third – about 13,000 – of the Belfast and Southampton tweets, whether from the UK or abroad, were racist or anti-immigrant, according to the Guardian analysis. When analysed separately, a quarter of the posts that were only about Southampton were racist or anti-immigrant, compared with a third of those that were only about Belfast.

One UK-based poster, writing a day after the Belfast stabbing, claimed they hoped the attacker was British-born because “race is the issue, not immigration status”. The post registered 2m views.

Valerie Wirtschafter, an expert on online foreign influence operations from the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank, said she believed violent events such as those in Belfast and Southampton were “a point of exploitation” in which “outside agitators” had an opportunity to make a disproportionate impact.

Their position was helped by X and other social media companies cutting content moderation, she said, but in particular by “algorithms and how they collide with the basic cognitive processes of humans. We are more attracted to things that are shocking.”

articles.title: Tears for Fears star admits he fell in love with another woman before his wife died
articles.excerpt: Matthew Nelson and Gunnar Nelson, the sons of late entertainer Ricky Nelson, have written a memoir, "What Happened to Your Hair?: How We Played Loud... Loved Proud... and Never Backed Down... Together...
articles.body_text:
Matthew Nelson and Gunnar Nelson, the sons of late entertainer Ricky Nelson, have written a memoir, "What Happened to Your Hair?: How We Played Loud... Loved Proud... and Never Backed Down... Together."

Tears for Fears star Roland Orzabal is opening up about the painful final years of his marriage, revealing that he fell in love with another woman before his first wife, Caroline, died after a long battle with an alcohol-related illness.

The "Everybody Wants to Rule the World" singer, who has written a new memoir, "Welcome to Your Life," admitted he reached his breaking point after spending years watching his wife’s condition deteriorate. Orzabal described that while walking away may have seemed cruel, he eventually saw "a clear way forward."

"Why was it important to be so candid? Well, because it’s the truth," the 64-year-old told Fox News Digital. "I didn’t want to write something false. And also, I always felt that somewhere out there is someone who’s going through what you went through."

'YOU'RE SO VAIN' SINGER CARLY SIMON SAYS PARKINSON'S AND CANCER DIAGNOSES KEPT HER FROM PUBLIC EYE

From left: Roland Orzabal and Curt Smith of Tears For Fears circa 1985 in New York City. Tears for Fears are best known for a string of ’80s hits, including "Everybody Wants to Rule the World," "Shout," "Head Over Heels" and "Mad World." (Robin Platzer/IMAGES/Getty Images)

"I’d spent years and years with Caroline in this state," Orzabal reflected. "It wasn’t just a year or six months. And yes, I had enough. I was shown a clear way forward."

In October 2016, Orzabal met writer and photographer Emily Rath while Tears for Fears were in Colorado to perform at Red Rocks. He wrote that his immediate reaction when he noticed her was, "That’s my wife."

"I’ve been around the world many times and had seen and met many attractive women, but I’d never heard those words before," he wrote. "They didn’t make sense, either, because I was already married, and this woman looked nothing like Caroline."

"Welcome to Your Life: Love, Death & Tears For Fears – An Iconic Musician's Journey Through Grief, Addiction, and Recovery" by Roland Orzabal is available now. (Dey Street Books)

Rath was 30 when she met the then-55-year-old Orzabal. "Ouch," he wrote. "If only I was half my age and she was older."

After exchanging numbers, the pair developed what Orzabal initially described as a "friendship between two creatives." Looking back, however, he acknowledged, "The truth is, I was falling in love with Emily before Caroline had died."

By then, Orzabal had spent decades with Caroline, whom he had known since they were teenagers.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Roland Orzabal's first wife Caroline. (Courtesy of Roland Orzabal)

Orzabal was around 14 years old when he first met Caroline Johnston. They married in Bath, England, in 1982, when the singer had just turned 21 and Caroline was 20. They had two sons.

Before Caroline’s physical and mental health deteriorated, the marriage had already endured significant strain. In the book, Orzabal describes a passionate but volatile relationship marked by frequent arguments. As his career took off, he spent long periods away and admits becoming increasingly "selfish," "hedonistic" and absorbed in his rock star persona.

By the mid-1990s, the marriage was in serious trouble. The couple discussed separation and sought marriage counseling. Orzabal says he was determined to keep his family together while acknowledging "the pain that I put Caroline through." Despite the turmoil, they stayed together.

British musician Roland Orzabal of Tears for Fears plays guitar during a performance at the Aragon Ballroom in Chicago on June 23, 1985. (Paul Natkin/Getty Images)

Things changed in the late 2000s, when the couple settled into what Orzabal describes as a predictable, day-to-day life where heavy nightly drinking became routine. Around 2011, friends began noticing a change in Caroline’s behavior.

"It was a slow process," Orzabal recalled to Fox News Digital. "She would say it’s menopause. 'It’s the menopause. I’m not eating because of the menopause. I’m weird because of the menopause. I’m depressed because of the menopause.' And she was always very emphatic, hard to argue with."

Roland Orzabal formed Tears for Fears with Curt Smith in 1981. (Courtesy of Roland Orzabal)

"I went along with this for many, many years until it was obvious that menopause was over, but the symptoms continued and got worse," he said. "It got worse and worse. We went to see several doctors, and they all said, 'It’s alcohol.' But even then I was in denial because I was a wine drinker. I thought, 'It isn’t doing me any harm, so why is it doing harm to her?'"

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Roland Orzabal married his first wife, Caroline Johnston, in 1982. The wedding took place around the same time his band Tears for Fears released their debut single "Mad World." (Pam Springsteen)

"To be honest with you, it wasn’t until the autopsy that I realized the truth," Orzabal admitted. "Terrible."

According to Orzabal, Caroline eventually struggled to eat solid food even as she continued drinking. She spent increasing amounts of time on the sofa, became anxious, stopped regularly cooking for their sons and alienated friends. Orzabal writes that her condition escalated to "seizures and hospitalizations," "bizarre ideation" and loss of normal bodily control. He described watching helplessly as she "slowly melted away."

According to the book, Roland Orzabal wrote, "Please Be Happy" about Caroline’s depression and deteriorating condition. (Pam Springsteen)

Orzabal writes that Caroline’s drinking became increasingly secretive, and he later discovered that she had been hiding bottles of vodka. He recalled seeing her jaundiced with "deathly red marks" on her face.

Roland Orzabal of Tears for Fears performs at Koninklijk Circus in Brussels, Belgium, on April 21, 1985. (Gie Knaeps/Getty Images)

"How much of a carer are you? Is that your natural bent?" Orzabal told Fox News Digital. "I would say with me, it probably wasn’t, but I did it anyway. And I think what it did was it would make me very angry inside, which wasn’t good. I had people talk to me about just leaving, which I would never have done. But I think in hindsight, it’s stupid to say now, but maybe I should have done something about it earlier or left. Sounds harsh."

Roland Orzabal and Curt Smith of Tears for Fears arrive at the German Radio Award 2022 ceremony in Hamburg, Germany, on Sept. 8, 2022. (dpa/picture alliance via Getty Images)

"I think the problem was that, one minute, she’d be fine," said Orzabal. "We would have a decent conversation. And then the next minute. She was doolally — not making sense, demented."

Orzabal wrote that as his feelings for Rath developed, he found himself confronting a choice about his future.

Roland Orzabal and his first wife, Caroline Johnston, had two children together: sons Pascal and Raoul. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)

"I was at a crossroads, a tipping point, if you like," wrote Orzabal. "A tipping point that would redefine my life. With all the things that were going on with Caroline, with all the visits to psychiatrists, to neurologists, to hepatologists, I was falling in love with a young, healthy woman who I believed loved me too and was the opposite of what I had left at home.

Tears for Fears at the Shepherd’s Bush Empire 2022. (Emily Rath Orzabal)

"... I had a talk with myself, out loud, pacing the room like some crazy man. I knew what was going to happen to Caroline: She would once again be committed and the whole process, the whole nightmare, would start again. And where would it end? I could choose the scenario, the illness, the misery and the frustration, or I could choose an alternative and leave her madness behind. ... I could choose life, or I could choose death. God strike me down, cancel me, whatever, but I chose life."

Orzabal told Fox News Digital that imagining a life beyond his wife’s illness left him with an agonizing sense of guilt.

Singer Roland Orzabal of Tears for Fears performs onstage during The Darker Waves Festival in Huntington Beach, California, on Nov. 18, 2023. (Scott Dudelson/WireImage)

"If you choose life at this moment, you were cruel," he said. "But I think it was the final straw because Caroline had already spent three months in a psych ward. I’d been there virtually every day going to visit her. And then, all of a sudden, that night I saw an alternative life for myself, which is hard to do — hard to take. But I did."

In 2017, Orzabal’s first wife of 35 years died. She was 54.

"I felt belief and disbelief," he said. "I couldn’t take it in because you have to go into action. I had to speak to my sons, my family. You’re clearing up the mess that death leaves."

WATCH: NELSON TWINS REFLECT ON FAMILY LEGACY AND THE TRUE COST OF FAME

In 2019, Orzabal said he entered InnerBalance, a rehabilitation center in Colorado, for treatment of his Ambien addiction. He said he began to forgive himself there.

"There’s this madness that comes with grief," he explained. "There’s the negotiation. 'What if I did this?' 'What if I did that?' And then, what happens when you no longer have that person to negotiate with? You no longer have that person to get angry. That’s all gone, and you are only left with the feeling."

Roland Orzabal's first wife, Caroline, died in July 2017 at the age of 54. According to multiple reports, she developed alcohol-related dementia. (Courtesy of Roland Orzabal.)

"I left out a lot of details, especially when it came to Caroline," he continued. "It was a lot worse, but I wanted to be respectful of those who’ve passed on. I wanted to respect her name. She’s my sons’ mother. So no, I couldn’t put the gruesome details at all. Even though it sounds bad, it’s much worse."

Roland Orzabal and Emily Rath on their wedding day. (Tara Marolda)

Orzabal and Rath married in 2020. They had a daughter, Eula, in 2025.

"Emily has been an amazing support system for me," said Orzabal. "It depends on your belief system - I think that if you believe in the soul, then [Caroline] would completely understand. When I think about the person she was ... she would understand."

Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Trump appoints staff secretary Will Scharf as new White House counsel
articles.excerpt:
Scharf, who helped president win approval for $400m ballroom, to replace David Warrington on 1 September

Donald Trump announced on Sunday that ⁠Will ​Scharf, the staff secretary who helped secure app...
articles.body_text:
Scharf, who helped president win approval for $400m ballroom, to replace David Warrington on 1 September

Donald Trump announced on Sunday that ⁠Will ​Scharf, the staff secretary who helped secure approval for the $400m White House ballroom project, will become ⁠White House counsel and assistant to the president.

Effective 1 September, Scharf will replace David Warrington, who will be leaving the administration to join the private sector. Warrington ​formerly served ​as a ​personal counsel and a ​lawyer ‌for Trump’s ​2024 campaign.

Trump noted that Scharf previously served as a federal prosecutor and represented him in a number of cases, including at the supreme court. Scharf also led the National ‌Capital Planning Commission, which approved the president’s construction ​of the White House ballroom.

“Will is Tough, Strong, and Smart! He also loves our Country, and respects the Law,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Will Scharf will do a great job as White House Counsel!”

The shakeup in the White House counsel’s office comes at a critical juncture – just months ahead of the midterm elections, where Trump’s Republican party will be fighting to hold on to control of Congress.

Democrats have vowed to pursue investigations into Trump and his administration if they are successful in November.

The White House counsel’s job is to advise on legal and policy questions related to the presidency. The office is the primary White House contact for the justice department, and it handles presidential pardons, works on judicial appointments and reviews legislation. The office also helps investigate and manage congressional investigations into the administration and lawsuits against the president when he is sued in his official capacity.

Trump in July 2025 had named Scharf as chair of the National Capital Planning Commission, the executive branch agency with jurisdiction over construction and major renovations to government buildings in the region.

Trump’s ballroom won final approval from the NCPC in April, though a divided federal appeals court ruled Friday that construction on the project must stop because Congress had not approved it. Trump has vowed to appeal to the supreme court.

The project is already well on its way and has begun to rise above ground on the east side of the White House.

The Associated Press and Reuters contributed reporting

articles.title: WWE's Chelsea Green dealt more bad luck, reveals broken orbital bone less than week after winning title

WWE star Matt Cardona names a few people who pro wrestling fans should look out for on the indies in an interview with Fox News Digital.

Chelsea Green has overcome serious obstacles to get to the top...
articles.body_text:
WWE star Matt Cardona names a few people who pro wrestling fans should look out for on the indies in an interview with Fox News Digital.

Chelsea Green has overcome serious obstacles to get to the top of the WWE women’s division.

She’s suffered numerous injuries over the last 12 months or so, including a heart issue that landed her in the hospital and in need of a procedure. Still, she managed to put those problems in the rearview to become the interim WWE women’s champion last weekend at SummerSlam.

COMPLETE PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE ON FOX NEWS DIGITAL

Interim WWE Women's Championship Chelsea Green makes her entrance during SmackDown at Xfinity Mobile Arena in Philadelphia, Pa., on Aug. 7, 2026. (WWE via Getty Images)

On Friday, Green was in a tag team match with Tiffany Stratton as they went up against Fallon Henley and Lainey Reid. Green told her followers that she suffered a broken orbital bone during the match as her string of bad luck continues.

"I did get injured last night. Stuff happens. It’s live television. It’s wrestling. It’s an occupational hazard," Green said in a video posted to her Instagram. "I ended up in the emergency room and I have a broken orbital bone. It looks amazing all things considered. It feels awful but looks pretty amazing."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Chelsea Green makes her way to the ring during SmackDown at Oakland Arena in Oakland, Calif., on July 24, 2026. (WWE via Getty Images)

"I have no idea what that means for me. Usually, you guys have seen me play into every single injury but this feels different, obviously. This feels very different. It feels frustrating. I’m upset. I feel like if I didn’t have bad luck, I’d have no luck at all. So, I just need to take a bit more time to process and to heal from, obviously, the head trauma that is going on right now and then we’ll see what happens. We’re just gonna take it day by day. So, world domination continues. We’ve just had a minor blip."

It’s unclear whether Green will be forced to relinquish the interim championship already. She outlasted four other women in a ladder match at SummerSlam to win the title.

Chelsea Green celebrates after winning the Interim WWE Women's Championship during SummerSlam at U.S. Bank Stadium on Aug. 2, 2026, in Minneapolis, Minn. (WWE via Getty Images)

Meanwhile, Rhea Ripley also revealed last week that she underwent knee surgery and could be out for a few more months. Ripley is the WWE women’s champion, which was why the interim belt was introduced going into SummerSlam.

Ryan Gaydos is a senior editor for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez announces decision to freeze her eggs
articles.excerpt:
US congresswoman to share journey online as she criticizes Trump administration’s attacks on reproductive care

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has announced she is going to freeze her eggs and will be shari...
articles.body_text:
US congresswoman to share journey online as she criticizes Trump administration’s attacks on reproductive care

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has announced she is going to freeze her eggs and will be sharing the process online.

The progressive New York congresswoman, 36, revealed her decision to undergo fertility treatment in a series of Instagram stories this weekend. “This is a choice that I am making to feel more in control of my life,” Ocasio-Cortez said.

Ocasio-Cortez said she had been saving for the procedure for a very long time, and said there was not a lot of information for women interested in doing so.

“As women in general, we are not taught about our bodies, we are not prepared for our own lives, whether that is in puberty, whether that is in pregnancy, whether that is in perimenopause, menopause, whether that is in so many different aspects of our lives,” she said in one of the stories.

Ocasio-Cortez recognized the balancing act that comes with undergoing fertility treatment with her work as a congresswoman. Ocasio-Cortez told viewers that she would be taking her shots in the dressing room before a scheduled ABC interview on Sunday.

“I want you all to see that,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “Because women can do anything. And I think it’s badass that I’m gonna be giving myself shots in the green room, get my glam on, roll out, talk international events, domestic policy, elections, pop out, live my life, do my thing.”

Ocasio-Cortez also showed the medicines and tools, such as syringes and alcohol wipes, used in the process, which involves injecting multiple forms of medication over a period of time that typically lasts around 10 days or more. She joked she would not be injecting herself on a live feed, quipping: “Maybe I should start an ASMR egg-freezing channel.”

“Don’t be weird about this, even I know though all of you will be,” she said with a slight smile moments before finding an injection site on her abdomen.

She exhaled, injected the medication, and then remarked: “That wasn’t so bad!”

During her Sunday interview on ABC, Ocasio-Cortez discussed her decision further.

“In this political environment where this administration is denying reproductive care to women across the country, from abortion rights to the ability to carry out a healthy pregnancy, I think it’s important for us as leaders to have these conversations and share these processes, especially for working women across the country and normalize them,” she said.

Ocasio-Cortez’s announcement drew praise.

Amanda Litman, co-founder and president of Run for Something, a political action committee that supports young progressive candidates, said on X: “I’m just so grateful for her honesty & vulnerability.”

Xochitl Hinojosa, a Democratic strategist, responded to Litman’s post by saying: “THIS. We don’t talk about women freezing their eggs or what women have to go through to start a family. Thank you @AOC for your bravery.”

articles.title: Lions announce Teddy Bridgewater has retired again, leaving team in middle of training camp
articles.excerpt:
Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins and star defender Maxx Crosby got into a heated exchange during practice on Friday. (This video contains AI-assisted content)

NFL veteran quarterback Teddy ...
articles.body_text:
Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins and star defender Maxx Crosby got into a heated exchange during practice on Friday. (This video contains AI-assisted content)

NFL veteran quarterback Teddy Bridgewater has once again retired from the game.

Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell told reporters on Sunday that Bridgewater, who was competing for the backup role to Jared Goff in the quarterbacks room, has decided to step away from the team in the middle of training camp.

The Lions officially placed Bridgewater on the reserve/retired list ahead of their Sunday practice.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

FILE - Detroit Lions quarterback Teddy Bridgewater (10) is seen on the sideline during the second half of an NFL football game against the Minnesota Vikings, Dec. 24, 2023 in Minneapolis. (AP Photo/Stacy Bengs, File)

Campbell added that he believes retirement could stick this time for Bridgewater, who had previously retired following the 2023 season. But he quickly rejoined the Lions for the 2024 season.

"I think he can only truly answer that, but I feel like this is where it’s at for sure right now," Campbell said, via ESPN. "This is where it needs to be and where he felt. And his biggest worry was letting us down. That’s the type of guys he is, and he’s not.

RUSSELL WILSON ANNOUNCES RETIREMENT FROM NFL AFTER 14 SEASONS

"That’s as far as it can get. He meant a lot."

As a result, the Lions were reportedly quick to sign another journeyman, Josh Dobbs, to a $1.425 million contract with $475,000 fully guaranteed, per NFL Network. Dobbs is familiar with Detroit, having been on the team’s practice squad during the 2022 campaign.

Dobbs has also recently backed up Drake Maye with the AFC-winning New England Patriots a season ago. He is a dual-threat quarterback, having the ability to use his legs to pick up crucial yardage, which is the opposite of Goff’s game as a true pocket-passer.

As for Bridgewater, he joined the Lions again as an unrestricted free agent in March after backing up Baker Mayfield with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in 2025. Bridgewater was expected to back up Goff this year, but the Lions have to pivot now.

One of the many reasons Bridgewater remains someone NFL teams want in their locker room is due to his mentorship abilities, understanding his role as a backup and helping the starter on a weekly basis before, during, and after the season. That includes working with Goff in 2023 and 2024, as he developed into one of the best pure passers in the league in an explosive Lions offensive scheme.

Teddy Bridgewater of the Detroit Lions looks to throw the ball against the Jacksonville Jaguars during a preseason game at Ford Field in Detroit, Mich., on Aug. 19, 2023. (Getty Images)

Bridgewater, who was a first-round pick to the Minnesota Vikings in 2014 out of Louisville, was a Pro Bowler early in his career. In just his second season, he got the nod after going 11-5 with 3,231 passing yards, 14 passing touchdowns, while rushing for 192 yards with three scores.

But Bridgewater’s career was derailed, as a starter at least, when a horrific knee injury led to a left knee dislocation and a torn ACL during a practice just before the start of the 2016 season.

FERNANDO MENDOZA REVEALS TOM BRADY'S NO-NONSENSE MENTORSHIP PLEDGE AHEAD OF NFL DRAFT

Bridgewater would move on to the New Orleans Saints in 2018, getting six starts across two seasons before getting a heavier workload with the Carolina Panthers in 2020. He went 4-11 in Carolina before going 7-7 with the Denver Broncos the following year.

Bridgewater also played a season with the Miami Dolphins in 2022, going 0-2 in his only two starts with the franchise.

If this is officially Bridgewater’s last time on an NFL football field as a quarterback, he threw for 15,182 yards with 75 passing touchdowns over 83 games. He owned a 33-32 record as a starter across 11 seasons.

Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Teddy Bridgewater (10) during an NFL game against the Carolina Panthers on Dec. 21, 2025, at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, N.C. (Icon Sportswire)

"I've known Teddy a long time and the human being is unbelievable," Campbell said. "Certainly, the player, everything that he's about. The type of teammate he is, the way he prepares ... always played the game up here and had a huge heart.

Scott Thompson is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Hasan Piker stands by 'intentionally provocative' claims that Hamas is 'a thousand times better' than Israel
articles.excerpt:
The ‘Fox News Sunday’ panel discusses progressive streamer Hasan Piker’s growing influence within the Democratic Party as midterm elections loom.

Far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker defended his rhe...
articles.body_text:
The ‘Fox News Sunday’ panel discusses progressive streamer Hasan Piker’s growing influence within the Democratic Party as midterm elections loom.

Far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker defended his rhetoric calling Hamas "a thousand times better than the fascist settler colonial apartheid state" of Israel on Sunday despite acknowledging it was "intentionally provocative."

"I say that on purpose," Piker told Rolling Stone Magazine. "I want to force people to really think about what I’m saying. I want to challenge them to think about it a little bit."

Piker made the comment in an X post from January and has since doubled and tripled down on the claim while facing backlash. Though he conceded that he would likely alienate fewer people by simply saying Israel was "worse" than Hamas, Piker told the magazine that it wasn't his style.

MARK HALPERIN CALLS HASAN PIKER A 'HORRIBLE PERSON' AS DEMOCRATS FACE PRESSURE TO DISTANCE FROM STREAMER

Hasan Piker, a streamer and creator, previously claimed that Hamas was "a thousand times better than the fascist settler colonial apartheid state" of Israel.  (Sportsfile via Getty Images)

"First of all, everyone says that," Piker said. "I’m not interested in the many bad things Hamas has done. I’m trying to get people to understand why someone becomes Hamas. Do I agree with everything they do? Of course not. I’ve called out their war crimes myself. But the point is to make people identify from their perspective. Palestinians have lived under this brutal occupation for 75 years. Put yourself in their shoes."

In the same article, Rolling Stone Magazine reported that the Democratic Party had a more favorable opinion of Palestinian people than the Israelis with the Israeli government ranking only three points higher than Hamas, suggesting Piker's opinions were more mainstream than they appeared. Piker joked that the backlash he faced for his comments were a result of "having the correct position too early."

CONTROVERSIAL STREAMER HASAN PIKER'S LECTURE AXED BY UNIVERSITY OF WASHINGTON AMID FREE SPEECH QUESTIONS

Still, he didn't regret his hyperbolic comments made on his livestreams or elsewhere.

"In some ways it is a performance. But existence is a performance," Piker said. "I could speak in sanitized, academic language all day — but that wouldn’t be as entertaining or reach as many people. So, I speak in a way that people understand. And sometimes I push buttons."

Hasan Piker has repeatedly defended his comments despite facing backlash. (Sam Barnes/Web Summit via Sportsfile via Getty Images)

Fox News Digital reached out to Piker for comment.

During an April appearance on "Pod Save America," Piker doubled down on his Hamas comparison despite pushback from co-host Jon Favreau.

"I've also said I'm a harm-reduction voter," Piker said. "I'm a lesser-evil voter and, therefore, I would vote for Hamas over Israel every single time because I'm looking at the situation as a paramilitary organization that has a political party as well, a political bureau as well that is entirely comprised not as an alien force but of orphaned children that have, you know, had their parents killed by an apartheid state that has been dominating the lives of Palestinians for 80 years at this point and have done a genocide at this point as well."

DAVID MARCUS: DON'T BLAME CONSERVATIVES. IT WAS THE LEFT THAT CANCELED HASAN PIKER

During an interview with CNN last week, Piker denied that he supported all of Hamas' actions but insisted that Palestinians "have a right to resist militarily."

"Well, I wouldn't say I express support for all of Hamas's actions or anything," Piker said. "I do say that the Palestinian resistance largely does have an internationally recognized right to resist. Do they violate that sometimes with war crimes? Absolutely. And Hamas certainly has as well. But at the end of the day, Palestinians do have a right to resist militarily."

The Anti-Defamation League (ADL) has previously denounced Hasan Piker's comments. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo)

In a previous comment to Fox News Digital, the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) condemned Piker's comments along with Democratic officials who continue to ignore them.

"Hasan Piker repeated multiple times that ‘Hamas is a thousand times better than Israel,’ while also shrugging off ‘war crimes.’ That is a person with more than 11 million followers sincerely expressing support for a designated terrorist organization, on a mainstream platform, to thunderous silence from the Democratic officials who continue to campaign and appear alongside him," an ADL spokesperson said.

Lindsay Kornick is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to lindsay.kornick@fox.com and on Twitter: @lmkornick.

articles.title: Credit to the QVC host who went viral for a live NSFW slip-up for handling it like a pro 'the show must go on'
articles.excerpt:
Steve Smith Sr can't come to grips with what Brandon Aiyuk has been doing this offseason.

Saying the show must go on when you make a mistake live and actually doing it are two different things. Credi...
articles.body_text:
Steve Smith Sr can't come to grips with what Brandon Aiyuk has been doing this offseason.

Saying the show must go on when you make a mistake live and actually doing it are two different things. Credit to QVC's Toni Brattin for pulling it off like a true professional. As a result, she gave the internet a gift.

The host was taking the QVC audience through a live demonstration of her "Salon Select" wig when she accidentally let "blow job" fly out of her mouth instead of "blowout" while describing the look the product provides.

Denis Simioni, founder and president of Estee Lauder Cos.' Ojon unit, left, and Shawn Killinger, a QVC program host, pitch Ojon products during a QVC show filmed in West Chester, Pa., on Friday, Feb. 18, 2011. Estee Lauder Cos. and Simioni are launching a marketing campaign touting the scientific properties of the brand as the New York-based cosmetics company steps up its expansion into hair care. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Almost 30 years under your belt can't fully prepare you for everything. But she did a decent job of keeping it together. She was talking texture and wave pattern when she let slip, "It looks like you went and got a blow job... a blowout at your salon."

VALERIE BERTINELLI APOLOGIZES AFTER DROPPING F-BOMB ON LIVE TV

She caught the mistake immediately, whispered "Oh my God," and managed to collect herself enough so that she could finish her thought and hand it off to her co-host.

After handing it off, Brattin couldn’t help but shake her head and kneel down behind the display table. It's one of those moments that brings everyone together and a relatable moment that the internet can't help but run with.

Brattin told TMZ of her viral blooper that she was hoping the producers were going to switch to another camera. That would have been helpful, but when it didn't happen, she powered through.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON’T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

QVC was very understanding of the mistake. They were able to laugh about it and knew that she wasn’t dropping words like "blow job" on their customers on purpose with any sort of malicious intent.

General view of the atmosphere at the Project Runway All Stars Season 3 premiere party presented by The Weinstein Company and Lifetime in partnership with Marie Claire, QVC, Mary Kay and Alterna Haircare at Hudson Common at the Hudson Hotel in New York City on Oct. 22, 2013. (Getty Images for The Weinstein Company)

OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

The company even showed up in the comments of the viral clip. They wrote on Instagram, "Kuddos to @terriconnqvc for handling this like a pro. Is there an award for Best Live Blooper Recovery??"

I agree. Credit to Toni Brattin for handling her "blow job" slip-up like a pro. It's a funny moment and there's no need to overreact.

articles.title: CNN stands by Iran war reporting after retired general challenges ‘unnamed sources’ on air
articles.excerpt:
Retired Brig. Gen. Mark Kimmitt criticized CNN’s use of unnamed sources in its Iran war coverage, while the network told Fox News Digital that it stands by its reporting.

CNN stood by its reporting i...
articles.body_text:
Retired Brig. Gen. Mark Kimmitt criticized CNN’s use of unnamed sources in its Iran war coverage, while the network told Fox News Digital that it stands by its reporting.

CNN stood by its reporting in a statement to Fox News Digital on Sunday after retired Brig. Gen. Mark Kimmitt challenged the network during a Saturday interview over its anonymous sourcing on the Iran war, including claims involving negotiations and Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine.

"We stand by our reporting," a CNN spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

Joseph Holstead, public affairs adviser to the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, declined to comment on CNN’s report or Kimmitt’s assessment but agreed with Fox News Digital’s characterization that CNN’s sources lacked firsthand knowledge of the conversations described in the report.

"We are not going to comment on it nor the opinion of a commentator," Holstead said to Fox News Digital in a statement.

Retired Brig. Gen. Mark Kimmitt criticized CNN’s reliance on unnamed sources in its reporting on the Iran war. (Getty Images)

US OFFICIAL SAYS JD VANCE MADE 'GREAT PROGRESS' IN IRAN TALKS, CALLS SNUB REPORTS 'FOREIGN PROPAGANDA'

CNN did not respond to Fox News Digital's questions about how it vetted the anonymous sources or Kimmitt’s claim that earlier anonymously sourced information about the negotiations was inaccurate.

Kimmitt raised the accuracy concern after CNN anchor Omar Jimenez asked about the network’s report that Caine was privately seeking an "off-ramp" because further military escalation could backfire.

"I read the CNN article and I saw quotes from unnamed sources that last week were saying there were no negotiations going on, and that proved not to be true," Kimmitt said.

By the time Kimmitt appeared on the network, President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance had publicly confirmed that negotiations were underway.

Trump said Thursday that he was personally involved in the discussions, while Vance told Fox News Digital on Saturday that American officials were speaking with Iran about restoring oil and gas traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

RNC national spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre defended Trump’s approach in a statement to Fox News Digital, portraying his Iran policy as effective and politically popular.

"President Trump’s ‘Peace through Strength’ foreign policy has been effective in preventing Iran from developing a nuclear weapon – something voters overwhelmingly support," she said. "The American people trust President Trump and voters will continue to gravitate toward our candidates who are in line with his efforts to strengthen our national security and keep American communities safe."

CNN told Fox News Digital that it stood by its reporting after Kimmitt challenged the network’s sourcing on air. (Getty Images)

TRUMP SAYS IRAN'S MISSILES 'AREN'T THE PROBLEM' AFTER WHITE HOUSE MADE THEM CENTRAL TO WAR RATIONALE

CNN’s Friday article did not report that negotiations were nonexistent. Citing three sources familiar with the matter, it reported that Caine had privately told senior Trump administration officials that airpower alone was unlikely to accomplish Trump’s objectives and that some options for escalating the conflict carried substantial risks.

One of the unnamed sources summarized Caine's position in the CNN report.

"Caine is looking for an off-ramp," the source said.

CNN reported that Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine privately sought an "off-ramp" from the conflict with Iran. (Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images)

TRADE VESSEL STRUCK BY PROJECTILE IN STRAIT OF HORMUZ AMID US-IRAN TALKS

The article also included an on-the-record response from Caine spokesman Joseph Holstead, who rejected anonymous descriptions of the chairman’s private discussions while declining to disclose what Caine had told Trump and other senior officials.

"We do not discuss the Chairman’s confidential conversations with the President, the Secretary, or other senior leaders, nor do we comment on anonymous, agenda-driven characterizations of those conversations by sources who were not privy to them," Holstead said.

Kimmitt's criticism extended beyond CNN's sourcing. The former general said the United States had not yet accomplished its central objectives involving Iran's nuclear program, missile capabilities and support for regional proxies.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"Look, I think it’s fair to say that we are not close to achieving our strategic objectives of ending the nuclear program, ending the missile program, and cutting off support for the proxies," Kimmitt said. "We do have the situation with the Strait of Hormuz. Those issues are undeniable."

Kimmitt also said Caine had to consider the threat from China, continued support for Ukraine and the military resources available to other combatant commanders while advising the president about Iran.

Jimenez responded that CNN reporters also preferred officials to attach their names to information.

"Hey, General, you said something that we preach all the time. I sure wish more folks would go on the record, too. But that’s me as a reporter," Jimenez said.

The sourcing dispute unfolded as the Trump administration continued negotiations intended to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Fox News Digital reported Friday that U.S. Central Command had halted attacks after 13 consecutive days of strikes against Iranian military targets while Washington and Tehran pursued an agreement.

Fox News Digital reached out to Kimmitt for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

CJ Womack is an associate editor at Fox News.

CJ joined Fox News Digital's team in 2026, which highlights the vital role journalism plays in shaping politics and culture. He has years of experience analyzing and reporting on the news media.

CJ graduated from Long Beach State University in 2025 with a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science and a minor in Journalism.
