A ‘Fox News @ Night’ panel discusses Democratic politicians campaigning alongside streamer Hasan Piker.

Hasan Piker, a close ally of Abdul El-Sayed, is calling for "Marxist-Leninist" punishment for those who criticize Michigan’s Democratic Senatorial candidate. As radicals and anti-Semites like Piker flood the Democratic Party, establishment figures are struggling to justify their alliance with extremist candidates.

Ironically, Democrats are now fulfilling the false narrative that they used against President Donald Trump after the Charlottesville protests. They are maintaining that there are "many fine people" in the Democratic Socialists of America party, despite its leaders seeking to destroy our constitutional system, open our borders, defund the police and embrace virtual anarchy. Now, some of these fine people are calling for moderates to be purged as radicals take over the Democratic Party.

Hasan Piker, a streamer and creator, appears during day two of Web Summit Vancouver 2026 at the Vancouver Convention Centre in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada, on May 13, 2026. (Sportsfile via Getty Images)

In 2017, the media manufactured a controversy by suggesting that Trump had praised neo-Nazis and Klansmen in 2017 as "fine people" in Charlottesville, Va. It was demonstrably false, but became the accepted truth in the media. In reality, Trump condemned the neo-Nazis, and the statement about "fine people on both sides" was in reference to the people on both sides of the debate over the removal of historic statues.

MARK HALPERIN CALLS HASAN PIKER A 'HORRIBLE PERSON' AS DEMOCRATS FACE PRESSURE TO DISTANCE FROM STREAMER

That narrative took on an added hypocrisy when some of the loudest voices later endorsed a candidate with an actual Nazi tattoo who allegedly assaulted women, mocked wounded veterans, and praised terrorists. However, he promised to deliver Maine and bring figures like Chuck Schumer and Elizabeth Warren back to power.

Democratic Party leadewrs like Kamala Harris and Pete Buttigieg brush off El-Sayed’s allies, including Mohammad Baqer Qazwini, a prominent Muslim cleric who gave a sermon that called for followers to vote for El-Sayed while also calling upon them to pray for the death of President Donald Trump and to celebrate the death of Sen. Lindsey Graham.

Darializa Avila Chevalier defeated longtime Rep. Adriano Espaillat in New York’s 13th Congressional District Democratic primary. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images; Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Then there is the Democratic House candidate in New York, Darializa Avila Chevalier, a prison abolitionist who boasted about how she wiped her hands on the American flag in lieu of a napkin.

MEET THE FAR-LEFT INSURGENTS WAGING WAR ON THE DEMOCRATIC ESTABLISHMENT IN 2026 MIDTERMS

Chevalier and other DSA candidates are being welcomed in the Democratic Party despite anti-American views and a DSA platform calling for the destruction of our constitutional system, including scrapping the Supreme Court, the presidency and the Senate. Many are also overwhelmingly anti-Israel, with many, like Piker, displaying virulent anti-Semitism.

When asked about the extreme agenda of these candidates, Schumer and others repeat the mantra that they need to win in the upcoming elections. In other words, the DSA is opposed to the core institutions and values of this country, but it could be useful in returning them to power.

What is interesting is that the establishment does not appear to care what these radicals represent for their party, but the radicals care deeply about what the establishment represents. This week, former DNC Vice-chair David Hogg told establishment figures that the "big tent" of his party is not big enough for them. When asked about Democratic moderates, Hogg replied, "They don’t have the right values."

Piker has even grander plans for our post-constitutional republic, calling for mass arrests, demanding pledges from establishment figures to "arrest and prosecute every prominent member of the Trump administration" who engaged in what he views as corruption as well as "every ICE agent who committed crimes on the job."

FORMER DNC VICE CHAIR DAVID HOGG CLAIMS DEMOCRATIC MODERATES 'DON'T HAVE THE RIGHT VALUES'

Piker also wants to purge any Democrats who do not support El-Sayed, calling them "haters" who deserve to be punished:

"There are haters in our ranks. Notice how whenever someone comes out and says, ‘Yeah, that’s actually a bad association,’ immediately it’s weaponized by the Republicans. You can’t be out here saying like, ‘Oh, I’m a centrist Democrat. And I think Abdul is a bridge too far.’ That must be punished."

Piker, who likes to parade around in a Mao jacket, seems to be longing for the good old days of party purges under Stalin and his contemporaries in the Comintern.

A memo from a major liberal grassroots group called out Democratic lawmakers like Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for their passive approach to resisting President Trump. (Kayla Bartkowski/Getty Images)

He notably accused critics of the sin of "factionalism." Since the Jacobins of the French Revolution, factionalism has been the scourge of revolutionaries. In my book, Rage and the Republic, I discuss the difference between the American and French Revolutions. Where James Madison saw factions as a natural part of a democratic system, the Jacobins sought them as a traitorous and reactionary element. Madison saw compromise as the best solution to factions, while the Jacobins saw the guillotine as the final solution.

BERNIE SANDERS, DSA REVEAL DEMANDS FOR DEM PARTY AFTER SOCIALISTS SWEEP NEW YORK ELECTIONS

Piker is right out of that Jacobin tradition, calling moderate Democrats "Koch payroll liberals" and "irredeemable." (Notably, the Jacobins also pushed for some of the same DSA demands such as a unicameral legislature).

Of course, conservatives can show the same intolerance for RINOs (Republicans in Name Only), but there is an added menacing element to communists calling for mass expulsion or punishment of moderates from their party. It is chillingly familiar.

Mao regularly purged the Communist Party of those not following the party lines, declaring, "Serious offenders should be punished by law, and when they are Party members they should also be dealt with according to Party discipline."

Establishment figures continue to use the "big tent" narratives to brush off questions about the radical agenda and associations of these candidates. The only thing that they have in common is the desire for power. Once these candidates win, figures like Schumer will discover that this tent is not nearly as big as they think.

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM JONATHAN TURLEY

Jonathan Turley is a Fox News Media contributor and the Shapiro Professor of Public Interest Law at George Washington University.

He is the author of the new book "Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution" (Simon & Schuster, Feb 3, 2026), on the 250th anniversary of the American Revolution.on the 250th anniversary of the American Revolution.

He is a nationally recognized legal scholar who has written extensively in areas ranging from constitutional law to legal history to the Supreme Court. He has written over three dozen academic articles that have appeared in a variety of leading law journals.

Professor Turley also served as counsel in some of the most notable cases in the last two decades including the representation of whistleblowers, military personnel, former cabinet members, judges, members of Congress, and a wide range of other clients.

Professor Turley testified more than 50 times before the House and Senate on constitutional and statutory issues, including the Senate confirmation hearings of cabinet members and jurists such as Justice Neil Gorsuch. He also appeared as an expert witness in both the impeachment hearings of President Bill Clinton and Donald Trump.

Professor Turley received his B.A. at the University of Chicago and his J.D. at Northwestern. In 2008, he was given an honorary Doctorate of Law from John Marshall Law School for his contributions to civil liberties and the public interest.

articles.title: Iran-aligned Houthis claim they attacked oil refinery in Saudi Arabia
articles.excerpt:
Drone strike comes after Riyadh signs defence pact and Tehran issues tough demands to reopen strait of Hormuz

Yemen’s Tehran-aligned Houthis have claimed responsibility for an attack on a refinery in...
articles.body_text:
Drone strike comes after Riyadh signs defence pact and Tehran issues tough demands to reopen strait of Hormuz

Yemen’s Tehran-aligned Houthis have claimed responsibility for an attack on a refinery in Saudi Arabia, two days after the kingdom signed ⁠a defence pact with Turkey ⁠and Pakistan in response to ​growing regional instability caused by the US-Israel war on Iran.

The attack early on Sunday came after Iran issued tough new demands to reopen the strait of Hormuz, and the United Arab Emirates said one of its ships had been targeted by an Iranian missile, as a deal to open the strategic waterway remained out of reach.

Iran’s supreme national security council said the strait would not open until the US corrected its “behaviour”. The US must never threaten Iran again and permanently end the war with Tehran and its armed allies in the region, said the statement from the council’s secretary, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, a former commander in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

He added that the US must also end the naval blockade of Iranian ports and withdraw its military from the area, “completely compensate” Iran for war damage, lift sanctions and “unconditionally” release frozen assets.

There was no immediate comment from the US. According to the memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed by the US and Iran in June, a timetable to end sanctions and a plan for compensation would be part of a final peace deal, and negotiations would address frozen assets.

The Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said on Saturday that Iran and Oman were close to reaching an agreement on navigation through the strait of Hormuz, “specifically the determination of a transit route”. But the waterway’s reopening was contingent on other conditions, Araghchi said, in remarks shared on social media. He blamed the situation on what he called the US violation of the June MoU.

Oman, which is mediating and has made relatively few comments on the Hormuz talks, said on Saturday that the discussions were continuing “in a positive and constructive atmosphere”. It condemned attacks on ships in the strait.

When it comes to decision making in Tehran, the final say rests with the supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not been seen in public since an airstrike killed his father and predecessor on the first day of US-Israel war on Iran.

State media said on Sunday that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, met Khamenei in late July. Pezeshkian has given differing accounts in recent ⁠weeks about his access to the supreme leader, saying in July that interactions with ​the Khamenei were “increasing day by ‌day”, only to note weeks later that communicating with him was “very difficult”.

With Iran and the US still arguing over the parameters for peace, the Houthis last month declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea, citing what they said was a Saudi siege on them, an allegation Riyadh denies.

The Saudi energy ministry said a fire had broken out at Aramco’s Jazan refinery early on Sunday but was later extinguished with no injuries and authorities were dealing with the ⁠incident, without giving a cause.

The Houthis used a drone to target the refinery in south-west Saudi Arabia, Yahya Saree, a military spokesperson for the rebel group, said in a post on X. They had struck Aramco sites before in ​Jazan, which processes 400,000 barrels of crude oil a day. They had also hit Yanbu, an oil export hub ‌on the Red Sea.

In a separate statement, Saree said the Houthis had carried out missile and drone strikes on the Yemeni Red Sea port city of Mocha, which is controlled by the country’s internationally recognised, Saudi-backed governing body in Aden.

The UAE said on Saturday that a ship affiliated with its state oil company had been targeted by an Iranian missile. There was no immediate comment from Iran, whose IRGC has previously attacked ships, saying they had not coordinated their passage through the strait with Tehran.

Tehran and its allied Shia armed groups have been striking Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states and blockading their ‌energy shipments since the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran on 28 February.

The escalation of the conflict, which has disrupted global energy supplies and rattled the world’s economy, prompted Saudi Arabia on Friday to form an alliance with US allies Turkey and Pakistan.

The accord is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression and stipulates that an armed attack against any of the three would be regarded as ⁠an attack on all.

The Turkish foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, said the alliance was not directed against Iran or ​any other country, but rather served as a general ​pledge to support the security of Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. It was ​not clear whether or how either Pakistan or Turkey would join in any Saudi response to the latest attacks.

articles.title: Bride cautions others before wedding day about risky beauty treatments: 'Pain wasn't worth it'
articles.excerpt:
'The Five' co-hosts discuss the growing trend of young couples opting for courthouse weddings instead of more extravagant ceremonies.

A bride-to-be who wanted to look "like a princess" on her wedding...
articles.body_text:
'The Five' co-hosts discuss the growing trend of young couples opting for courthouse weddings instead of more extravagant ceremonies.

A bride-to-be who wanted to look "like a princess" on her wedding day ended up looking far worse than that after a severe allergic reaction to a fake eyelash treatment.

Polly Bibby, 26, an illustrator, decided to try classic eyelash extensions ahead of her big day compared to her usual minimal makeup look.

She had a patch test done, she said, according to Kennedy News & Media — and since she suffered no reaction, she went ahead with the procedure in early July, before her wedding day.

DOCTORS WARN OF ‘LOOKSMAXXING’ DANGERS AFTER INFLUENCER’S LIVESTREAM EMERGENCY

After getting the treatment done — which cost her about $88, she said — she was initially happy with her "dressier" appearance.

Just a few hours after the appointment, however, her eyes became watery and sore. She shrugged it off as symptoms of hay fever.

Polly Bibby, pictured, was left with red, raw and swollen eyes after suffering an allergic reaction to eyelash extensions. (Kennedy News & Media)

But when her eyes started to sting and then stick together due to a yellow discharge, alarm bells began going off. She called an urgent care medical line and was advised to head to the nearest hospital emergency room.

A shocking photo shows her red, raw and swollen eyes. After being seen by a nurse in the eye unit at Hinchingbrooke Hospital in Hinchingbrooke, Cambridge, it was confirmed she'd suffered an allergic reaction to the eyelash extensions.

WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS LINKED TO 'OZEMPIC EARS' AND OTHER COSMETIC COMPLAINTS, SURGEONS SAY

She was given a course of antibiotics and antihistamines, and told to wait three days for the swelling to go down before getting the false lashes removed.

"To keep the eyes safe, [artificial] lashes should be applied by an experienced aesthetician in a sanitary setting, with chemicals that are safe for your skin," said Rebecca J. Taylor, M.D., a board-certified ophthalmologist in Nashville, in a statement on the American Academy of Ophthalmology website.

"The procedure does come with risks, namely trauma to or infection of the eyelid or cornea; allergic reaction to the glue; and permanent or temporary loss of eyelashes."

Many brides opt for special beauty treatments for their wedding day. But one suffered a severe allergic reaction to an eyelash extension procedure.  (iStock)

Infection can also result, Taylor said, from inadequate hygiene in the salon or damage to the eye during application.

Even though her skin is now slowly healing, Bibby of Cambridgeshire, in the United Kingdom, feared her eyes would still be red by the time she said "I do" to her to 29-year-old fiancé, Benjamin May.

She said she's been sharing her experience to warn other brides about getting certain treatments so close to their big day.

"I don't wear that much makeup," she told Kennedy News & Media. "Getting married is the biggest day of your life, so I just wanted to test out different makeup and actually feel like a princess for the day."

She said it was a trial for her wedding, as she'd "never had my eyelashes done before."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

About four or five hours after the appointment, her partner looked at her eyes, she said, and thought they were a little red.

"By that evening, they had gone red, raw and were stinging. The only way I can describe [how I looked] is the man from 'The Goonies' with the big puffy eyes called Sloth. I just didn't look like myself. I looked like a different person."

Bibby, shown here, was given a course of antibiotics and antihistamines and told to wait three days for the swelling to go down before having her false lashes removed. (Kennedy News & Media)

She said her eyes were "burning," and "it got to the point where I was losing my vision and I couldn't see at all."

Every time she blinked, she said, her "eyes were sticking together as I had discharge building up [in] my eyes ... a sticky yellow discharge pretty similar to when babies have conjunctivitis."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

She said the medical staff who treated her were "quite taken back and shocked by it."

During the removal of the false lashes, she said it felt like "acid was being poured onto her face."

"I didn't realize it would happen to me."

She said, "I was screaming, crying and tensing up. My eyes are still red, scabby and very 'rashy.' The eyelids themselves are really swollen, and I've still got quite blurry vision."

She also said, "When people joke around and say things [can] go wrong [on your wedding day] — I didn't realize it would happen to me."

"I won't be getting eyelash extensions for the big day," said Bibby (not pictured) ahead of her big day, after suffering an allergic reaction. (iStock)

Ahead of her wedding, she said, "I won't be getting eyelash extensions for the big day. Going through that pain was not worth it. If I knew in hindsight, I'd just use mascara."

She added, "I'd hate for anyone else to go through this."

Kelly McGreal is a production assistant with the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Former DNC fundraiser says major donors won’t back Kamala Harris again as party faces divisions
articles.excerpt: Former DNC fundraiser Lindy Li joins 'My View with Lara Trump' warning that the Democratic Party is deeply in debt. Li points to Kamala Harris's multi-billion dollar campaign spending and a rapid shif...
articles.body_text:
Former DNC fundraiser Lindy Li joins 'My View with Lara Trump' warning that the Democratic Party is deeply in debt. Li points to Kamala Harris's multi-billion dollar campaign spending and a rapid shift toward progressive socialism as the main reasons contributors are refusing to support the party.

A former Democratic National Committee (DNC) fundraiser warned Saturday on "My View with Lara Trump" that major donors are unlikely to support former Vice President Kamala Harris in another presidential run, arguing the party is struggling with internal divisions, fundraising problems and a weak 2028 field.

Lindy Li contended that political donors view their contributions as a "business proposition" and will not continue backing candidates or organizations they believe mishandled their money.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris speaks during a panel discussion at the Austrian World Summit of the Schwarzenegger Climate Initiative on June 16, 2026, in Vienna, Austria. (AFP via Getty Images)

KAMALA HARRIS IS THE 'FAIRLY OBVIOUS' 2028 PRESIDENTIAL FRONTRUNNER, DEMOCRATIC INSIDERS SAY

Li criticized the party’s post-election accountability and said donor frustration is contributing to broader Democratic fundraising problems.

"There's been no accountability. The autopsy that they sent out was basically a sham, and they couldn't even stand behind it. They didn't even mention the fact that Kamala Harris is a terrible candidate," she said.

"Kamala Harris is living in fantasyland… [thinking] that big donors would bet on her again," she added. "She should just go away because the American people do not want her agenda."

Former Vice President Kamala Harris speaks at the 38th Annual Michigan Democratic Women's Caucus Legacy Luncheon on April 18, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Bill Pugliano/Getty Images)

SEN MARK KELLY WARNS FAR-LEFT POLICIES THAT ‘DON’T MAKE SENSE’ COULD COST DEMOCRATS SEATS

Li noted roughly $2.5 billion was spent between Harris’ campaign operation and the pro-Harris Future Forward super PAC. Federal filings show Harris’ principal campaign committee alone reported about $1.18 billion in disbursements during the 2023-24 cycle.

Li made the case that Democratic fundraising troubles are connected to dissatisfaction with the party’s drift leftward, criticizing Democrats for embracing socialist policies.

"This is why donors like me left the party in droves. And this is why they are so… broke. They literally had to put up their own headquarters… as collateral. They can't even get a text back from donors. So I don't want to hear anything about a big tent. You should not be normalizing socialism like this," she said.

Former U.S. Vice President Kamala Harris speaks onstage during the Fortune Most Powerful Women Gala 2025 at Washington National Cathedral on October 14, 2025 in Washington, DC. (Getty Images)

The former Democratic fundraiser also criticized party leaders for succumbing to pressure from the party’s left flank, arguing that Sen. Chuck Schumer only labeled Democrats a "big tent party" because he knows that if he doesn't, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., would primary him.

"He's trying to race her to the bottom. It's just ridiculous," she said. "And Americans already rejected it in 2024," Li said.

Max Bacall is an associate editor for Fox News Digital covering media, culture and comedy.

articles.title: Middle East crisis live: Netanyahu rejects Trump’s Gaza plan and vows no withdrawal until Hamas disarms
articles.excerpt:
Israeli prime minister says he will not support 15-point plan hailed by Donald Trump

Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected a Gaza plan hailed by US president Donald Trump, vowing no ...
articles.body_text:
Israeli prime minister says he will not support 15-point plan hailed by Donald Trump

Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected a Gaza plan hailed by US president Donald Trump, vowing no military pullout of Gaza until Hamas is “genuinely” disarmed.

“Israel rejects the 15-point document,” Netanyahu said, referring to a plan endorsed in late July by Hamas.

The Israeli military “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens,” Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting, Reuters reports.

The document, the latest stage in a US-led ceasefire announced in October that has reduced but not ended Israeli operations in Gaza, said Hamas would surrender weapons to a nascent Palestinian governing body.

The plan said Israel would begin pulling out forces in tandem with the disarmament, an idea adamantly rejected by Israel which also wants Hamas to destroy its weapons.

Netanyahu said that Israel was speaking with the US about its objections. “They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters,” he said.

Netanyahu said that Hamas must give up all of its weapons, a goal that Board of Peace members say is not realistically achievable. “We are talking about real disarmament, not fictitious disarmament,” Netanyahu said.

President Trump’s former defense secretary Mark Esper slammed Iran’s list of demands for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, calling them “ridiculous” and saying they “should be rejected out of hand.”

These include “demands such as the withdrawal of all US forces from the region, reimbursement for the costs of the war, the fact that we would end our blockade, we would end sanctions,” Espter said on ABC News’ This Week. “So it’s gone beyond the pale.”

Esper’s comments on ABC come as Iran maintains a stranglehold on the important waterway. For Esper, Iran’s demands show “that they believe that they have the upper hand, they believe they are winning, and they are already.”

“That’s what we’re up against right now.”

Iran has effectively instituted a blockage in the strait since the US-Israel war started in February and wants to charge tolls to ships that want to travel through. Iran has attacked vessels that it claims tried to get around this blockade.

Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected a Gaza plan hailed by US president Donald Trump, vowing no military pullout of Gaza until Hamas is “genuinely” disarmed. The Israeli military “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens,” Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting.

Here are the other key updates from today:

The US must pressure Israel to accept the next phase of the Gaza plan, a Hamas official said, after Netanyahu rejected the US-backed agreement. “We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons,” Hamas political bureau member Bassem Naim said.

A Houthi drone salvo targeted a Saudi oil refinery on the Red Sea coast. The Iran'-backed group’s military spokesman Yahya Saree said the Houthis had “succeeded in targeting the Aramco refinery in Jazan on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast with a drone”.

Attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen killed at least four troops from the internationally-recognised government forces and injured 20 more personnel, two military sources said. The initial toll came from strikes on the Yemeni city of Mokha and surrounding areas, as well as Khokha, south of the port city of Hodeida, the sources said on condition of anonymity, after the Houthis announced they had targeted military forces and equipment on the Red Sea coast.

Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian met the country’s supreme ⁠leader Mojtaba Khamenei around the start of the president’s third year in office in late July, state ⁠media said, ⁠and ​a paramilitary leader promised footage of Khamenei in the future. Khamenei was reportedly seriously injured in the ​February strike that killed his father and predecessor, Ali Khamenei on the first day of the US-Israeli war on Iran. The promise to release footage of the leader by paramilitary Basij ⁠Organisation deputy Qasem Qoraishi appeared to be aimed ​at quashing speculation about his health.

Along with his rejection of the US Gaza plan earlier, Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed once again to prevent Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons, regardless of the course of diplomacy with Washington and Arab states.

“I want to emphasise once again: with an agreement or without an agreement, as long as I am prime minister, Iran will not have nuclear weapons,” Netanyahu said at the cabinet meeting.

Both the US and Israel have said a goal of their war on Iran is to stop it obtaining a nuclear weapon. Iran has always maintained its nuclear program is peaceful.

Strikes by Iran-backed Houthi rebels on Sunday killed at least 11 people, a medical source in the Yemeni port city of Mokha told AFP, after an earlier drone salvo targeted a Saudi oil refinery on the Red Sea coast.

Residents in Mokha confirmed to AFP they heard blasts in the area, with one saying they “heard explosions from drones and air defences over the port and city”.

Another resident said they heard “six consecutive explosions” at the port.

The Houthis control vast swathes of Yemen, including the capital Sanaa and areas on the border with Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea provinces.

The group’s military spokesman Yahya Saree said the Houthis had “succeeded in targeting the Aramco refinery in Jazan on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast with a drone”.

He added the attack on the facility operated by Saudi Arabia’s state-owned oil firm was launched in response to incursions by drones from the Gulf monarchy into northwest Yemen.

One major sticking point between the two sides over the Gaza plan is disagreement over timing commitments.

Israel has said that Israeli troops in Gaza would not move before Hamas disarms, while Hamas ‌has insisted that Israel halt attacks before it begins implementing the part of the agreement dealing with its arms.

Hamas said it agreed to the plan in order ​to spare the people in Gaza a possible resumption of war, ​but it added that the implementation of the deal would depend on Israel first meeting its own commitments, including withdrawal.

Hamas avoids the use of the term “disarmament” and said the group agreed to hand ⁠over weapons to be stored by the US-backed National Committee for the Administration of Gaza under the supervision of Trump’s ​Board of Peace.

Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s rejection of the plan and vow not to withdraw until Hamas disarms was met with praise by far-right finance minister Bezalel Smotrich.

“We went to war with a central goal: the destruction of Hamas,” he said in a statement. “The (military) cannot withdraw even a milimetre from the Gaza Strip. The Gaza Strip cannot begin any process of reconstruction before the complete dismantling and demobilization of Hamas and the Gaza Strip.“

The US plan that would see Hamas disarmed and Israeli withdrawal from Gaza was announced at the end of July. Here’s a recap of the details of that plan from when it was announced:

double quotation markAnnouncing the agreement in a social media post, Trump said it involved the “complete disarmament” of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza and was “a monumental step toward ending the fighting”.

Israel has pointed to Hamas’s failure to disarm as justification for its continued strikes and refusal to allow any reconstruction in Gaza, and for Israeli forces’ steady edging forward from the demarcation line agreed in October.

The 14-point plan, posted by the Board of Peace (BoP) on X, urges Israel, Hamas and other Palestinian factions to halt all military operations, and calls for an international verification committee (IVC) to be set up. It outlines a 14-day period after all parties have accepted the roadmap, with a timetable and implementation mechanisms to be worked out.

Control of Gaza would then be handed to a National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, a panel of Palestinian professionals and experts set up by the BoP in January who have been waiting in Cairo since then to take over. The NCAG would take over all administrative functions, backed by the new police force and the ISF. That would enable a “process to decommission and store heavy weapons, military production sites, depots of weapons, and tunnels”.

The disarming of Hamas and other groups would be “gradual, sequential and time-bound” and would be “linked to an Israeli withdrawal, in phases, from the areas under its control in Gaza”. The ISF would operate between NCAG and Israeli-controlled areas of the territory, while internal security would be the responsibility of the NCAG and its police force.

You can read Julian Borger’s full report at the link below:

The US must pressure Israel to accept the next phase of the Gaza plan, a Hamas official told AFP, after Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he rejected the US-backed agreement.

“We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons,” Hamas political bureau member Bassem Naim told AFP.

Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian met the country’s supreme ⁠leader Mojtaba Khamenei around the start of the president’s third year in office in late July, state ⁠media said on Sunday, ⁠and ​a paramilitary leader promised footage of Khamenei in the future, Reuters reports.

Pezeshkian has given differing accounts in recent ⁠weeks about his access to Khamenei, who has not been seen in public since he succeeded his father in the ⁠role in March.

On 21 July, the president said interactions with ​the supreme leader were “increasing day by ‌day”, but in ‌early August he said communicating with Khamenei was “very difficult”.

The late July ‌meeting covered military affairs and the economy, including securing resources, managing foreign exchange and energy use, as well as economic ties with foreign partners, according to state media.

Khamenei was reportedly seriously injured in the ​February strike that killed his father and predecessor, Ali Khamenei on the first day of the US-Israeli war on Iran. The promise to release footage of the leader by paramilitary Basij ⁠Organisation deputy Qasem Qoraishi appeared to be aimed ​at quashing speculation about his health. Senior Iranian sources have said he suffered ⁠facial disfigurement and other injuries ​in the ​strike.

Attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen killed at least four troops from the internationally-recognised government forces and injured 20 more personnel, two military sources told AFP.

The initial toll came from strikes on the Yemeni city of Mokha and surrounding areas, as well as Khokha, south of the port city of Hodeida, the sources said on condition of anonymity, after the Houthis announced they had targeted military forces and equipment on the Red Sea coast.

Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected a Gaza plan hailed by US president Donald Trump, vowing no military pullout of Gaza until Hamas is “genuinely” disarmed.

“Israel rejects the 15-point document,” Netanyahu said, referring to a plan endorsed in late July by Hamas.

The Israeli military “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens,” Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting, Reuters reports.

The document, the latest stage in a US-led ceasefire announced in October that has reduced but not ended Israeli operations in Gaza, said Hamas would surrender weapons to a nascent Palestinian governing body.

The plan said Israel would begin pulling out forces in tandem with the disarmament, an idea adamantly rejected by Israel which also wants Hamas to destroy its weapons.

Netanyahu said that Israel was speaking with the US about its objections. “They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters,” he said.

Netanyahu said that Hamas must give up all of its weapons, a goal that Board of Peace members say is not realistically achievable. “We are talking about real disarmament, not fictitious disarmament,” Netanyahu said.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Corp said they will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until the United States meets Tehran’s conditions, including compensation for war damages.

The IRGC said their strategy was to maintain the closure “until the enemy accepts all our conditions ... the strait is now actually a theatre of war for us and not just a waterway”.

Iran’s security chief Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr on Saturday laid out a list of demands for reopening the strait, including an end to the “war and aggression against Iran and its allies in Lebanon, Palestine, Yemen and Iraq”.

He also demanded the lifting of a US counterblockade of Iranian ports, the end of sanctions, the release of frozen assets and compensation for wartime damage, according to remarks reported by the Tasnim news agency.

Iran has imposed an effective blockade of the strait since the US and Israel attacked in late February, and wants to charge tolls for passage, striking ships it accuses of attempting to circumvent its preferred route.

Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said discussions with Oman over transit and management of the strait were “approaching the final stages”, but added that the reopening of Hormuz “is subject to other conditions and compensation for the violation” of an interim June agreement with the US.

Iran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian has said he believes now is the best time for an agreement with the US. “There is cohesion, strength, and unity in the country, and as far as I know, Iran is considered victorious and powerful in this war,” Iranian news agencies quoted him as saying.

Oman condemned what it described as repeated attacks on vessels while transiting the strait, without assigning blame, and said that ​negotiations with Iran on arrangements for shipping through Hormuz were “positive and constructive”.

The UAE said on Saturday that Iran had attacked a carrier affiliated with the UAE’s state oil company with a missile as it transited the strait of Hormuz. No injuries were reported. The UK maritime trade monitor UKMTO said a ‌vessel had caught fire after being hit by an unknown projectile but the fire was put out and there was no reported environmental impact. There was no immediate comment from Iranian authorities.

US Central Command said on Saturday it had allowed more than 30 ships through for humanitarian aid since the current blockade started. US forces have turned away 53 ships, disabled two vessels and boarded two others, Central Command said in a statement on social media.

articles.title: China expresses ‘grave concern’ as internal documents reveal suicide warning before death in Melbourne immigration detention
articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: Serious questions raised about whether Chinese citizen was properly monitored at centre run by US prison giant

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The US private p...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: Serious questions raised about whether Chinese citizen was properly monitored at centre run by US prison giant

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The US private prison company running Australia’s immigration system was warned that a newly detained Chinese citizen expressed suicidal ideation and had a history of self-harm less than 24 hours before she died by suicide in a Melbourne detention centre, internal documents show.

The death has raised serious questions about whether the detainee was properly monitored and whether she was placed in an appropriate room, given her state of mind.

It has also triggered an intervention from Australia’s biggest trading partner, Guardian Australia can reveal.

The Chinese embassy has confirmed it has “lodged solemn representations and expressed grave concern to the Australian side” about the circumstances of the death.

“China will closely follow the case and safeguard the safety and legitimate rights and interests of Chinese citizens,” an embassy spokesperson said.

China’s public intervention creates a fresh headache for the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, who is already furious about a string of security lapses involving the government’s new immigration contractor, Secure Journeys, a local subsidiary of the US-based prison multinational Management and Training Corporation.

In May the Guardian revealed that a series of failures had allowed the escape of high-risk detainees, caused ill-equipped staff to be stabbed and hospitalised and triggered multiple investigations, one of which warned that MTC’s “minimalist staffing model” was putting workers and detainees at risk.

Burke took the extraordinary step of hauling in the global president of MTC for a face-to-face dressing down in September 2025, just six months after the company was awarded the $2.3bn onshore immigration detention contract.

On 10 July Australian Border Force issued a short statement saying a detainee had been found dead in the Melbourne immigration detention centre that morning.

The detainee was a Chinese citizen in her mid-30s who had been picked up the day before for allegedly overstaying an English-language studies visa, internal documents seen by the Guardian show. She had no criminal history.

The ABF transferred her into the custody of Secure Journeys on the afternoon of 9 July.

The ABF made clear to Secure Journeys that she had previously attempted self-harm and had “recently thought about self-harm/suicide”, the documents show.

She was found hanging in her room in the Broadmeadows residential precinct, part of the Melbourne immigration detention centre, early the next morning.

Victoria police are investigating the death, which they described as non-suspicious. The coroner’s court of Victoria said it had directed police to prepare a brief of evidence.

The best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know.

If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods.

The Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.

If you don't already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.

SecureDrop, instant messengers, email, telephone and post

If you can safely use the Tor network without being observed or monitored, you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via our SecureDrop platform.

Finally, our guide at theguardian.com/tips lists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.

There were 360 reported incidents of threatened and actual self-harm across Australia’s onshore immigration detention network between July 2025 and March 2026, according to parliamentary records. There have been at least two deaths this year.

A Secure Journeys spokesperson said the company offered its “deep condolences to the family and friends of the female detainee” but could not comment further due to the investigation.

“Secure Journeys’ commitment to maintaining safe and secure operations, as well as both staff and detainee welfare remains our top priority,” the spokesperson said.

The Department of Home Affairs offered sincere condolences to the woman’s family and friends. “Due to our privacy obligations to the deceased and the ongoing investigation into this matter, it would not be appropriate to comment further,” a spokesperson said.

China experts described the embassy’s statement as “firm but not excessive”.

The Australia-China Relations Institute’s director, Prof James Laurenceson, said the fact that representations had been made and the embassy had expressed “grave concerns” showed it was taking the death seriously.

But Laurenceson said he didn’t read the embassy’s statement as “excessively aggressive”.

“It is the case that Australia and China have been trading tersely worded diplomatic statements more frequently in recent months over everything from Taiwan, China’s maritime claims in the South China Sea, its cyber operations, the Jimmy Lai case, Darwin Port, and more,” he said. “But I am not convinced that China’s statement in this case should be interpreted as some sort of diplomatic slap back for Australian complaints about Chinese actions in other contexts.”

MTC’s performance in running Australia’s onshore detention network has triggered multiple investigations, including by the federal work safety regulator Comcare.

Internal documents show Comcare has set up a dedicated inspection program to scrutinise immigration detention, citing an “increase in notifiable incidents, the severity and the profile of the reported incidents involving the [contractor]”.

The regulator privately warned the department this year that it had received numerous reports of “serious injury or illness to both workers and others (detainees)”, “self-harm ideations and death involving detainees” and “detainee on detainee violence”.

One of Comcare’s key concerns is that the risk-assessment system used in the centres is not effective and is putting staff and detainees at serious risk of violence and other harms.

Understaffing has been a key concern since MTC took over.

A March report by the National Preventive Mechanism, an independent monitor of places of detention, reported that “critically” low staffing levels were compromising the centres’ safety.

The understaffing is also causing seriously ill detainees to miss medical appointments because MTC lacks workers to escort them to health centres.
