TRUMP WEIGHS IN ON LIV GOLF, PGA TOUR AFTER SAUDIS PULL FUNDING OF STARTUP LEAGUE

That's a huge problem, seeing as the PIF was LIV's only funder.

However, LIV Golf CEO Scott O'Neil announced this week that the tour has an as-yet-unnamed investor lined up.

"LIV Golf has an agreement in place with a lead investor, signed by the investor and approved by the Board, to anchor the transaction and play a key role in supporting the path forward for the League’s next era, driven by and for the players," O'Neil said.

articles.title: Turkiye says Mecca defence pact not aimed at Iran
articles.excerpt:
Turkish leaders have insisted that the new trilateral defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan is not directed at Iran.

Turkiye’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Saturday that the pact does n...
articles.body_text:
Turkish leaders have insisted that the new trilateral defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan is not directed at Iran.

Turkiye’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Saturday that the pact does not identify Iran, or any other country, as a common threat.

The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement was signed on Friday by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, stating that an armed attack on one of the three countries would be considered an attack on them all.

“There is no common threat that we have put in writing,” Fidan told Turkey’s state-run Anadolu agency, adding that countries that do not attack the signatories would not be considered targets.

Fidan described the pact as “technically” similar to NATO’s Article 5 collective-defence clause, under which an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.

But the response would depend on the circumstances.

A country under attack would have to request assistance and specify what kind of support it needed, Fidan said. That could range from intelligence and logistics to ammunition or the deployment of military units.

The alliance will also establish political and military committees, bringing together foreign and defence ministers and military chiefs, as well as a secretariat in Saudi Arabia.

Fidan said the three countries would work on joint training, intelligence sharing, logistics, threat assessments and military interoperability.

Defence-industry cooperation is also expected to be a notable part of the pact. Fidan said it was one of the main issues discussed by the three leaders in Mecca, including how the countries could benefit from each other’s military technologies.

The Turkish minister said preparations for the agreement had been under way for nearly two years and eight months, suggesting it was not drawn up simply in response to the current tensions involving Iran.

Despite Ankara’s assurances, some Iranian officials have questioned the agreement and warned Saudi Arabia against relying on its new partners for security.

Mahmoud Nabavian, a member of Iran’s parliamentary National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, said Saudi leaders should understand that cooperation with Turkiye and Pakistan would not guarantee their security.

Another commission member, Ebrahim Rezaei, similarly dismissed the pact as a “paper agreement”.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi did not directly mention the agreement in a message on X on Friday, but he called on regional states to rely on themselves and pursue what he described as “true brotherhood”.

At the same time, he stressed the strength and readiness of Iran’s armed forces.

Fidan portrayed the agreement as part of a broader effort to give regional countries greater responsibility for their own security.

“External hegemons coming into the region do not solve the problems; they make them more acute,” he told Anadolu.

He described Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan as the “core countries” of the initiative and made clear that Ankara wants the arrangement to expand.

“Under our president’s vision, we should not remain limited to three countries,” Fidan said. “We should grow and, if necessary, bring all countries under this umbrella.”

Several countries have already expressed interest, according to Fidan, who said he expected Egypt, which he described as a “natural partner”, to join once outstanding technical issues were resolved.

For now, many of the practical details remain to be worked out, including how the three militaries would coordinate in a crisis.

But the planned committees, permanent secretariat and focus on interoperability and defence-industry cooperation suggest the pact is intended to develop beyond a simple mutual defence declaration.

articles.title: Utah wildfire blocks rescuers from reaching firefighting helicopter crash site
articles.excerpt:
Fate of two passengers onboard helicopter that went down Friday morning remains unknown after more than 24 hours

The fate of two passengers onboard a firefighting helicopter that crashed Friday morni...
articles.body_text:
Fate of two passengers onboard helicopter that went down Friday morning remains unknown after more than 24 hours

The fate of two passengers onboard a firefighting helicopter that crashed Friday morning in Utah remains unknown after more than 24 hours, as one of the country’s largest wildfires continues to grow, preventing authorities from safely reaching the accident site.

The Sikorsky S-64 helicopter, contracted by the US Forest Service, was responding on Friday to the Widemouth 2 fire, a blaze sparked in late July by lightning, when it crashed in a remote area of central Utah.

Widemouth 2 has swept through more than 114,600 acres (46,400 hectares) and is 24% contained, as of Saturday. That figure marked a jump from early on Friday, where the fire’s scope was reported as reaching more than 105,000 acres, according to state data.

The chopper’s crash ignited a new blaze, state authorities said at a news conference on Friday evening. The accident site is within the fire’s perimeter.

“Ground resources attempted to respond immediately, but access to the scene was compromised by the emergent fire,” the US Forest Service wrote in a Saturday statement. “Without a safety zone, the Incident Management Team determined not to place lives at risk until the area is deemed safe.”

Federal officials have advised the public to refrain from speculating on the nature of the crash, as search-and-rescue teams wait for fire conditions to subside to safer levels.

In a Saturday daily report, however, the US National Interagency Fire Center, a coalition of state and federal agencies, said the helicopter’s “pilot and one crewmember were fatally injured”. At a Saturday morning briefing, a moment of silence was observed to honor the passengers.

The US Forest Service has declined to confirm their status.

“There have already been many false reports and rumors, and the victims deserve the highest level of respect and avoidance of speculation,” the agency wrote.

Investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) were en route to Richfield, a city roughly 160 miles (250km) south of Salt Lake City, as of Friday. When they are able to reach the crash site, they will document the scene, before retrieving the aircraft.

The western US states have faced a deadly wildfire season. In June, three firefighters died, as they battled a blaze along the Colorado-Utah border. A fourth firefighter later died from burn injuries sustained during the emergency response.

articles.title: WNBA faces discipline dilemma after Carrington's 'White privilege' post targeting Indiana Fever
articles.excerpt: OutKick host Dan Dakich criticizes the WNBA and media for mishandling star Caitlin Clark, arguing the league, after 30 years, fails to capitalize on her popularity. He cites 'petty jealousies, racism,...
articles.body_text:
OutKick host Dan Dakich criticizes the WNBA and media for mishandling star Caitlin Clark, arguing the league, after 30 years, fails to capitalize on her popularity. He cites 'petty jealousies, racism, and sexism' as reasons for negative narratives and limited support for the 24-year-old athlete. Dakich suggests this impacts both Clark and the sport's potential growth.

Chicago Sky guard DiJonai Carrington was ejected for a Flagrant 2 foul on Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham on Saturday afternoon.

Then Carrington presumably went to the locker room and fired off a strong accusation.

A post on Carrington's Threads account shortly after her ejection read: "WHITE PRIVILEGE @indianafever."

WNBA COACH TORCHES LEAGUE’S OFFICIATING AFTER LATEST BIZARRE NO-CALL: ‘IT’S A F------ JOKE’

Chicago Sky guard DiJonai Carrington commits a flagrant 2 foul against Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Following an ejection, a player went to the locker room and made an apparent race-based accusation. It's hard to imagine that happening in another major professional sports league without a harsh punishment from the league.

The Fever went on to beat the Sky, 90-86, but that seemed like a secondary story at best.

Carrington was tossed late in the first quarter after striking Cunningham across the head while the Fever guard attempted a layup. Officials reviewed the play and upgraded the foul to a Flagrant 2, which carries an automatic ejection. Cunningham had to be restrained following the play and appeared to show her teammates that her mouth was bleeding.

The timing of Carrington's post certainly appeared to suggest that she believed race, or "white privilege," played some role in what happened.

WNBA SUDDENLY WANTS TO STICK TO BASKETBALL AFTER YEARS OF MAKING POLITICS PART OF THE PRODUCT

While Carrington didn't specifically write, "The referees are racist," it's hard to find an alternative interpretation. Unless, since she tagged the Indiana Fever, she thinks the Fever organization is racist.

Either way, the WNBA finds itself in a terrible spot.

Either the league has to impose a harsh punishment on Carrington, which potentially angers other players in the WNBA and certain corners of the sports media, or it does nothing and risks reinforcing the perception that different racial standards apply, despite Commissioner Cathy Engelbert recently telling Congress that the league applies its rules and disciplinary processes consistently across all games and all players.

Chicago Sky guard DiJonai Carrington arrives at Wintrust Arena before a WNBA game. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

OutKick contacted the WNBA, the WNBA Players' Association and the Chicago Sky shortly after Carrington's post.

The league was asked whether it interpreted the message as an allegation that race or racial bias played a role in Carrington's ejection, whether it had spoken with Carrington about the post and whether it was reviewing the matter for potential discipline.

The Sky were similarly asked what Carrington meant, whether she was alleging racial bias in the officiating decision and whether the organization stood by her characterization.

OutKick also contacted the WNBPA, asking whether the union believes race or racial bias played a role in Carrington's ejection, whether it has evidence of racial disparities in WNBA officiating and whether it stands by Carrington's "WHITE PRIVILEGE" characterization.

None of the organizations responded prior to publication.

WNBPA SAYS IT DID NOT ASK WNBA TO DROP USA 250 ALL-STAR PATCH AFTER UNION OFFICER PUBLICLY OBJECTED

Complaints about officiating are part of professional sports. Players think they get fouled too much, coaches think opponents get favorable whistles, and fans are convinced every referee has a bet on their favorite team's opponent.

But claiming "white privilege" immediately after an officiating decision is different. It introduces the idea that officials aren't simply making good or bad basketball calls, but that race might influence how those calls are made.

If that's what Carrington meant, she should say it clearly and explain what evidence she has.

If that's not what she meant, that's pretty easy to clear up, too.

And there's another important piece of context in this specific incident.

Sophie Cunningham has become one of the WNBA's most polarizing players after publicly stating that she doesn't believe biological men should compete in women's sports. Her position has generated rallies at Fever games, subsequent counter-protests and open disagreement from others inside the WNBA, including the players' association.

So, it's entirely possible Carrington's message was aimed at something broader than the officiating.

Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham fights with Chicago Sky guard DiJonai Carrington after being Carrington fouled Cunningham with a hit to the Fever guard's head. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

The WNBA can't spend years embracing players speaking publicly about politics, race, gender and social issues, then treat a player's "WHITE PRIVILEGE" accusation as something that doesn't deserve a suspension.

And the WNBPA has a problem, too. On Friday, the union said "hate, abuse, and demonization of any person or group of people, including transgender people" fuels "fear, division, and harm."

Well, if "any person or group" actually means any person or group, then the union can’t carve out an exception when one of its own players invokes "WHITE PRIVILEGE" against another team.

Carrington not only posted that accusation publicly, but she did it during a game and presumably from inside a WNBA locker room. She tagged another WNBA franchise.

The league, the players' association and the Sky were given an opportunity to explain what she meant or, at minimum, say whether they asked her.

For now, Carrington's two-word accusation is left to speak for itself.

articles.title: Four killed in helicopter crash in Brazil’s Rio de Janeiro
articles.excerpt:
At least four people have been killed in a helicopter crash in the Brazilian city of Rio de Janeiro, according to a statement from the Colombian consul in the country.

Saturday’s crash involved a pil...
articles.body_text:
At least four people have been killed in a helicopter crash in the Brazilian city of Rio de Janeiro, according to a statement from the Colombian consul in the country.

Saturday’s crash involved a pilot and three Colombian women who were members of the same family.

They were reportedly on a sightseeing flight over Tijuca National Park, a densely forested, mountainous area on the edge of the city.

In the aftermath of the crash, Rio de Janeiro Mayor Eduardo Cavaliere called for more oversight of helicopter flights, a popular tourist activity. He even suggested such flights could be suspended “for a week or two”, as new safety measures are implemented.

“My solidarity to the families of the victims of the helicopter accident that happened today near Vista Chinesa within the Tijuca National Park,” Cavaliere said in a social media post.

He added that he had been in contact with Brazil’s National Civil Aviation Agency, ANAC.

“City Hall has requested that ANAC take immediate action to intensify oversight and ensure safety in helicopter flights that are circulating with increasing frequency in our city,” Cavaliere explained.

“We place the entire apparatus of City Hall at the disposal of ANAC to support the measures and actions that may be necessary.”

The crash took place near Vista Chinesa, a lookout point crowned by a small bamboo pagoda. Tijuca National Park is a top destination in Rio de Janeiro, famous for its Christ the Redeemer statue and sweeping vistas of the coastal city.

Diana Paez, the Colombian consul general in Rio de Janeiro, told the news agency AFP that the three women on Saturday’s flight were part of a family that had travelled to the city to celebrate a girl’s 15th birthday.

The group of six had split up since the helicopter could only fit three people. The girl’s grandmother, aunt and cousin died in the crash.

Helicopter rides have become a popular way for tourists to see the city and its various monuments from above, a practice that has attracted growing concern over safety.

Six people were recently killed when two helicopters collided in midair over the city. That incident took place over the western suburb of Recreio dos Bandeirantes on June 14.

articles.title: Crews recover 19 bodies from rubble of destroyed Gaza building
articles.excerpt:
Nineteen bodies, most of them women and children, have been recovered from under the rubble of a destroyed residential building in Gaza City, Gaza’s civil defence said in a statement.

The recovery, w...
articles.body_text:
Nineteen bodies, most of them women and children, have been recovered from under the rubble of a destroyed residential building in Gaza City, Gaza’s civil defence said in a statement.

The recovery, which concluded on Saturday, is the latest in a slow, largely manual campaign to retrieve the dead from beneath Gaza’s ruins. Such efforts are hampered by a chronic shortage of the heavy machinery needed to clear broken concrete.

Mohammed Abu Dan, who oversees recovery efforts, said that work had ended at the “Karam” building in Gaza’s western area after four consecutive days of searching.

Specialised medics and civil defence crews would now move to a new site elsewhere in Gaza City, he said, to resume search operations.

Civil defence officials have repeatedly said crews are relying on rudimentary tools and exhausting manual labour in the absence of heavy equipment capable of shifting the concrete slabs left behind by Israeli strikes.

Gaza’s Health Ministry says more than 8,000 people remain missing under rubble across the territory.

Since the ceasefire took hold on October 11 last year, at least 1,254 people have been killed, 4,121 wounded and 804 bodies recovered from rubble, according to the ministry’s latest count.

The overall death toll since October 2023 stands at more than 73,300, with more than 174,000 wounded.

The recovery operation follows a mass funeral held in Gaza City on Tuesday for 112 people from the Abu Sharia and al-Hasayna families, whose remains were pulled from the wreckage of a residential block in Gaza’s Sabra neighbourhood, which was destroyed in an Israeli strike in November 2023.

articles.body_text:
The supermodel tells Fox News Digital at The Paley Center Gala in New York the healthy habits she prioritizes in summer.

Molly Sims is enjoying a beach day with her kids.

The 53-year-old model and actress took to Instagram to share how she and her family spent "a perfect beach day" together.

She posted a series of photos on her Instagram stories featuring her children swimming in the ocean and building sandcastles, as well as one of her in a mismatched bikini with the words, "Oh hey," written over it.

In the photo, Sims can be seen flaunting her toned abs in a black bikini top and blue bikini bottoms, which she paired with a chunky chain necklace with a heart charm with the letter "M" on it, as well as black sunglasses and a black hat.

Sims shared photos of herself and her kids from their "perfect beach day." (Molly Sims Instagram)

KRISTIN CAVALLARI FLAUNTS HER TONED FIGURE IN BIKINIS DURING EUROPEAN SUMMER VACATION

She also shared a photo of herself after leaving the beach in a white dress with black polka dots, which she paired with the same gold chain necklace, gold hoop earrings and minimal makeup.

"Nothing like getting ready for dinner after a day in the sun," she wrote over the picture, adding a sun emoji.

Sims shared she and her family had "a perfect beach day." (Molly Sims Instagram)

Sims later cleaned up and wore a white dress with polka dots after leaving the beach. (Molly Sims Instagram)

Sims recently made waves when she appeared in the pages of the 2026 Sports Illustrated Swimsuit Issue. (Alexander Tamargo/Getty Images for Sports Illustrated)

She has never been one to shy away from posting bikini photos on social media, often taking to Instagram to share photos from various vacations, whether she was in Cabo San Lucas, Mexico, or on a mountain vacation in the snow.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Sims previously credited bone broth as her secret to staying fit. (TheStewartofNY/GC Images)

In February 2023, Sims took to her Instagram stories to share how she keeps her body bikini ready, noting her secret is bone broth, and she showed a picture of a mug filled with it.

She wrote, "Anti-ageing [sic], good for digestion and gut, helps my joints after workouts, better sleep... this has been game changing for me."

articles.excerpt:
Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Antonio Banderas is getting real about why he ditched Los Angeles to move back to his hometown in Spain.

During a recent interview ...
articles.body_text:
Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Antonio Banderas is getting real about why he ditched Los Angeles to move back to his hometown in Spain.

During a recent interview with People, the 65-year-old explained he originally moved to Los Angeles to be with Melanie Griffith after the two fell in love. She had two young children at the time and couldn't relocate to Spain.

"Those were beautiful, exciting years. But I always had this sense of provisionality that it was not going to last my whole life," Banderas said. "I knew that Málaga was there, my hometown. I was not supposed to be in Malibu, but in Málaga."

Griffith and Banderas went on to marry in 1996, just one year after making a connection on set of the 1995 movie "Two Much." Not long after tying the knot, the two welcomed their daughter, Stella, in September 1996.

Banderas always knew he would return to his hometown in Spain after moving to Los Angeles to be with Melanie Griffith. (Carlos Alvarez/Getty Images)

'FIRE COUNTRY' STAR DIANE FARR LEAVES LOS ANGELES AFTER 30 YEARS TO START HER 'THIRD ACT'

The two were married for 18 years before Griffith filed for divorce in June 2014, citing irreconcilable differences. They went on to finalize their divorce a little over a year later, in December 2015.

"When we separated, we were always very sincere. And now she is, if not my best friend, one of my best friends," Banderas explained.

While married to Griffith, Banderas was stepfather to her two children, Alexander Bauer and actress Dakota Johnson.

When speaking to E! News in February 2025, Banderas admitted he "would love to work with Dakota someday," not only because she is his family, but "because she's a good actress."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Banderas said he would love to work with Johnson on a film. (Amy Sussman/Getty Images)

"She's a good actress in many different ways, because she's a great comedian, too," he said. "She developed now her career more in drama, but I remember when she did a TV show called Ben and Kate that I got a lot of fun [out of seeing] her on the screen, because she got the rhythm of comedy, too."

Banderas is currently starring in the Anthony Bourdain biopic "Tony," but got his big break in mainstream American films in the 1993 movie "Philadelphia."

He went on to star in "Interview with the Vampire," "Desperado," "The Mask of Zorro" and others, including "Pain and Glory" in 2020, which earned him an Academy Award nomination.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

During an interview with The Times in March, Banderas reflected on the early days of his career, and recalled being told upon his arrival in Hollywood that he was there "like the Blacks and the Hispanics, to play the bad guys."

Banderas recalled being told he would never play anything except a villain in Hollywood. (Juan Naharro Gimenez/Getty Images)

"The problem was, a few years later, I had a mask, hat, sword and cape and the bad guy was Captain Love, who was blond and had blue eyes," he said. "Even more important is 'Puss in Boots,' because it's for young kids. They see a cat that has a Spanish, even an Andalusian accent, and he's a good guy."

Lori A. Bashian is an entertainment news writer at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Hormuz talks positive, Oman says, as Iran warns deal would not open strait
articles.excerpt: Oman has said positive talks have been taking place with Iran over an agreement to secure a shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, as Tehran warned that any deal would not see an immediate reope...
articles.body_text:
Oman has said positive talks have been taking place with Iran over an agreement to secure a shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, as Tehran warned that any deal would not see an immediate reopening of the vital waterway.

Both sides suggested on Saturday that discussions were progressing, but a timeline on any deal being finalised remained unclear. Oman's foreign ministry warned against attacks on shipping that could hamper that.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said talks were in their final stages but the reopening of the strait remained "subject to other conditions".

Tehran has effectively blockaded the waterway, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and natural gas usually flows, since the US and Israel began attacking it in February.

Talks in recent days have focused on the possibility of a deal between Iran and Oman on a new route through the strait, which they would both have responsibility for and is hoped would lead to progress in resuming shipping traffic.

But Araghchi said a full reopening of the typically busy maritime route depended on other conditions being met, of which he provided a cursory appraisal.

He said the conditions included Iran receiving compensation from the US for what Tehran described as violations of the deal both sides signed in June to cease fighting and advance talks to end the war.

That deal - called a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) - quickly fell through, as did diplomatic talks, with tit-for-tat attacks resuming just days after it was signed.

Separately, Mohammad Baqer Zolqadr, Iran's security chief, told the semi-official news agency Tasnim that the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen until the US "corrects" its behaviour.

He said the US needed to meet six Iranian demands, including a halt to threats against Iran, removal of its naval blockade of Iranian ports and release of Iran's frozen assets.

Another blockade, on Saudi Arabia's ports in the Red Sea, had been imposed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis since 20 July.

Earlier this week, US President Donald Trump said a deal with Iran "could be soon", but Vice-President JD Vance appeared to be more sceptical on Saturday, telling Fox News that work remained to be done even if progress was being made.

"We're really in the middle of the game here," he said. "This thing is not over."

Vance added that "we're applying a whole host of tools - diplomatic, economic [and] military tools - to ensure that we get the best outcome for the American people".

Additionally, he claimed that the "same amount of oil" will emerge from the Gulf as did before the US military operation began on 28 February, although he offered no details.

"What we're really working through now is how you can actually set up a traffic scheme so that the ships can pass through safely," he added.

One of the main points of disagreement between Tehran and Washington has been Iran's reported threat to impose a fee on vessels wishing to cross the strait.

Reuters - citing an Iranian official - previously reported that Tehran was seeking fees of between 5% and 7% of the price of cargoes from vessels who travel through it.

Vance downplayed those reports, saying: "The Iranians have told us they have no plans to toll the Strait of Hormuz."

Oman's warning against attacks on ships in the strait came as the United Arab Emirates (UAE) said on Saturday that Iran had targeted a tanker affiliated with Adnoc, its state-owned oil company, as it passed through.

The UAE's foreign ministry said in a statement that a "hostile Iranian attack" had hit an Adnoc tanker "with a missile". It added that there were no casualties.

Later on Saturday, the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency also reported a ship being struck by "an unknown projectile" off the coast of Oman, causing "a fire that has been extinguished" but no casualties.

It is unclear whether UKMTO was referring to the same ship as the UAE.

articles.title: America’s best fast-food burger revealed — and it’s not available in every state
articles.excerpt:
California chef Andrew Gruel demonstrates how fresh and frozen burger patties stack up in flavor and texture, revealing why one earned higher marks for moisture, beefy taste and overall quality.

The ...
articles.body_text:
California chef Andrew Gruel demonstrates how fresh and frozen burger patties stack up in flavor and texture, revealing why one earned higher marks for moisture, beefy taste and overall quality.

The best fast-food burger in America can’t be found in every state, but it’s been named a fan-favorite for the third year in a row.

The Double Char burger from Habit Burger & Grill earned first place in USA TODAY’s 2026 10 Best Readers’ Choice Awards, marking the third consecutive year the chain's burger earned top honors.

Habit was also voted the best fast-casual restaurant for the second year in a row.

"Charring burgers over an open flame since 1969, Habit Burger & Grill started in Santa Barbara, California, and has grown to include over 350 restaurants," USA TODAY reported. "Order the Double Char from the Habit’s California-inspired menu and get ready for two freshly chargrilled beef patties, caramelized onions, fresh lettuce, and tomato, pickles and mayo on a toasted bun. You can also add cheese."

The fan-favorite burger in America is from Habit Burger & Grill, according to a new survey. (iStock)

About the restaurant itself, USA TODAY reported that Habit Burger & Grill has been offering "a diverse array of menu items spanning from chicken clubs to Caesar salads to ahi tuna filets, but the restaurant chain really shines when it comes to red meat," highlighting the Charburgers and the way they’re cooked individually over an open flame as their particular appeal.

The annual readers’ choice contest includes several travel and lifestyle categories nominated by a panel of experts and voted for by USA TODAY readers.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

In-N-Out’s Double-Double burger came in second place on the survey, due, according to USA TODAY, to the item's "freshly baked bun made with slow-rising sponge dough, two slices of American cheese, two patties of 100% American beef, onions, tomato, lettuce and a proprietary spread recipe unchanged since 1948."

Coming in at number three was Freddy's Original Double, which USA TODAY noted is a classic sandwich offering "two savory steakburger patties loaded with cheese, onion, pickles and a healthy dose of mustard."

The Double Char burger from Habit Burger & Grill is not available in every state but is a favorite among Americans. (iStock)

The Papa Burger from A&W, "with two 100% beef patties and two slices of melted American cheese, plus lettuce, tomato, onion, pickles and A&W Papa Sauce on a lightly toasted bun," came in at number four.

Rounding out the top five was Culver’s double ButterBurger Cheese.

"This burger made Wisconsin a serious contender in the burger wars," USA TODAY reported. "It’s made with fresh, never-frozen beef seared to order and topped with real American cheese made in Wisconsin."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Shake Shack’s SmokeShack cheeseburger, the cheeseburger from Five Guys, Burger King’s Whopper, Wendy’s Son of Baconator and Whataburger’s Double Meat Whataburger also made the top 10 list, in that order.

In-N-Out’s Double-Double burger and Freddy's Original Double earned second and third place, respectively, in USA TODAY’s 2026 10Best Readers’ Choice Awards. (iStock)

Habit Burger is owned by Yum! Brands, the parent company of Taco Bell, KFC and Pizza Hut. According to the chain’s website, there are more than 380 Habit locations across 14 states and internationally.

Habit Burger locations include Arizona, California, Florida, Idaho, Maryland, Massachusetts, Nevada, New Jersey, North Carolina, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Utah, Virginia and Washington.

Teresa Mull is a freelance writer with the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

At least 200 people evacuated as wildfire rages near Lake Garda

At least 200 people have been evacuated after a wildfire broke out near Italy’s Lake Garda. Authorities said the fire started in the municipality of Tignale on the western shore of the lake. Lake Garda is one of the country’s most popular tourist destinations.

articles.title: Lebanese soldiers injured while Israeli troops intrude on southern town
articles.excerpt:
Three Lebanese soldiers have been wounded while trying to defuse unexploded ordnance in the southern village of Zawtar al-Gharbiyah, the Lebanese army said.

Hours earlier on Saturday, the village may...
articles.body_text:
Three Lebanese soldiers have been wounded while trying to defuse unexploded ordnance in the southern village of Zawtar al-Gharbiyah, the Lebanese army said.

Hours earlier on Saturday, the village mayor and Lebanon’s state-run National News Agency (NNA) said Israeli troops had entered and built an earth barrier overnight.

Mayor Abed Ezzeddine told the AFP news agency that residents were surprised to see the barrier, around 100 metres from the village square. The village had been placed under the control of Lebanon’s army as part of a June agreement with Israel.

A Lebanese military source called the move a violation of the framework accord, but the Israeli military told the AFP agency that it was “not aware of such an event in this area”.

“An Israeli occupation army force advanced into the village of Zawtar al-Gharbiyah shortly after midnight … and erected a new earthen barrier near the town square,” NNA reported. An AFP correspondent confirmed seeing the barrier blocking a road at the eastern entrance.

The Lebanese army had deployed to Zawtar al-Gharbiyah on July 21 and around 50 families have since returned to the village, Mayor Ezzeddine said. Israeli troops were on the outskirts of the village before the deployment.

The village is one of two “pilot zones” where the Lebanese army is deploying under a US-sponsored framework agreement signed with Israel on June 26 . It envisions a phased Israeli withdrawal in return for the disarmament of Hezbollah.

Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Tyre in southern Lebanon, Ihab al-Aqadi, said Israel had escalated the pace of its attacks over the past few days, in parallel with negotiations between Beirut and Tel Aviv in Rome.

He described Zawtar al-Gharbiyah as a pilot area that the Lebanese army was trying to clear of mines, with teams also removing rubble to pave the way for residents to return.

Al-Aqadi said the nearby town of Mansouri was shelled by Israeli artillery on Saturday. It had effectively remained sealed off by gunfire, with residents unable to return after evacuation orders and intermittent shelling. A bulldozer clearing roads there had been damaged by a bomb explosion the day before, he added.

He said the shelling and incursions extended across the frontier: Israeli bulldozing in occupied Zawtar al-Sharqiyeh towards the Ali al-Taher area of Nabatieh al-Fawqa; two drone strikes on open ground in Mayfadoun; and continued ground incursions in Kfar Shouba, in the Hasbaya district and Haddatha in Bint Jbeil district.

Villages along the line of contact had become uninhabitable, among them Nabatieh al-Fawqa and Mansouri, al-Aqadi said.

He added that Lebanon was holding firm on the ceasefire and pressing Israel to halt the destruction of border villages, while preparing for a new round of talks in September.

Israel said a soldier was wounded in southern Lebanon on Saturday. The military, cited by Israel’s Channel 12, said the soldier sustained moderate injuries in an “operational incident” and was evacuated to hospital for treatment. Israel Army Radio reported that he was a combat engineer from the 607th Engineering Battalion who was hit by shrapnel from Israeli fire in the border village of Tayri.

Lebanon and Israel concluded a seventh round of direct, US-mediated talks in Rome on Thursday. President Joseph Aoun said Beirut had made “positive progress” on border and prisoner issues.

articles.title: Australia is the planet's extinction hotspot, but one animal offers a glimmer of hope
articles.excerpt:
"Eyes peeled," comes the order from the front passenger seat.

Obediently, we scan the ends and tops of logs, looking between low scrub and patches of vivid wildflowers for a flash of stripes or a dar...
articles.body_text:
"Eyes peeled," comes the order from the front passenger seat.

Obediently, we scan the ends and tops of logs, looking between low scrub and patches of vivid wildflowers for a flash of stripes or a dart of movement.

Eluding us is the numbat, a rare Australian marsupial which could be the love-child of a chipmunk and an anteater.

Numbats were once populous across the bottom half of the continent, but Dryandra Woodland – in the south-western corner of Australia – is one of the few places they remain.

As we slowly roll along bush tracks, researchers explain how this annual trip helps plot the species' survival.

Classified as endangered until this month, numbats have been bouncing back. This team's efforts have seen them scratched off the international red list of threatened species - a rare glimmer of hope in a country facing an extinction emergency.

This part of Australia is the front line of that crisis: a last stand for many species driven to the brink by feral pests, disease, urban development, habitat destruction and climate change.

Winging over our car at one point is the endangered Carnaby's cockatoo. On an island just off the coast is one of the last surviving pockets of the world's rarest marsupial, the Gilbert's potoroo. Diving in the sapphire waters around it is the increasingly scarce Australian sea lion.

Dryandra Woodland is one of the few places you can still find wild numbats

Australia has long been celebrated as a nature haven, home to some of the world's most unique plant and animal species. More than 80% cannot be found anywhere else.

But it has arguably become the extinction capital of the world, losing roughly four species every decade - and the decline is only worsening.

Dedicated volunteers and under-funded conservationists have been slowing the army of increasing threats, but experts fear that without urgent action and political courage, the biodiversity Australia says it loves is headed for a bloodbath.

"It's not even a case of imagining it, it's happening in front of our own eyes," Professor Euan Ritchie tells the BBC.

Tony Friend has spent five decades trying to save the numbat

If spotting a rare creature in the wild wasn't challenging enough, the numbat is a squirrel-sized camouflage connoisseur, explains Tony Friend, the godfather of conservation in the state of Western Australia.

"They just slept in today," jokes Rob McLean, president of the Numbat Taskforce, a volunteer group which makes a lot of Tony's thinly-resourced work possible.

For two weeks each spring, as the young start venturing from their burrows, this team drives a daily circuit and records every numbat spotted. They log GPS coordinates, measure the distance to the road, and use a complicated equation to estimate the density of the animals in these woods and, from that, broader population health.

One person sits in concentrated silence at each window, another perched in the back of the pick-up truck, ducking for the occasional limb branching from trees which rise around us.

Through the trunks, we get the occasional glimpse of the razed farmland which tightly fences this pocket of protected woodland. On the side of one trail is a machine which detects and sprays feral cats and foxes with poison, another reminder of the perils numbats face.

"This year's been a bit of a feast," Rob admits.

For hours on end, we cruise around, seeing parrots, wallabies, a goanna and a couple of echidnas - but no numbats.

Tony arrived at Dryandra back in the 80s to find a numbat population fewer than 50. Many of the culprits then were the same as those still driving extinctions across the nation today.

Feral cats kill an estimated three billion animals in Australia each year

Swathes of critical habitat are being cleared for development or industries like farming, mining and timber.

Leaving a trail of destruction in their wake are introduced pests: fire ants, cane toads, rabbits, foxes, feral cats.

Invasive weeds like lantana are choking the Australian bush, chlamydia has sent koalas to the edge of existence across much of the country, while the skin-eating chytrid fungus has caused seven frog extinctions here and counting.

The changing climate is creating unliveable conditions for some species, like native flying foxes which are dropping out of trees in their thousands due to extreme temperatures.

For others it is eliminating their food or their homes.

Climate change is also driving natural disasters which fry and drown both plants and animals with now frightening regularity.

The infamous Black Summer bushfires of 2019-20, for example, killed an estimated three billion animals. The successive years of record-breaking flooding which followed were so widespread it's impossible to estimate the impact on wildlife.

The Carnaby's black cockatoo is another species barely hanging on in south-western Australia

Many species once abundant across the continent are now isolated to increasingly small and disjointed patches, each impact compounding and leaving them more vulnerable to the next.

There are small, yet determined, efforts to slow the momentum of decline.

As a young numbat scoffs his breakfast – custard with "termite sprinkles" – at Perth Zoo, a keeper explains how this stud's upcoming release at Dryandra will help boost genetic diversity.

"When you get that feedback: your babies have got babies, it's very satisfying," Vicki Power says.

Breeding programmes like this have also made setting up additional populations of an array of threatened species possible.

But many cannot survive in the true wild, where large-scale predator control remains an endless battle, and are instead sent to fenced nature reserves, themselves high-maintenance undertakings facing problems like in-breeding and overpopulation.

Habitat protection or restoration projects have been ramping up, but they are not keeping pace with destruction, particularly in the most critical areas.

Scientists are also trying to fight disease, though that's an expensive and laborious endeavour, which for most species buys only a little more time. Others are preserving genetic material in case we ever work out how to resurrect species from the dead.

Scientists agree that we're living though the world's sixth mass extinction event, and the first caused by humans. But Australia is at the front of this trend.

It leads the world in mammal extinctions, and medals when it comes to the loss of other species classes too.

"Despite Australia being one of the wealthiest countries per capita in the world and having more than its fair share of world-leading scientists… we have a truly awful record of conserving species," Ritchie says.

The Australian government's official extinctions list sits at 67, but researchers are confident at least 100 plant and animal species have been lost forever.

They suspect the true figure is far higher. The country is still discovering species which have already been wiped out.

Though the rate of extinction in Australia has stayed stable, at around four per decade, the number of threatened species is still climbing quickly, and the deterioration of many is only gathering speed.

This trajectory has some scary flow-on effects, experts warn. Australia's biodiversity "underpins everything", ecologist Jack Pascoe says.

Think food production, tourism, construction – much of the economy. Potential scientific breakthroughs could be stymied: in medicine, agriculture and even climate change adaptation. And for First Nations Australians, the decline also threatens their culture.

"We think of ourselves as custodians of all life on Earth… so there's a much more personal and social feeling of loss that comes when these things are not doing well or we lose them forever," Pascoe, a man from the Yuin Aboriginal nation, says.

Though environment protection is a state responsibility, the federal government oversees matters of national importance.

Labor took office in 2022, promising no new extinctions under its watch, and it has sought to make nature protection a defining feature of its second term.

"It's well understood that nature is facing many challenges in the world today, both here in Australia, and overseas… we are losing biodiversity at an alarming rate," Environment Minister Murray Watt told the BBC in a statement.

His party has significantly increased Australia's emissions reduction efforts and massively boosted renewable energy projects. There is some praise for their work on drawing critically endangered mammals back from the brink. And the passage of revamped environment laws last year was heralded as the most significant reform in a generation.

The country also has an ambitious goal to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.

But there's limited optimism that this will be a real turning point.

The new laws are only the scaffolding of change. The substance of it is still being worked out – in the form of National Environmental Standards (NES) and a federal watchdog to enforce them.

And many in the sector say the problem is not so much the regulatory tools available, but rather the political will to use them.

Successive governments have failed to adequately protect the environment over the past 30 years, Australia's longest serving environment minister tells the BBC.

​​That includes his own administration. "We should have done more too," says Robert Hill, who lead the last major reforms in 1999 under John Howard's conservative coalition.

Vicki Power and Tony Friend have spent decades trying to save the numbat

Many of the challenges of his era still haunt leaders today.

The nation's wealth has largely been built off the back of its natural resources – often at the expense of the environment. Those riches still underpin the economy and help fund government spending on essentials like healthcare and housing.

Then there's the added pressure applied by industry and the competing interests of states - whose stake in regulatory controls blurs the lines of accountability and increases bureaucratic hurdles.

These battles leave even the toughest environmental advocates within governments bruised.

For example, the Albanese government last year rushed through laws protecting salmon farming after lobbying by Tasmanian state officials, silencing opposition from within and ignoring advice from its own department concerning the impact of the A$1.4bn (£733m; $989m) industry on the survival of the Maugean Skate, an endangered ray.

"The axe falls on the environmental outcome if there's the alternative of an economic one," Hill says.

"Even if [the federal government] does want to act, it's still got to have the political strength to turn its aspirations into reality."

The Albanese government passed legislation to protect salmon farming after lobbying by Tasmanian state officials

There is also a belief that greater regulation alone will achieve little.

Too much conservation work currently relies on philanthropists' cash and devoted volunteers, those in the sector say, and much more languishes on the to-do list due to a lack of money.

The federal government directly spends about A$700m on nature protection, a fraction of the A$33bn – or 1% of GDP – conservationists say it should be. That is an eyebrow-raising figure, people like Paul Elton concede, but one they argue is reasonable.

According to his research – which the government disputes – more than A$26bn is still being spent on subsidies for things like mining, intensive agriculture or fuel despite Australia signing global pledges to wind them back.

"For every dollar the government is spending on positive biodiversity conservation action, there's A$26 being spent on subsidies that are causing harm to nature," he tells the BBC.

Minister Watt didn't directly respond to questions about conservationists' demands, but said: "We remain committed to long-term environmental recovery, in partnership with state and local governments, community and environmental groups."

Though public sentiment is shifting, there's scepticism the government will prioritise the environment amid competing demands and compounding crises until voters force them to do so.

"The community will say to you, we should spend a lot of money on the environment. And then if you say, 'Well, what are you prepared to sacrifice to ensure that funding base?', then they're no longer interested," Hill says.

In the face of so many challenges and what they see as little progress, advocates admit it's hard to hang on to hope.

"We know what the problems are. We know how to address them. We know when we spend money on the environment, it pays back many times over," Ritchie, a mammal ecologist, says.

"It's like being a doctor and seeing all these sick people in the community and you know how to fix them, but no one will let you do that."

Volunteer 'Jacko' keeps watch from the back of the truck

Small wins, like the future of the numbat, keep them fighting.

There are now around 3,000 nationwide, and in Dryandra numbers have increased ten-fold. The animal has recently been taken off the international endangered species list and is now classified as near-threatened.

It takes five hours, but finally synchronised cries of excitement come from the driver's seat and the back of the pick-up truck. The cause of the commotion stands frozen and alert at the end of a hollowing log.

"It's not a competition," Rob says. Chuckling, he points at his rival spotter: "But I beat him by a second."

The dam has broken. Over the next little while we see eight numbats, including two pairs of babies, blinking at us in the dusky light.

This year's full count, Tony later tells me, is one of the best yet.

"But I remind people they're not out of the woods yet," Tony says.

The relief at the numbat's revival is tempered by worry this will make it harder to access the funding and support needed to cement those gains.

The woylie, or brush-tailed bettong, is a cautionary tale. It recovered slightly and was taken off the threatened list only to be added again a decade later, in a worse state.

"We can't walk away," Tony says, "and say 'no, they're fine,' you know?"

"It's got to be accepted that continued work is needed to keep that animal on the planet."

articles.title: US slams Chinese ‘nature reserve’ as effort to claim South China Sea
articles.excerpt: The United States has slammed China over a territorial dispute with the Philippines in the South China Sea, a key maritime region that has emerged as a flash point for questions of regional sovereignt...
articles.body_text:
The United States has slammed China over a territorial dispute with the Philippines in the South China Sea, a key maritime region that has emerged as a flash point for questions of regional sovereignty.

In a statement on Saturday, the US State Department said China was seeking to deny Filipino fishermen access to the area surrounding the Scarborough Reef, near the island of Luzon.

It also rejected China’s claims that the area constituted a “nature reserve”, dismissing the assertion as a bid by Beijing to advance its territorial ambitions.

“The United States rejects China’s ongoing attempts to enforce its destabilizing ‘national nature reserve’ at Scarborough Reef and deny Filipino fishermen access to their traditional fishing ground,” the statement reads.

“This is yet another unilateral attempt by China to use dubious environmental and legal pretexts, backed by coercion, to advance its sweeping territorial and maritime claims in the South China Sea at the expense of its neighbors.”

The statement concluded with a line that the US “stands with our Ally, the Philippines, in support of a free and open Indo-Pacific”.

In recent weeks, tensions have flared in the South China Sea, after Chinese ships fired water cannon on Filipino fishing vessels near the Scarborough Shoal.

The area has been claimed by both China and the Philippines as each country’s sovereign territory, in a decades-long dispute.

The Philippines has brought its case to the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague, which largely dismissed China’s sweeping claims to the area as unlawful under international maritime law.

But China refused to participate with the arbitration panel and has instead advanced what is widely called the “nine-dash line”: a looping border that asserts Chinese sovereignty across much of the South China Sea.

China has become more assertive in the region in recent years, constructing artificial islands and intercepting Philippine fishermen in the contested waters.

Critics speculate that China is seeking to translate its claims over the South China Sea into greater economic heft and military power. The sea is not only a strategic zone for military operations, but more than $3 trillion worth of goods pass through the area annually.

The US has sought to use such territorial disputes to advance its own position in Asia, and it frequently weighs in on the side of its allies in the region in the face of aggressive manoeuvring from Beijing.

In April, for instance, the US held joint military operations with Canada and Australia in the region, reiterating its “support of a free and open Indo-Pacific”.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also condemned certain Chinese activities in the area, including the use of water cannon against Filipino vessels.

“The whole world saw it, and it’s disturbing,” Rubio told reporters on the sidelines of the ASEAN meeting in Manila in July.

“We have a role, and we’re not going to abandon our allies,” he added. “We’ve made that abundantly clear.”

articles.title: ‘Debilitating’: Hunter Biden speaks out about father Joe Biden’s cancer
articles.excerpt: Hunter Biden, the younger son of former United States President Joe Biden, has offered an update on his father’s cancer diagnosis in a wide-ranging interview that also reflected on some of the more co...
articles.body_text:
Hunter Biden, the younger son of former United States President Joe Biden, has offered an update on his father’s cancer diagnosis in a wide-ranging interview that also reflected on some of the more controversial moments of the Biden presidency.

In a Friday night appearance on the BBC show Newsnight, Hunter Biden told host Paddy O’Connell that his father’s condition was “debilitating”.

“It’s really hard, Paddy, and it’s really sad to watch,” the younger Biden said.

“The only thing that I say about my dad about his health right now is I wish he would complain more because it’s not good. The cancer has spread. It’s metastasized into his bones and further. It’s very painful.”

In May 2025, the former president revealed that, days earlier, during a physical exam, doctors had discovered he was suffering from an aggressive form of prostate cancer that had already spread to his bones.

The announcement came approximately 10 months after the elder Biden dropped out of the 2024 presidential race. Biden, the incumbent in the election, had all but secured the Democratic Party’s nomination, sweeping the primaries, but concerns about his advanced age had been mounting.

A turning point came on June 27, 2024, when Biden faced Republican candidate Donald Trump for the first presidential debate of that year’s election season.

Though Trump and Biden are relatively close in age, Biden appeared comparably stiff on stage, walking to his podium with short, uneasy steps. He then appeared to lose his train of thought in the middle of answers.

At one point, he answered a question about national debt by stumbling over his words, then announcing, “We finally beat Medicare.” He was 81 years old at the time.

His wife Jill Biden later said she worried her husband was having a stroke. While she said she has never seen the Democratic leader act like that before or since, Trump has used the lingering questions about Biden’s health to cast doubt on the legitimacy of his policy decisions.

Trump went on to win the 2024 presidential election, earning a second term in office. He had previously lost to Biden in the 2020 race.

Democrats, meanwhile, have continued to speculate how their odds might have been different had Biden dropped out earlier — or not run at all. The topic remains a point of division within the party.

O’Connell asked Hunter Biden whether he watched his father’s now-infamous debate. The younger Biden responded that he had viewed it alone in a room in his house in California.

“Like everybody else, I was shocked,” he said. “I could tell as soon as my father came out that something was wrong. I’ve never seen him with kind of the hundred-yard stare that he had.”

Like his stepmother Jill, Hunter Biden framed the incident as an anomaly: “The reason that was so shocking is because it had never happened before, and it hasn’t happened since.”

He also speculated that the Democratic leader’s cancer diagnosis the following year may have contributed to his debate performance.

“Nine months later, he was diagnosed with stage-four prostate cancer and stage-four metastatic bone cancer, none of which we knew,” he said.

Hunter Biden has himself been the subject of numerous controversies during his father’s presidency.

Republicans have long accused the younger Biden of leveraging his father’s political status to further his personal business pursuits.

He has also struggled with drug addiction, and in June 2024, during his father’s re-election bid, he was convicted of three felonies for owning a gun while under the influence of drugs, and lying about his addiction on his firearm application forms. Such charges are typically rare.

That same year, Hunter Biden also pled guilty to federal tax evasion charges, for failing to pay $1.4m from 2016 to 2019.

Though Joe Biden had pledged on the campaign trail not to pardon his son’s crimes, he abruptly reversed course in the final weeks of his presidency.

“From the day I took office, I said I would not interfere with the Justice Department’s decision-making, and I kept my word even as I have watched my son being selectively and unfairly prosecuted,” Biden wrote on December 1, 2024, with less than two months remaining in his term.

“In trying to break Hunter, they’ve tried to break me, and there’s no reason to believe it will stop here. Enough is enough.”

Suggesting that his son would be a target for political persecution, Joe Biden granted him a “full and unconditional pardon” for any actions taken from 2014 up to that point.

It was part of a spate of unconventional pardons Biden granted before leaving office. His brother James Biden was also pardoned, as was his former chief medical adviser Anthony Fauci and the Congress members involved in the investigation of the Capitol attack on January 6, 2021.

Biden suggested that his pardons were motivated by the fear the incoming Trump administration would launch a campaign of political prosecutions against perceived political rivals.

Observers, however, have questioned the broad nature of the pardons, and some critics, particularly on the right, have suggested they amount to government corruption.

O’Connell presented that allegation to Hunter Biden in their interview. In response, the younger Biden acknowledged that the pardons were controversial.

“Was it good for our Constitution? Was it good for the American people? Was it good for my dad’s legacy? No, on all counts,” he said. “It’s something that is easily criticised and for good reason, and I can’t pretend otherwise.”

But Hunter added that his father’s fears about Trump have been borne out.

“I think that Donald Trump has proven to be exactly who my dad thought he was going to be, as it relates to the revenge and retribution that he would seek on his political enemies,” he said.

articles.title: Yemen’s government forces attack Houthis amid renewed shelling of Marib
articles.excerpt: Yemeni government forces have launched attacks on Houthi positions across multiple front lines, hours after the group renewed its shelling of Marib city, raising fears that years of relative calm coul...
articles.body_text:
Yemeni government forces have launched attacks on Houthi positions across multiple front lines, hours after the group renewed its shelling of Marib city, raising fears that years of relative calm could give way to wider conflict.

A military spokesman said the attacks on Saturday targeted the Houthis’ “capabilities and forces” along “multiple axes and along the line of contact”, describing the operation as necessary to “protect unarmed civilians”.

The military operation came after Houthi missile and drone attacks on the provinces of Hadramout and Marib killed at least 30 government soldiers and wounded 15 others on Thursday.

Deputy Information Minister Mohammed Gezan said Saturday the Houthis had “resumed shelling civilian neighbourhoods in Marib city with missiles and drones.”

The renewed shelling of Marib, a city hosting more than 2 million of Yemen’s nearly 5 million displaced people, followed an attack on Friday that killed two civilians and wounded 14 more, according to Yemen’s Health Ministry.

The Houthis said they were targeting a military camp on the city’s outskirts, while the Yemeni army said it repelled a separate attack Friday evening without casualties.

Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa, said it marked the first time in months the government forces had announced a counteroffensive, framing it as retaliation for a Houthi shift towards preemptive strikes on army positions in Marib and Hadramout.

The Houthis, Mawry said, claim they are acting on suspicions that government forces are coordinating with Saudi Arabia on a broader offensive against Houthi-held territory.

Elisabeth Kendall, a Middle East specialist and president of Girton College at Cambridge, said the escalation carries a “looming possibility” of tipping Yemen back into full-scale conflict.

“The civil war in Yemen never really technically ended,” she told Al Jazeera, noting that the 2022 truce had expired.

Kendall pointed to recent troop movements and clashes as signs that “all the warning signs are there”, though she said government forces are now more unified than in previous years – a shift that could work in the government’s favour if Saudi Arabia intervenes decisively.

The United Nations has called for de-escalation, condemning both the Houthi missile attacks and the group’s continued strikes on oil tankers in the Red Sea.

articles.title: Maher blasts Rand Paul for releasing Fauci’s COVID diaries as PR expert suggests a new course for the Senator
articles.excerpt: Comedian Bill Maher criticized Sen. Rand Paul for releasing Dr. Anthony Fauci’s private COVID-19 diaries and pursuing a contempt referral, arguing that Paul’s actions conflict with his longtime libert...
articles.body_text:
Comedian Bill Maher criticized Sen. Rand Paul for releasing Dr. Anthony Fauci’s private COVID-19 diaries and pursuing a contempt referral, arguing that Paul’s actions conflict with his longtime libertarian views on privacy and government overreach.

Comedian Bill Maher is taking aim at Sen. Rand Paul for what the host says betrays Paul's own brand.

During Friday's episode of HBO's "Real Time," Maher accused Paul, R-Ky., of breaking with his libertarian views by releasing Fauci's pandemic-era diary and threatening to hold him in contempt of Congress. Meanwhile, a public relations expert told Fox News Digital that Paul should focus on why the diary matters rather than how he obtained it.

"Stop threatening to put everyone in jail who you just don’t like," Maher said more broadly about politics.

"Rand, babe, your entire brand is ‘Senator Right to Privacy,’" he added. "You’re the libertarian guy, the Fourth Amendment guy. It’s your family legacy."

BILL MAHER BREAKS WITH THE LEFT TO HAMMER ANTHONY FAUCI AFTER EXPLOSIVE SENATE HEARING

Comedian and television host Bill Maher arrived for the 27th Mark Twain Prize for American Humor gala at the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts on June 28, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Alex Wroblewski/AFP via Getty Images)

Maher’s comments come on the heels of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which is led by Paul, voting 8-5 to refer Fauci for contempt after he repeatedly invoked the Fifth Amendment during a Senate hearing regarding his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic last week.

Fauci, who received a preemptive pardon from then-President Joe Biden last year, exercised his right against self-incrimination a total of 111 times during the hearing while being questioned over his leadership as the White House chief medical adviser during the pandemic.

In the days before the hearing, Paul released more than 1000 pages of Fauci's private "COVID diaries" — medical notes and personal reflections Fauci wrote and stored on his government computer.

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

Senator Rand Paul, R-Ky, a Republican from Kentucky and chairman of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, speaks during a hearing in Washington, DC, US, on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. Anthony Fauci declined to testify in a Senate committee hearing on his role in the US response to Covid-19, invoking his 5th Amendment rights. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The move was blasted by Maher, who argued Paul's decision to publish the documents directly contradicted his longtime political platform of personal privacy and limited government intrusion.

"Your entire political career has been about warning us about government overreach," Maher said, speaking directly to Paul. "You printing someone's diary? It's like [Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez] wearing a gown that says, ‘Tax the poor.’"

Fauci's diaries were located and stored on government servers.

Jason Mudd, CEO of Axia Public Relations, told Fox News Digital that the criticism surrounding Paul's release of Fauci's private diary is unfounded, while adding he would advise Paul to change approach to explaining why the document is important.

"If Sen. Paul were my client, I’d tell him to stop defending how he got the diary and start defending why it matters," Mudd said. "A public official’s notes on a government computer aren’t a private citizen’s journal, and that distinction should have been his first sentence, not his fifth."

Maher’s comments come after he previously made headlines by suggesting that his "vote is in play" after voicing his discontent with the socialist direction the Democratic party is heading.

"Politically, Bill Maher carries resonance with a fairly non-tribal group of viewers. While that means he can often piss off both sides, it also means he can be seen as above the partisan back-and-forth, without a specific left or right agenda," media expert Kaivan Shroff told Fox News Digital.

DAVID MARCUS: BILL MAHER'S NO REPUBLICAN, HE'S JUST A RARE DEMOCRAT WHO THINKS

Dr. Anthony Fauci is sworn in during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs committee hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, DC, on July 29, 2026.  (Alex Wroblewski / AFP via Getty Images)

Shroff added that Maher's words carry more weight when he criticizes both sides of the political spectrum because of his willingness to call out his own party.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"Maher can spend one week arguing that Democrats have lost the plot and the next saying Republicans have gone too far," Shroff said. "That gives moments like this outsized significance: when someone who has repeatedly criticized Fauci and the left still looks at what Rand Paul is doing and says it crosses a line, it gives permission to viewers who aren’t particularly sympathetic to Fauci to reach the same conclusion."

"In a polarized media environment, the messenger can matter as much as the message," Shroff added.

Fox News Digital reached out to Senator Paul and Dr. Fauci for comment.

Julia Bonavita is a media and culture writer for Fox News Digital, and a Fox Flight Team drone pilot. You can follow her at @juliabonavita13 on all platforms and send story tips to julia.bonavita@fox.com.

articles.excerpt:
'It's going crazy': Eyewitnesses capture forest fires raging across British Columbia

Thousands of people were forced to flee their homes as a fast-moving wildfire in a remote part of western Canada s...
articles.body_text:
'It's going crazy': Eyewitnesses capture forest fires raging across British Columbia

Thousands of people were forced to flee their homes as a fast-moving wildfire in a remote part of western Canada spread rapidly, doubling in size since it was first detected on Friday.

The Bald Range fire now occupies more than 36 sq miles (95 sq km) across the Summerland and Okanagan-Similkameen districts of British Columbia, according to the BC Wildfire Service.

Erick Thompson, an emergency official with the Regional District of Okanagan-Similkameen, said this was one of the "quickest-moving, largest fires in such a short time" he had seen in the fire-prone region.

The fire remained "out of control" as of Saturday morning.

The Bald Range wildfire burns, as seen from a vehicle, northwest of Summerland, British Columbia, Canada

As the fire approached, Summerland's entire population of around 12,000 people was ordered to evacuate, along with about 8,000 residents of  neighbouring Peachland. Power was also lost across Summerland, city officials said early Saturday.

On Friday evening, Thompson had been giving updates on the rapidly-spreading fire from the emergency operations centre. But in a video posted from his car the next morning, he said he had left the centre to evacuate his own family.

"I had to leave the EOC to come and get my family to leave this area. We're heading south," he said.

It was not yet clear how many structures had been destroyed in the blaze.

Okanagan also has a lot of horses that residents have been struggling to evacuate.

Those unable to rescue their animals left their gates open in the hope  the animals would find their own way to safety, local residents told Canadian broadcaster CBC.

Some owners also painted markings on their animals to make them easier to identify later, CBC reported.
