articles.title: Caribbean hot spot gripped by water crisis, and tourists scramble to reschedule plans
articles.excerpt:
Dominica, Antigua and Barbuda are listed in the new travel ban from the Trump administration citing Citizenship by Investment concerns. Shown in this clip, the Antigua coastline.

Puerto Rico is imple...
articles.body_text:
Dominica, Antigua and Barbuda are listed in the new travel ban from the Trump administration citing Citizenship by Investment concerns. Shown in this clip, the Antigua coastline.

Puerto Rico is implementing water rationing measures in San Juan amid an intense drought, raising questions for American tourists visiting the Caribbean island.

More than 180,000 water customers will face 48-hour water outages on an alternating schedule starting Friday, according to The Associated Press.

Historical weather data shows that July was the driest month for San Juan in more than 120 years, as well as the second-hottest month on record.

CRUISES THROWN INTO CHAOS AS DROUGHT STRANDS SHIPS, LEAVES PASSENGERS SCRAMBLING

The U.S. Drought Monitor reports that nearly 25% of Puerto Rico is experiencing a severe drought and another 36% is under a moderate drought, per the AP.

The situation is raising concerns among some tourists regarding upcoming trips to the island.

Puerto Rico is implementing water rationing measures in San Juan as an intense drought affects parts of the Caribbean island. (Erika P. Rodríguez for The Washington Post via Getty Images)

On a Reddit forum dedicated to Puerto Rico travel, one tourist said that, though the person's hotel was equipped with an emergency water supply, they were still worried about the shortage.

"Can someone please be realistic about what it’d be like to visit during this?" the Reddit user asked. "Will it affect restaurants and bars? Should we cancel even though we likely won’t get anything refunded?"

DISNEYLAND GUESTS LEFT SCRAMBLING AFTER WATER OUTAGE SHUTS BATHROOMS AND RESTAURANTS

In response, other users offered mixed assessments of how the rationing could affect visitors.

"Hotels have cisterns and generators," one person wrote. "However, you should prepare to be flexible in your outlook, as it is a crisis."

Water rationing in San Juan is raising concerns among some tourists who have upcoming trips planned to Puerto Rico. (Ricardo Arduengo/AFP via Getty Images)

"Hotels are probably the ones less affected by all of this," a different Reddit user advised. "Businesses and restaurants will [definitely] have to adjust, like they've had to in the past. Droughts don't happen every year but they are common."

"Good luck is all I have to say," another person said. "Have family [that] were told about upcoming water shutoffs."

VACATION HOT SPOT FACES NEW CDC TRAVEL WARNING AS OUTBREAK CASES CONTINUE CLIMBING

Others were less concerned about how the drought could affect travelers.

Biggest "issues you’ll encounter [are] no ice in drinks, or car washes available," a Reddit user said.

"We didn’t feel good about going and canceled [our trip]."

"Pools are unaffected, restaurants might use paper plates," another said.

The person behind the original Reddit post later updated the thread to say the travelers canceled their trip.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"We didn’t feel good about going and canceled," the Reddit user said. "We got refunds on some things, not others, and hope to be back another time."

Reddit users offered mixed assessments about how Puerto Rico's water rationing measures could affect tourists visiting the island. (Ricardo Arduengo/AFP via Getty Images)

Water-related advisories have also affected travelers in other tropical destinations.

Earlier this year, Hawaii officials issued multiple brown water advisories across the state's islands in the aftermath of a storm.

At the time, there were concerns about heavy rain runoff carrying pesticides, sewage and animal waste into the ocean, which raised concerns about E. coli and salmonella.

More than 180,000 water customers are expected to face alternating 48-hour outages during water rationing measures in Puerto Rico. (Ricardo Arduengo / AFP via Getty Images)

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"If the water is brown, turn around," the Hawaii Department of Health Clean Water Branch said.

The Associated Press contributed reporting.

Andrea Margolis is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital and Fox Business. Readers can follow her on X at @andreamargs or send story tips to andrea.margolis@fox.com.

articles.title: US appeals court upholds injunction pausing Trump’s White House ballroom
articles.excerpt: In a sharply worded opinion, the United States Appeals Court for the District of Columbia has upheld an injunction against the construction of President Donald Trump’s White House ballroom, citing the...
articles.body_text:
In a sharply worded opinion, the United States Appeals Court for the District of Columbia has upheld an injunction against the construction of President Donald Trump’s White House ballroom, citing the need for congressional approval.

The appeals court voted on Friday by a margin of two to one, with judges Patricia Millett and Bradley Garcia forming a majority. The third judge on the panel, Neomi Rao, dissented.

The lengthy opinion began with a reflection on the White House’s role as the “people’s house”. Congress, the judges explained, wields control over the building and its surrounding property, and the president is only a temporary tenant.

“The President has no — and claims no — constitutionally assigned authority over that property, which is designed and maintained for the use of all Presidents, current and future, and for the American people,” Garcia and Millett wrote.

They then proceeded to describe the series of events that led to October’s abrupt demolition of the century-old East Wing of the White House, flattened to make way for Trump’s long sought-after ballroom.

“We are aware of no instance in American history in which a President, unilaterally and using privately collected funds, demolished substantial portions of the White House that Congress authorized to be built and American taxpayers paid for. Until now,” they wrote.

Allowing the ballroom construction to proceed will cause “permanent and irreversible harm” to the “historic, architectural, and aesthetic interests” represented by the plaintiffs, according to the ruling.

Millett and Garcia — who were appointed by Democratic presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden respectively — therefore upheld a lower court decision to pause construction while litigation proceeds.

“The Defendants have not shown that Congress delegated that authority to either the President or the National Park Service,” the judges wrote.

“Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help.”

Their injunction, however, came with a 14-day stay on its implementation, to allow the Trump administration to appeal to the Supreme Court.

On his social media platform Truth Social, Trump quickly fired back that the Supreme Court was precisely where he planned to take the case.

“We will be immediately appealing to the United States Supreme Court,” Trump wrote at one point in his lengthy, 487-word post.

“The Military and Secret Service are viewing this horrendous, politically motivated, and unlawful ruling as a National Security threat to our Nation in that the entire Complex is being built for the protection of our Country and, additionally, all future Presidents.”

Trump has repeatedly argued that the ballroom is necessary for national security purposes, creating a space for presidents to securely hold events.

Critics, however, have denounced the ballroom as an unnecessary and destructive vanity project undertaken without following the correct legal protocol.

The idea for a new ballroom stretches back to 2011, when Trump, then known primarily as a real estate magnate, told ABC News of his ambitions to build an opulent White House ballroom to host state dinners.

He had emerged at the time as a critic of then-President Obama, and he renewed his pitch to build a White House ballroom during his first successful presidential bid in 2016.

But the idea languished during Trump’s first term. However, after being sworn in for a second term in 2025, Trump quickly resumed his push for a ballroom, along with other projects designed to reshape the Washington, DC, landscape.

When Trump publicly discussed the ballroom proposal in July 2025, he pledged its construction would not be destructive.

“It won’t interfere with the current building. It will be near it, but not touching it, and pays total respect to the existing building,” he said at the time.

But last October, without advance notice, construction crews began levelling the East Wing, which was first built in 1902.

The nonprofit National Trust for Historic Preservation was among the groups that expressed outrage at the sudden demolition.

Plans also emerged showing that the ballroom would be approximately 90,000 square feet, or roughly 8,361 square metres, a size that would dwarf the main structure of the White House.

In December, the National Trust filed a lawsuit, arguing that Trump exceeded his authority by unilaterally destroying the East Wing and erecting a ballroom.

On March 31, US District Court Judge Richard Leon, an appointee of Republican President George W Bush, sided with the National Trust and issued an initial injunction to pause the construction.

“Unless and until Congress blesses this project through statutory authorization, construction has to stop,” Leon wrote at the time.

He did, however, offer a carve-out to allow any construction that was necessary for national security — though he clarified that his exception did not allow for the ballroom project as a whole to proceed.

On Friday, the National Trust applauded the appeals court’s decision to maintain Judge Leon’s injunction, pausing the ballroom’s construction while litigation proceeds.

“This is a great day for our country and for the American people’s right to voice their opinions about the historic places they cherish, including the White House,” the trust’s president, Brent Leggs, said.

“From the beginning, our position has been clear and consistent: the law states that only Congress can authorize the construction of a ballroom at the White House.”

But Trump and his allies have argued that the ballroom as a whole is a critical national security asset. In recent months, they have suggested the structure would be six storeys deep, with bomb shelters, an underground military hospital, secret military facilities and drone-related protective materials on the roof.

Trump also quoted extensively from the appeals court’s dissent, issued by Rao, one of his judicial appointees.

“The district court issued an extraordinary injunction halting all construction of the ballroom. This was a blatant abuse of discretion,” Rao said, reflecting on Leon’s decision.

She added that she believes the National Trust has no standing and that the district court had let “aesthetic displeasure” outweigh “the government’s security interests”. She also framed the construction as a matter of executive authority.

“Because the injunction is beyond the proper province of the federal courts, construction should be allowed to continue,” Rao wrote.

But her colleagues on the appeals court ruled otherwise — and even suggested that the ballroom project might continue, should Trump prevail in the overall litigation.

The injunction, after all, only pauses the construction while the lawsuit unfolds, they wrote.

“This ruling does not even necessarily mean that the Defendants may not ultimately construct the ballroom,” Garcia and Millett said.

“What it does mean is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court’s expeditious litigation without securing Congress’s authorization, as the Constitution and laws require.”

articles.title: The Colorado Buffaloes are once again getting roasted online for looking like a Pop Warner team
articles.excerpt:
Dan Dakich shows respect for Deion Sanders speaking up about the challenges he's faced since getting bladder cancer.

It's been a while since I talked about the Colorado Buffaloes football team — thei...
articles.body_text:
Dan Dakich shows respect for Deion Sanders speaking up about the challenges he's faced since getting bladder cancer.

It's been a while since I talked about the Colorado Buffaloes football team — their spring game, to be exact.

College football had been gone for three months at that point and every Power 4 program's spring game was basically like an oasis in a desert when it came to the cravings of the fans.

At that time, the Buffs were making headlines for the physical makeup of their team, and since no one else had anything to talk about, the mighty mites of Boulder got the microscope put squarely on them.

OKLAHOMA SOONERS QUARTERBACK JOHN MATEER LOOKS ABSOLUTELY JACKED JUST IN TIME FOR FALL CAMP

LaJohntay Wester #10 of the Colorado Buffaloes celebrates with Travis Hunter #12 and Shedeur Sanders #2 after his first quarter touchdown against the Oklahoma State Cowboys at Folsom Field on November 29, 2024 in Boulder, Colorado. (Dustin Bradford/Getty Images)

Folks on the internet picked Colorado apart for their lack of size, comparing them to a high school football team.

Now, summer workouts have concluded and fall camp is in full session, so let's check in on the Buffaloes and see what they've been doing in the weight room all offseason.

Surely Coach Prime had his guys in the lab getting jacked all summer long, right?

Hmm, that's weird. Why would the Colorado football official X account post a video of a local Denver-area Pop Warner team running passing drills?

MICHIGAN STATE'S SPRING GAME SHENANIGANS ARE A CRIME AGAINST HUMANITY

Oh, wait, I've just received an urgent update that says this is, in fact, the actual Colorado Buffaloes football team practicing for the 2026 season.

Nov 23, 2024; Kansas City, Missouri, USA; Colorado head coach Deion Sanders watches his players warmup prior to the game between the Kansas Jayhawks and the Colorado Buffaloes at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium. (Nick Tre. Smith-Imagn Images)

What exactly does the strength and conditioning coach do at Colorado, anyway?

The comments section under the post is filled with people who are questioning why a Power 4 football team looks like a solid 6A high school program from Texas.

I was only half kidding when I questioned why the Colorado account was posting Pop Warner clips, too.

When I scrolled past this initially, all I saw was the size of the players and the field they were playing on, so I had to do a legitimate triple take to make sure what I was seeing was accurate.

For crying out loud, even the ref in the background looks like a high school student they got as a volunteer for a summer job.

Speaking of the Colorado X account, I feel bad for the social media admin in charge of posting this.

You know that young man or woman was thinking, "This is going to get us torched online."

And, you know what? They were absolutely right.

Julian Lewis of the Colorado Buffaloes carries the ball for a gain in the first half against the Arizona State Sun Devils at Folsom Field (Dustin Bradford/Getty Images)

From everything I could find, the Buffs are projected to finish at or near the bottom of the Big 12, and without knowing too much about what the team has returning aside from former five-star signal caller Julian Lewis, I can see why.

Coach Prime better hope his players are as fast as he was when he played college football, because they certainly aren't overpowering any of their opponents this season.

articles.title: ‘It didn’t need to end this way’: mother of US teen trafficked and killed decries police failures
articles.excerpt:
Robyn Cory says daughter Kristen was not protected, amid questions about why it took six years to identify remains

The family of Kristen Galvan, a 15-year-old Houston girl who was sex trafficked and ...
articles.body_text:
Robyn Cory says daughter Kristen was not protected, amid questions about why it took six years to identify remains

The family of Kristen Galvan, a 15-year-old Houston girl who was sex trafficked and murdered, says law enforcement failed her twice by not protecting her after she gave forensic interviews about her traffickers, and later by taking more than six years to identify her remains.

The Texas attorney general’s office announced on 28 July that Kristen’s remains had been positively identified using advanced DNA testing conducted over the past year. Parts of her skull, clothing and an earring were found beneath a bridge beside a jogging trail in Missouri City, about 10 miles outside Houston.

The remains were recovered by law enforcement on 29 January 2020 about three weeks after she disappeared.

Kristen was bound with duct tape, beaten and stabbed to death, said Robyn Cory, her mother. The rest of her body has never been recovered. An investigation into her homicide is ongoing, the Texas attorney general’s office has said.

The Guardian reported in January that Kristen’s death was first confirmed to her family through mitochondrial DNA extracted from one of her molars, with testing verifying a mother-child relationship with Cory.

Kristen’s case generated significant media attention and has been featured in several television documentaries about missing people.

Kristen, who was also known by her nickname “Kiki”, was an honor-roll student who dreamed of joining the military. Her life changed in 2019 when she was groomed by a sex-trafficking gang through a boy acting as a scout at her school. Before long, gang members began contacting her on Instagram, showering her with compliments and invitations to parties as they worked to groom her.

On 1 November 2019, she was lured away from home by the gang, who sex trafficked her to buyers over social media and forced her to walk Houston’s red-light district. Nine days later, police found her there and brought her back to her family. She arrived home deeply traumatized and fearful her traffickers would harm her or her family unless she went back to them.

“Kristen screamed at me, ‘They’re going to kill you. They have pictures of you all. They’re going to kill my brothers.’ I didn’t realise the hold they had over my child,” Cory said.

At that time, Kristen also gave written statements that provided evidence that helped convict three men who trafficked her, and her phone was taken into custody.

But Houston police did not offer the family witness protection, Cory said. She believes this could have saved her daughter’s life. The Guardian has viewed an email sent by her family to Houston police on 27 November 2019, seeking an update on the arrest of her trafficker, which said that Kristen was very concerned for her safety, as well as the safety of her family.

“Two months before my baby was murdered, we were pleading with them for help,” Cory said. “We knew we were in danger. This could have all been prevented if she had been given protection after she gave evidence against her traffickers.”

Two law enforcement officials not involved in the case, who spoke to the Guardian, said providing witness protection to trafficking victims – particularly those whose traffickers have gang affiliations – is widely considered best practice.

“If Kristen’s case had been taken seriously as an endangered trafficking victim rather than just a runaway, her life could have been spared,” said Betty Simons, a private investigator who worked on Kristen’s missing persons case for six years. “It didn’t need to end this way.”

The Houston police department and the US attorney’s office for the southern district of Texas, which prosecuted Kristen’s trafficker Aryion Jackson, did not respond to requests for comment from the Guardian.

As a precaution, her family relocated Kristen to her grandparents’ home in Spring, in Montgomery county, Texas. Kristen went missing again in early January 2020 and was never seen again.

Cory and Simons say Kristen’s disappearance was not treated with sufficient urgency by the Montgomery county sheriff’s office. The family requested an Amber alert – an emergency notification issued to the public when authorities believe a child is believed to be missing and in danger – but the request was denied.

“I begged for an Amber alert, but law enforcement mislabelled her as a runaway. They don’t look for runaways,” Cory said.

Cory also requested that investigators ping Kristen’s phone to try to determine its location in the days following her disappearance. She said that request was also denied.

Montgomery county sheriff’s office, which led the missing-person investigation, did not respond to requests for comment about its efforts to locate Kristen after she went missing. The sheriff’s office said in a press release that it assigned Kristen’s case to a human trafficking unit on 16 January 2020, which is two weeks after she went missing and seven days after she is believed to have been murdered.

Despite Kristen’s remains being found three weeks after her disappearance in Missouri City, investigators said they were unable to identify them using conventional DNA testing.

“Missouri City police department attempted to identify the remains, but their condition prevented the development of an STR [short tandem repeat] profile, making advanced DNA testing necessary,” said the Texas attorney general’s office in a statement.

Last week, Cory and Simons met with the medical examiner on Kristen’s case, who said that DNA testing could have been conducted when her remains were first found, which contradicts the statement from the attorney general’s office, they said. The Texas attorney general’s office and Missouri City police department did not respond to a request for comment.

Additionally, Cory said investigators told her in 2025 that no soft tissue sample had been collected before her daughter’s remains were chemically processed, with the “flesh scrubbed off them”, for a forensic facial reconstruction sketch artist. She says investigators told her that extracting DNA after that process became significantly more difficult.

“How do you find a deceased missing child in your city and not properly sample DNA? She should have been identified years ago, in my opinion,” said Cory.

The Missouri City police department did not respond to questions.

In 2021, a profile of an unidentified Jane Doe was listed on the Department of Justice’s National Missing and Unidentified Persons System (NamUs), a database of missing, unidentified and unclaimed individuals. It estimated the victim to be between 12 and 18, of Hispanic and American Indian heritage, which Kristen has from both lineages.

Cory said the case file included a forensic facial sketch that bore a striking resemblance to Kristen. She says her requests to detectives with the Montgomery county sheriff’s office and the FBI to investigate whether the Jane Doe was her daughter weren’t acted upon.

In a 29 July press release, the Montgomery county sheriff’s office said it only received a tip that the Jane Doe might be Kristen on 8 July 2025.

Yet, the Guardian has viewed text messages between Cory and law enforcement from 2022 in which she asked investigators to examine the Jane Doe profile. Cory also first mentioned the profile to the Guardian in an interview in 2024.

“I had saved the Jane Doe profile because I always found myself awake at 4am, going back and just staring at the sketch,” Cory said. “I kept asking but they would never test her.”

The Montgomery county sheriff’s office did not respond to questions about the discrepancy in the timeline.

Cory said the breakthrough came in early 2025 after the Montgomery county sheriff’s office cold case division took over the investigation and acted on her request to investigate the Jane Doe profile. The detective then located the Jane Doe’s remains at the attorney general’s Office, which had held them since 2022.

Cory said she was very grateful for the investigative work detectives at the cold case unit Montgomery county sheriff’s office, Missouri City police department and the attorney general’s office have done over the past two years. But she says she still has unanswered questions about what efforts were made during the first four years after her daughter disappeared by law enforcement officers previously working her daughter’s case.

“Nobody listened until the cold case detective did in March 2025,” said Cory. “The new detectives on the case have moved mountains.”

During her five-year search for Kristen, Cory helped recover and rescue other trafficked girls. She also advocated for safety improvements along Houston’s Bissonnet Street, an area long associated with trafficked sex workers. Her work contributed to the installation of barriers designed to disrupt trafficking activity.

“The Galvan family’s unwavering commitment to seeking answers not only ensured Kristen was never forgotten but also inspired advocacy that continues to benefit vulnerable children, victims and families throughout the Houston community,” the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children said in a statement.

Last week, Cory was permitted to spend time with her daughter’s remains at a medical examiner’s office. They were placed in a small square cardboard box with a lid and set on a desk in front of her. The box was labeled only with Kristen’s case number. Cory used a pen to write her full name, Kristen Marie Galvan, on the box and draw hearts, to give Kristen her name back, she said. She placed a bouquet of flowers on top.

“After all these years, I felt like I needed to be near her,” she said. “I carried the box. It was so light, but I could feel her with me.”

Cory is now planning a memorial at the site where her daughter’s partial remains were discovered in Missouri City. It will feature a cross illuminated with lights, she said, because “Kristen was scared of the dark”.

articles.title: The White House’s plan to vet potentially dangerous AI is cloaked in secrecy
articles.excerpt:
A Trump administration framework on AI testing leaves a lack of transparency – and plenty of open questions

After months of talking with tech industry leaders, the Trump administration finalized a fr...
articles.body_text:
A Trump administration framework on AI testing leaves a lack of transparency – and plenty of open questions

After months of talking with tech industry leaders, the Trump administration finalized a framework this week for how it will test new artificial intelligence models for safety and cybersecurity risks. So far, the White House is keeping details of the framework private, in a blow to transparency and potential boon for secretive AI companies.

On Tuesday, staff from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, Nvidia and Microsoft attended a private meeting with White House officials to review the AI framework. Multiple outlets have since reported that although the volunteer vetting process for new AI models has been settled, the White House does not plan to release its policy publicly and will only share testing criteria with a select few tech companies.

The Trump administration and tech industry’s opaque process for how they will check if new AI models threaten global cybersecurity has left numerous questions about how the framework will operate. It remains unclear what level of scrutiny models will face and what safety benchmarks they must meet, leaving businesses, foreign governments and the public in the dark.

The White House, OpenAI and Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.

Discussions over creating an AI cybersecurity framework began earlier this year after the release of Anthropic’s Mythos model, which the company withheld from public release in April over concerns that it could be used to hack into IT and financial systems. The model’s capabilities sparked a small geopolitical crisis over cybersecurity, as well as spurred the Trump administration to reconsider its hands-off approach to AI regulation in favor of slightly more oversight.

In June, the White House issued an executive order that called for AI companies to voluntarily submit their new models for government review up to 30 days before release. The order was a watered-down version of initial notions to make some parts of the vetting process mandatory. Tech moguls including Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg reportedly personally lobbied Trump against the mandate. The order also left an August deadline for determining the framework, which the White House and AI companies now appear intent on keeping to themselves.

The murky nature of the framework increases uncertainty for businesses reliant on AI models, as well as on foreign governments increasingly worried that frontier AI models can pose unexpected security risks. It also means that outside researchers and cybersecurity experts have little visibility into how the government is assessing new AI models, with only companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic privy to the process.

It is also unclear which companies’ models will be subject to government review, since the executive order does not define what qualifies as the advanced AI it targets. Open source models, which are free to download and use, for instance, will be excluded from the framework, according to Axios.

The framework comes amid persistent security concerns surrounding new AI models. Over the past month OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta have disclosed that their new models hacked into outside organizations during what were intended to be isolated security tests. OpenAI and Anthropic also agreed to delay the release of new AI products over cybersecurity concerns and fear that their models could be used to hack into financial systems or otherwise create harm.

Earlier this year, the Trump administration ordered the Center for AI Standards and Innovation to stop issuing public reports on AI model assessments while it worked out a framework. It is unclear whether those reports will resume now that the framework is finalized.

articles.title: Trump's pick for top law enforcement official gets crucial last-minute lifeline for confirmation
articles.excerpt: Fox News correspondent David Spunt reports on the Senate impasse over President Donald Trump's nomination of Todd Blanche for attorney general as Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis remain noncommittal....
articles.body_text:
Fox News correspondent David Spunt reports on the Senate impasse over President Donald Trump's nomination of Todd Blanche for attorney general as Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis remain noncommittal.

As Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche's confirmation appeared headed for sure defeat, one on-the-fence Senate Republican gave him, and President Donald Trump, a vital lifeline.

Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., has remained quiet throughout this and last week on how he would vote on Blanche, who barely survived his confirmation vote from the Senate Judiciary Committee. Now, after conversations with Trump's pick to lead the Department of Justice (DOJ), the pieces are in place to confirm Blanche.

"I will vote for Mr. Blanche," an emotional Cassidy said on the Senate floor. "I'll be criticized for this vote. What's new? But, the people of Louisiana can be assured that I worked hard to understand the issue and to make the right decision."

COLLINS DROPS THE HAMMER ON TRUMP'S PICK TO LEAD DOJ, JEOPARDIZING PATH TO CONFIRMATION

U.S. Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA) arrives for a meeting with Senate Republicans in the U.S. Capitol on June 28, 2025 in Washington, DC. Senate Republicans overnight released a new version of the "One, Big, Beautiful Bill," as they approach U.S. President Donald Trump's July 4 deadline. (Photo by Al Drago/Getty Images)

With Cassidy's green light, Blanche has a chance, even with Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., missing in action. But to be confirmed, Senate Republicans will need an assist from Vice President JD Vance. Still, it’s unclear whether the Senate will actually vote on Blanche on Friday, which could be the upper chamber’s grand finale of the summer before it exits Washington, D.C., for the remainder of August.

It comes after Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, announced that she would not support Blanche’s nomination to be the nation’s top prosecutor and law enforcement official, dealing another blow to his rocky confirmation process.

Her defection, despite a heavy lobbying effort by Blanche that saw him make the trek to Alaska, means that Senate Republican leadership can’t afford to lose anymore votes to get him across the finish line, given that , R-Ky., though now back home, has still not returned to the Senate.

Murkowski acknowledged Blanche’s visit to Alaska and heavy lobbying effort throughout the last few weeks, but it’s his connection to President Donald Trump’s nearly $2 billion anti-weaponization fund, and broader concerns of a weaponized Justice Department, that proved the nail in the coffin for her.

TRUMP'S AG PICK SURVIVES — FOR NOW — AS REPUBLICANS QUESTION IF WHITE HOUSE DEAL WILL HOLD

"The politicization — even weaponization — of the Department did not start with this administration but has accelerated during it," Murkowski said in a statement. "I take issue with the handling of the release of the Epstein files; the sweeping immunity protections granted to the President, his family, and their businesses; the statements that have been made to anti-abortion groups; and the repeated targeting of individuals ranging from former administration staff to sitting U.S. Senators."

"I am also keenly aware that the Department’s nearly $2-billion dollar slush fund—which likely would have rewarded January 6 protesters—is only off the table because this nomination is pending and the Senate has leverage," she continued. "Once we vote, that will end, and there is no telling what the future holds."

TRUMP THREATENS TO YANK HIS OWN AG NOMINEE AS GOP REVOLT GROWS

Senator Lisa Murkowski, a Republican from Alaska, speaks to members of the media following a vote outside the US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, on Friday, Oct. 3, 2025.  (Graeme Sloan/Getty Images)

To Murkowski’s latter issue, several lawmakers in both sides of the aisle acknowledge that though Blanche and the Department of Justice (DOJ) agreed to permanently rescind the fund in writing to Sens. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, there’s nothing stopping Trump from reviving it.

And he’s on several occasions made clear he wants to see it come back.

"The country needs an Attorney General who will check the worst impulses of this administration," Murkowski said. "I hope Mr. Blanche is able to achieve that, if confirmed, but I simply do not have confidence that will be the case."

Before making her decision, Trump already took a snipe at her during an interview with Punch Bowl News published Friday morning.

"I’m against Murkowski," Trump said. "I do more for Alaska than any president in history. No president’s done for Alaska what I’ve done. She’s not good."

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

articles.title: Cricket’s Shakib, an Hasina ally, will face trial in Bangladesh if secure
articles.excerpt: Bangladeshi cricket great Shakib Al ⁠Hasan, an ally of ousted Prime Minister Sheikh ⁠Hasina, says he is ready to return from a two-year exile, face trial on charges that include murder, and play a far...
articles.body_text:
Bangladeshi cricket great Shakib Al ⁠Hasan, an ally of ousted Prime Minister Sheikh ⁠Hasina, says he is ready to return from a two-year exile, face trial on charges that include murder, and play a farewell series if the government guarantees his safety.

Shakib, a former politician for Hasina’s Awami League, has been living in the United States since her government was toppled in a deadly student-led uprising in August 2024.

Now 39, ⁠the player has not yet retired from international cricket and said he still hopes to play a farewell series at home and represent his country at the 2027 Cricket World Cup, a one-day international tournament.

The former Bangladeshi captain’s case highlights the wider fallout from Hasina’s ouster, which has left dozens of her allies facing criminal charges and unable to return to Bangladesh.

His return would test whether Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s government will accommodate figures from ⁠the former governing party — an open question as Hasina herself has announced plans to go back in December despite having been given a death sentence there.

“If I get the clearance from the government that my security will be ensured, I am happy to go back, face the court trial and everything that’s needed to be done,” Shakib told the Reuters news agency by phone from Sri Lanka, where he is playing franchise cricket.

“I know I haven’t done anything,” he said, giving the most detailed account yet of his two years abroad. Hasina, who has been living in India, was sentenced to death in absentia over the crackdown on the Bangladesh protests that killed about 1,400 ‌people, according to the United Nations.

She has told Reuters that she and other Awami League leaders plan to return to Bangladesh voluntarily in December. Shakib said he wanted to go home immediately, but failing that would try to return alongside her.

“Whatever the captain says, we follow her,” he said. “I think they will decide it better, and we will follow the instructions given to us.” Shakib defended his virtual appearance at a Delhi news conference on Wednesday alongside Hasina, after which his unoccupied house in Bangladesh was attacked, saying he had called only for peace and Bangladesh’s progress and had no regrets.

He said he had written, through a lawyer, to the Bangladeshi interior, law and sports ministries under the previous interim government as well as to the police, seeking to have what he described as fabricated charges against him dropped, but had received no response. Shakib said he was keen to talk to Prime Minister Rahman about returning.

Turning to cricket, ⁠Shakib said he would not wait long to retire.

“I am playing most of the franchise leagues. I am feeling good, still enjoying the game, playing ⁠well also,” he said. “But … age is not on my side at this moment, so I cannot wait for too long.”

On one occasion in late 2024, Shakib said, he boarded a flight home on assurances from the interim government that he would be given security. He called officials from the airport lounge to confirm he was travelling, then was told mid-journey to turn back. He landed in Dubai and returned to New York, where he lives on Long Island with his wife ⁠and three children.

“I don’t know what changed in 12 hours,” he said, adding that the trip had been arranged over the previous five to seven days.

A later return plan collapsed after he posted a birthday message for Hasina on social media, which he said authorities cited as the reason for barring his re-entry. “I don’t understand how ⁠that is the criteria for not letting me into Bangladesh,” he said.

Shakib rejected suggestions made by previous officials that distancing himself from ⁠Hasina and the Awami League could ease his return. “There is no way I will consider that.”

In 2024, the then-interim government’s sports adviser, Asif Mahmud, said Shakib would be given security like any other cricketer, but he urged the player to clarify his political stance to reduce public anger over his Awami League ties.

He said two cases against him are currently active: one over the alleged killing of a protester during the uprising, and one brought by anticorruption authorities about alleged corruption. The murder case, he said, was filed ‌on a day in August 2024 when he was playing a match in Toronto.

“It’s a laughable case,” he said, adding that he has not yet appointed a defence lawyer.

His bank accounts have also been frozen for a year and a half pending investigation, he said, though he declined to name the banks or say how much money was being withheld.

“When someone is the highest-taxed player for the last 10 years and ‌paid all ‌the taxes and everything and his account has been frozen for a year and a half for investigation,” he said. “I will give you all the information you need, but if you don’t find anything, just release it.”

Shakib said that for two years he had not seen his parents, who have remained in Bangladesh but have not been allowed to leave.

“It’s been difficult for all of us, but we are surviving.”

On Thursday, Shakib said his house had been attacked after he joined Hasina’s first public media conference since her 2024 removal from power.

articles.title: Haitians face arrest and deportation after US removes TPS protections
articles.excerpt:
DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin says ‘We’re going after them right now’ despite threat of violence in home country

Hundreds of thousands of Haitians are faced with the prospect of imminent risk of arr...
articles.body_text:
DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin says ‘We’re going after them right now’ despite threat of violence in home country

Hundreds of thousands of Haitians are faced with the prospect of imminent risk of arrest and deportation – to a home country racked with crime, violence and political unrest – after the Trump administration officially stripped them of humanitarian protections that had allowed them to live and work legally in the United States for years.

US district judge Ana Reyes confirmed on Wednesday that her order blocking the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) from ending temporary protected status (TPS) for Haiti was no longer in effect. This followed the controversial supreme court ruling in June that upended judicial review of the program and opened the door for immigration enforcement to track down and detain Haitians en masse.

“We’re going after them right now,” the DHS secretary, Markwayne Mullin, said earlier this week. “These individuals can either self-deport or we’ll arrest you and send you back. It’s that simple.”

Enacted by Congress in 1990, TPS protects people who are already in the US when a natural disaster, epidemic, armed conflict or other extraordinary and temporary circumstance affects their country of origin, making it unsafe for them to return home.

TPS holders are eligible for work permits and have added an estimated $262bn to the US economy since 2001, according to the FWD.us advocacy organization, often pursuing careers in essential industries such as construction and health and elder care.

But since returning to office last year, the Trump administration has almost categorically terminated existing TPS designations for some of the most dangerous countries in the world – a policy change that eventually led the highest court to authorize ending the program for Haiti and Syria, despite both countries being on the state department’s “do not travel” advisory list.

“In a stunning contradiction, the administration advises Americans against all travel to Haiti – and instructs those who go anyway to draft a will and submit DNA samples so their remains can be identified,” said Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, president and CEO of the immigrant-serving non-profit Global Refuge.

He continued: “That is the government’s own assessment of the danger. To then compel hundreds of thousands of Haitians into such dire circumstances is an unconscionable abdication of our moral responsibility.”

More than 300,000 Haitians have lost TPS permission overnight and could endure deportation if they have not applied for another form of immigration relief, such as asylum in the US or a green card. For a wide swathe of people, no such pathway to citizenship exists, even if they have lived in the US for decades.

Even so, the thought of returning to Haiti’s life-threatening conditions is “unimaginable” for many Haitians in the US, PBS News reported.

“It’s not that we don’t want to go back to Haiti,” said Harriett Cecilia Joseph, a former TPS holder. “It’s just the situation [there] doesn’t allow us to.”

Already, removal orders for Haitians in the immigration courts have soared by 96% between March and June, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse (Trac). And immigration officials have started outfitting Haitians with ankle monitors to track their movements, making them easy to find and detain.

“They now face an impossible choice: remain without status and risk arrest and deportation, or return to a Haiti marred by gang violence, kidnapping and the collapse of basic services,” said Vignarajah.

Thousands of Syrians, although a much smaller group in the US than Haitians, may be at similar risk of repatriation after losing TPS and their affiliated work permits. At the same time, a US district court on Wednesday also allowed the federal government to end employment authorization for active TPS holders from El Salvador, Ukraine and Sudan, jeopardizing their livelihoods despite their ongoing protections against deportation.

With so many immigrants suddenly barred from the workforce, business owners are being forced to let go of employees in industries already hampered by significant labor shortages.

Meanwhile, Haitians and their champions are calling on the US Senate to extend TPS legislatively, through a proposal that already passed the House of Representatives in April.

“We work hard, we pay our taxes, we give back to our communities and we are a big part of the engine that keeps the United States workforce in many essential industries moving,” Josiane Valsaint, a Haitian who had TPS, wrote for the Guardian. “We deserve to stay here, with our families and loved ones.”

articles.title: It sounds like Tony Romo may never return to CBS
articles.excerpt:
Fox News national correspondent Kevin Corke reports on Tony Romo’s refusal to take a breathalyzer test on ‘The Will Cain Show.’

It sounds like Tony Romo may never return to CBS.

As OutKick reported ...
articles.body_text:
Fox News national correspondent Kevin Corke reports on Tony Romo’s refusal to take a breathalyzer test on ‘The Will Cain Show.’

It sounds like Tony Romo may never return to CBS.

As OutKick reported last week, Romo's OWI arrest put his future in jeopardy beyond the initial indefinite suspension.

Even before his arrest, there were doubts about whether CBS would keep Romo as its lead NFL analyst beyond this season, especially with the network set to air the Super Bowl in 2028.

Romo's stock has also fallen considerably over the past three seasons, with critics pointing to his lack of preparation, goofy antics, and increasingly forced banter with Jim Nantz.

According to Puck News, Romo's arrest could expedite his departure. The outlet reported on Thursday that the consensus around the sports media industry is that "Romo won’t be back."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

CBS Sports play-by-play announcer Jim Nantz (left), analyst Tony Romo (center) and sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson at press conference at the Super Bowl LVIII Media Center at the Mandalay Bay Resort and Casino on Feb. 6, 2024. (Kirby Lee/USA TODAY Sports)

CBS could also invoke a morals clause to fire Romo for cause over the arrest video. However, Romo is owed 18 million a year through 2030. Therefore, his legal team would almost certainly fight any attempt to void the deal.

Either way, CBS does not have to put Romo back on the air.

Romo's exit would open up one of the biggest jobs in sports media: calling games alongside Jim Nantz. J.J. Watt will replace Romo this season after a promising year in the booth. If Watt works well with Nantz, CBS would have every reason to consider keeping him there full-time.

J.J. Watt at Super Bowl LVIII. (Mary Kouw/CBS via Getty Images)

The Ellison-owned CBS also has deep pockets and could go after a bigger name ahead of the Super Bowl next season.

Troy Aikman, Kirk Herbstreit, and Greg Olsen all have contracts that expire after this season. Expect CBS to consider each of them.

Aikman is the most intriguing option and arguably the best NFL color commentator in the industry. That said, it would likely take around $25 million a year for CBS to poach Aikman away from ESPN.

Olsen is currently the No. 2 analyst at Fox, but possesses the talent to be a No. 1.

Herbstreit is more of a long shot. While he is Amazon's top NFL analyst, he is still best known for his work on ESPN's College GameDay and college football coverage. CBS no longer has the college football inventory to match that.

ESPN "College GameDay" analyst Kirk Herbstreit speaks before the Miami Hurricanes versus Ole Miss Rebels College Football Playoff Semifinal at the VRBO Fiesta Bowl on Jan. 8, 2026 at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Arizona. (Kevin Abele/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

As for Romo, it's hard to imagine another network wanting him in the booth, even with more streamers adding NFL games to their lineups.

articles.title: Unearthed clip of El-Sayed revealing his 'hate' for iconic Michigan town sparks online firestorm: 'Dark heart'
articles.excerpt:
El-Sayed made the remark in a 2020 documentary about his 2018 campaign. (Credit: How to Fix a Primary/Version One Productions, Oct. 2020)

Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed is facing p...
articles.body_text:
El-Sayed made the remark in a 2020 documentary about his 2018 campaign. (Credit: How to Fix a Primary/Version One Productions, Oct. 2020)

Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed is facing pushback online over a resurfaced clip where he says he "hates" arguably the most treasured location in the state.

In the documentary clip from 2020, resurfaced by The Midwesterner on Friday, El-Sayed can be seen walking through Michigan’s Mackinac Island during his failed run for governor.

"I hate Mackinac so much," El-Sayed says about the state’s most recognizable vacation spots which sits on an island in Lake Huron between Michigan's Upper and Lower peninsula's.

"It’s funny cause, like, if we win, this is gonna be, like, the summer home," El-Sayed added, referencing the governor’s summer residence on the island.

DEM SENATE HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED RECOUNTS SMASHING VODKA BOTTLE AFTER BEARD CRITICISM

Michigan Democratic Senate nominee is facing criticism online over a resurfaced clip of him saying he hates one of the state's most cherished locations. (Getty Images)

"I’m just gonna be like every time I’ve ever come here, I’ve hated it. Why am I here."

The clip went viral on social media on Thursday with conservatives blasting El-Sayed for looking down on the quaint village town.

MICHIGAN SENATE RACE: EL-SAYED’S TIES TO EXTREMIST FUEL ANTISEMITISM CONCERNS AMONG JEWISH VOTERS

Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed claps during a press conference in front of the Spirit of Detroit statue on Aug. 5, 2026, in Detroit. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

"The rising stars of the Democrat Party loathe America and seek to destroy it," Federalist Editor-in-chief Mollie Hemingway posted on X. "And unlike their spiritual forebears, they see less of a reason to hide it for political gain. "

"I got engaged on this island," Outkick founder Clay Travis posted on X. It’s an awesome place. Honestly, I don’t understand how anyone could hate northern Michigan in summer, absolutely beautiful, most underrated spot in the country."

"Wow hating Mackinac!" former Trump adviser Steve Cortes posted on X. "A place that is so iconic to Michigan, to America. Abdul has a dark heart."

"Abdul el-Sayed is a repellent terror-loving anti-Semite--and that's not even the worst thing about him," Commentary Magazine editor John Podhoretz posted on X. "He hates Mackinac Island, one of the most wonderful places on earth. A person who hates Mackinac Island has had his soul ripped from his body."

Visitors can also take in the sights on Market Street by bike — there's no cars allowed on Mackinac Island, anyway. (Getty Images)

"He would rather summer at his property in Dubai ," National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) spokesperson Sarah Gallagher posted on X.

"Bro has no soul," On Brand Strategies communications associate Carly Moran posted on X. "It’s literally Heaven on Earth. "

"Abdul speaks fondly of his Egyptian summers yet he shows utter disdain for one of Michigan’s most beautiful summer destinations," former Michigan GOP gubernatorial candidate Tudor Dixon told Fox News Digital. "He wants his history to be respected but belittles Michigander’s favorite memories. He doesn’t respect us and therefore he cannot represent us."

"Abdul El-Sayed hot mic: 'I hate Mackinac so much,'" conservative influencer account End Wokeness posted on X. "This is the most American place in MI."

Some, including journalist Brad LaPlante, defended El-Sayed’s comments as being taken "out of context."

"El-Sayed was talking about the Mackinac Policy Conference, an annual gathering of policy pros and insiders that he argues brings together well-connected and powerful people and shuts most voters out of politics," LaPlante wrote.

Others weren't so sure, including Michigan Young Republicans Board Member James Asher who responded in a post on X, "Brad, are you dizzy from the way you’re spinning this?"

Mackinac Island is beloved in large part because it has retained a character increasingly rare in American tourist destinations. Motor vehicles have been largely prohibited since the 1890s, leaving visitors to travel by foot, bicycle or the island’s famous horse-drawn carriages.

The island is littered with Victorian homes, historic hotels, waterfront streets, natural scenery and celebrated fudge shops which draw more than a million visitors from around the world each summer, while landmarks such as the Grand Hotel and Fort Mackinac have helped make the island an enduring symbol of Michigan history and culture.

Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed’s campaign for comment but did not receive a response.

El-Sayed responded to the post from End Wokeness on Friday afternoon saying, "Not sure about 'End Wokeness,' but I don’t think the most 'American place in MI' can be a place that…bans cars."

Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter at Fox News. Find him on Twitter @andymarkmiller and email tips to AndrewMark.Miller@Fox.com.

articles.title: Tennessee Titans revamped their mascot and social media certainly had some thoughts
articles.excerpt: On today’s episode of Don’t @ Me, Dan Dakich reacts to ESPN's Stephen A. Smith going off on Minnesota Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve for wearing a "Trans Kids Belong" shirt against Sophie Cunningham and the ...
articles.body_text:
On today’s episode of Don’t @ Me, Dan Dakich reacts to ESPN's Stephen A. Smith going off on Minnesota Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve for wearing a "Trans Kids Belong" shirt against Sophie Cunningham and the Indiana Fever.

It's a time of change for the Tennessee Titans. The team has a new stadium getting ready to open next year, and recently showed off some new threads that really scream, "Yeah, we used to be the Houston Oilers. What of it?"

So, with so much change, reimagining and upgrading happening within the organization, apparently they decided that the team's mascot, T-Rac, an anthropomorphic raccoon, needed a makeover as well.

And, as you may have expected, the citizens of social media had some thoughts.

JOSH ALLEN DELIVERS FULL-THROATED UNSOLICITED DEFENSE OF BUFFALO BILLS' HIDEOUS NEW UNIFORMS

Now, while the T-Rac revamp had likely been in the works for quite some time, the Titans couldn’t have picked a better time to unveil it.

Why? Because raccoon stock has never been higher, what with internet sensation Jimothy taking over to the point of getting his own theme night at a Seattle Mariners game.

Consider this a "before" photo of the Tennessee Titans newly revamped mascot, T-Rac. (Photo by Matthew Maxey/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images))

So, now people are really into raccoons, even if all they usually do is pick through garbage bins and spread the contents all over the alley behind my house.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

But, to that point, fans have strong feelings when it comes to the change, and while some liked T-Rac 2.0, his more realistic look was not met with unanimous approval online.

On one hand, it seems like a waste of breath to get worked up over the mascot.

On the other, I still haven't forgiven the AHL's Hershey Bears for making their mascot, Cocoa, all trim and fit, instead of fat and jovial like he was in my youth.

The original T-Rac kind of looked like a deep-cut 'Looney Tunes' character. (Photo by Jeff Dean/Getty Images)

I feel like this is always the reaction to a new mascot. I mean, for the first 24 hours that Philadelphia Flyers mascot Gritty existed, he was reviled.

Then he fell on the ice, shot a Rangers fan with a T-shirt cannon, threatened to kill the Pittsburgh Penguins mascot, and — what do you know? — he practically became a god in Philadelphia.

I think it's just a matter of time before all Titans fans are willing to take a bullet for T-Rac 2.0...

...unless this season gets off to a bad start, in which case he might become the scapegoat (scaperaccoon?).

articles.title: James Carville predicts 2028 Democratic primary will test true strength of party's socialist wing
articles.excerpt: Democratic primaries test progressive candidates as James Carville warns against far-left extremism ahead of the August elections. Democratic strategist James Carville strongly criticized controversia...
articles.body_text:
Democratic primaries test progressive candidates as James Carville warns against far-left extremism ahead of the August elections. Democratic strategist James Carville strongly criticized controversial streamer Hasan Piker. Former West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin also joins the criticism, claiming the radical left wants to dismantle everything we know as midterm elections loom.

Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville told Fox News Digital that 2028 will decide the future of the Democratic Party, not 2026, saying all he can do is try to advise them not to make the wrong choice.

In recent months, there has been a rising faction of far-left Democratic candidates winning primaries in multiple states, and some more moderate figures are alarmed.

"I am not going to be in the same party with Hasan Piker," Carville said on "The Sunday Briefing" referring to a streamer who has made controversial statements like claiming America deserved 9/11, something he later backtracked on. "If he becomes a force in a Democratic Party, I'm out of here. I have no intention of ever being in the same political party with that guy."

In the following days, Carville spoke to Fox News Digital about how the party stands at a historic crossroads. But he advises that 2028 will be the real test of the far-left's strength.

DEMOCRATIC STRATEGIST JAMES CARVILLE SAYS HE COULD BECOME A REPUBLICAN UNDER ONE MAJOR CONDITION

James Carville warned that the Democratic Party is at a historic crossroads that will be decided in the 2028 primary. (Cindy Ord/Getty Images for SCAD)

"This I believe 100 percent — the future direction of the Democratic Party is going to be decided by Democratic primary voters in 2028," he said.

"Everyone claims they're the ascendant ring, alright, on the 2028 presidential election, and this can only be resolved at the presidential level. It cannot be resolved at the state level," he said. "And I am sure that there will be robust representation from the DSA ring of the party, whatever you want to call it. I'm sure there'll be a robust number of candidates from what I would call the governing wing of the Democratic Party, but you call it what you want."

He asserted again that this is a matter of politics that must be decided by the base of the party itself. The 2028 primary promises to be a crowded contest, with figures ranging from Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to Gavin Newsom to Pete Buttigieg to Kamala Harris to Rahm Emanuel among those expected to vie for the nomination.

"And this can't be solved through op-ed pieces, it can't be solved through cable TV network packages, panels, it can only, and that's the way it should be, that the Democrats themselves have got to settle on the direction of their party, and they're going to have all the options, and we'll see just how popular this is," he said.

KAMALA HARRIS IS THE 'FAIRLY OBVIOUS' 2028 PRESIDENTIAL FRONTRUNNER, DEMOCRATIC INSIDERS SAY

Sen. Bernie Sanders, left, and James Carville. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Cindy Ord/Getty Images for SCAD)

When later asked about what would happen if the democratic socialist wing takes power, he repeated his past prediction that there will have to be a "schism" in the official party.

"I'm going to let Democratic voters determine the direction the party goes in, and if it goes in the direction of — I'm pretty confident it won't, but if it goes in that direction, then I'm going to be 82. OK, fine, go ahead, but not with me," he said. "Until Democratic voters choose the direction of the party, I'll try to do all I can to help them make the right choice, in my opinion."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

James Carville and democratic socialist demonstrators. (David Dee Delgado/Getty Images for The New York Times; Photo by Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

Alexander Hall is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Alexander.hall@fox.com.

articles.title: ‘Sopranos’ stars reunite in emotional farewell for Vincent Pastore
articles.excerpt:
Fox News national correspondent Bryan Llenas reports on the death of ‘Sopranos' star Vincent Pastore at age 80 on ‘Fox Report.’

Years after "The Sopranos" came to an end, its stars reunited for a hea...
articles.body_text:
Fox News national correspondent Bryan Llenas reports on the death of ‘Sopranos' star Vincent Pastore at age 80 on ‘Fox Report.’

Years after "The Sopranos" came to an end, its stars reunited for a heartbreaking reason – to say goodbye to Vincent Pastore.

Pastore was laid to rest Thursday in New York, surrounded by family and friends. His "Sopranos" co-star Steven Van Zandt served as a pallbearer, helping carry the late actor to his final resting place. Pastore's casket was draped with an American flag in honor of his time served in the Navy.

Pastore's daughter remembered the man best known for the role of Salvatore "Big Pussy" Bonpensiero as "a giving person."

"He was a man who lived out his dreams… but he knew how lucky he was," she said during the emotional funeral, Page Six reported.

'THE SOPRANOS' ACTOR VINCENT PASTORE DEAD AT 80

Pallbearers, including Steven van Zandt, carry the casket of actor Vincent Pastore during his funeral at Holy Family Church in New Rochelle, NY, on Aug. 6. (James Keivom)

"I think that’s why he tried to share as much of it with as many people as possible," she added. "Whether that was a big tip, always in cash, or by shaking hands with every cop on every corner."

Maureen Van Zandt attends Vincent Pastore's funeral on Aug. 6. (T.JACKSON / BACKGRID)

Van Zandt told the outlet he kept in touch with Pastore "quite often" before his death.

"We just happened to call him two days ago. The day before he died, we luckily just happened to call him," he said, referring to himself and his wife Maureen. "He was one of a kind, and we’ll miss him very much."

Days after his death, the actor's "right-hand man," Stephen Villano, told The Post that Pastore was not anything like the character he often portrayed on the screen.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Vincent Pastore rose to fame as a key character in "The Sopranos." (Getty Images)

"He said, ‘I’m an actor. I play a character.’ So people would think that this is the man, but that wasn’t the man," he said. "The man was generous, he was kind, he was caring," Villano said.

"He cared about his neighbors, he cared about charities, he cared about fundraisers," he said, specifically supporting veterans in the Bronx, U.S. troops and the police department.

"He supported St. Jude’s [Children’s Research Hospital] and he supported the NYPD," Villano added. "Widows, orphans, their Christmas parties…all the time, back the blue."

Mourners pay their respects to Vincent Pastore at his funeral on Aug. 6. (T.JACKSON / BACKGRID)

Pastore died Aug. 1, Fox News Digital previously confirmed.

"Vinny passed away either yesterday or today at home in The Bronx," his manager, Robert Attermann, said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"I had the privilege of representing Vinny for more than 30 years, long before 'The Sopranos' made him a household name," he added. "To the world, he will always be remembered as the unforgettable 'Big Pussy,' but to those of us who knew him, he was so much more."

Vincent Pastore is survived by his daughter Renee. (Cindy Ord/Getty Images)

In addition to Pastore's role on "The Sopranos," the actor also appeared in "Blue Bloods," "Law & Order," "General Hospital," "Bull," "Pair of Kings," "Hawaii Five-0" and most recently lent his voice on an episode of "Yellowjackets."

He also appeared in a number of movies, including "Goodfellas," "A Bronx Tale," "Carlito's Way," "Gotti," "Once Upon a Time in Brooklyn," "Mickey Blue Eyes" and others.

"He loved being an actor," Attermann said. "He was passionate about his craft and was always encouraging, respectful, and generous with young actors, taking the time to offer guidance and support whenever he could."

Fox News Digital's Lori Bashian contributed to this report.

NFL star Drew Brees prepares for his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction in August 2026, reflecting on his career and overcoming doubts about his physical traits. Brees also advocates for severe food allergy awareness, sharing his own challenges and discussing Neffy, a new needle-free epinephrine nasal spray, highlighting its ease of use for millions of children who battle allergies.

'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday–Friday on OutKick.com.

First weekend of August. We've made it. The NFL is BACK. My Red Sox haven't lost a game since the Biden Administration. Carrie Underwood and Cris Collinsworth were both on my TV last night.

It's not possible to have it any better than us today. The momentum is through the roof right now. I can feel it in my bones.

I think we're in for a special weekend. Let's roll.

NBC Sunday Night Football color commentator Cris Collinsworth talks with recording artist Carrie Underwood before a game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Las Vegas Raiders at Allegiant Stadium on Sept. 24, 2023, in Las Vegas, Nev. The Steelers defeated the Raiders 23-18. (Getty Images)

Welcome to a Friday Nightcaps — the one where Carrie returns for Year 14 and has NFL fans ready to run through a brick wall.

What else? I've got the return of Collinsworth memes (my favorite fall tradition), Jim Harbaugh with an all-time response on Colin Cowherd's show, and does this look like the face of a woman who wants transgenders in women's sports?

Grab some Zucchini for National Sneak Some Zucchini Into Your Neighbor's Porch Day — seriously — and settle in for a Friday 'Cap!

There really is a day for everything, isn't there? What a day! Who knew?

For those who want more info — how could you not? — SSZIYPD "offers gardeners a way to rid themselves of extra produce. For some, this day offers a way to rid their garden of an overproducing squash plant."

That, of course, is according to Google, which also tells me that this holiday was started by Tom Roy at wellcat.com after doing years of news & talk radio.

No idea who Tom Roy from wellcat.com is, but I'm all in. I'd gladly take a zucchini on my front porch today. I'm not expecting one, but what a delight it would be!

OK, that's enough produce talk. Let's get this class started with Carrie Underwood and NBC teasing the new anthem for the upcoming NFL season during last night's THRILLING Hall of Fame game:

There's been a lot of chatter about folks not happy that Carrie Underwood is back for a 14th year on Sunday Night Football.

That's nonsense. As OutKick's unofficial Carrie Underwood—SNF reporter, I can assure you this is fake news. Yes, I'm aware Fox had a story on this yesterday.

That did not come from this department. It's a big house, folks.

Recording artist Carrie Underwood films a promo on the field before a game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Las Vegas Raiders at Allegiant Stadium on Sept. 24, 2023, in Las Vegas, Nev. (Getty Images)

Anyway, Carrie is back, the vibe has shifted back to a more rock 'n' roll theme this season, and all is well once again.

"This season, we’ve drawn inspiration from Carrie’s deep, well-documented love of rock music — a perfect fit since our Sunday Night Football anthem was born from pure rock ‘n’ roll: Joan Jett and the Blackhearts’ ‘I Hate Myself for Loving You,’" said Tripp Dixon, creative director for the SNF opening theme.

"We’ve worked to match these two rock frequencies of past and present as they come together in Carrie’s high-energy performance. The greatest players and teams in the NFL will take it from there."

Amen, Tripp. And yes, Carrie can still very much sling the fastball at 43. Elite stuff.

Carrie Underwood is back for SNF, Angel Reese celebrates Barbie Night & NFL WAGs are training-camp ready

Speaking of ... let's welcome back another member of Sunday Night Football — Cris Collinsworth!

More importantly, the return of Collinsworth memes:

Lordy. How great was Tirico last night, by the way? Is he the best announcer in the game right now?

You could probably throw Ian Eagle, Joe Davis, and even Al Michaels in there, even though Al doesn't quite have the zip on his fastball that Carrie still has on hers.

Of course, as a miserable Dolphins fan, I've grown used to Andrew Catalon. We get him about 12 times a year. Still better than dramatic Jim Nantz!

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

OK, let's rapid-fire this Friday class into a big weekend. First up? Just an all-time moment here between Colin Cowherd and Jim Harbaugh earlier this week:

Amazing. I have no earthly idea what Jim is trying to say, but I very much enjoyed the journey from Point A to Point B.

"Evolvement ... is that a word? Is that a word, Colin?"

Colin Cowherd tries to follow Jim Harbaugh's train of thought. (Screenshot)

That was Golden State's Gabby Williams back in May, saying she would welcome a transgender player on her team. With a straight face!

And then, of course, she plays the predictable, "it's not really an issue" card. Folks, I've said it before and I'll say it again now:

If you meet someone from the "it never happens" crowd, you will know right away that you have a fraud on your hands. It's the easiest way to weed one out. It's straight out of the left's playbook.

Gabby Williams #15 of the Chicago Sky arrives before a game against the Indiana Fever on Aug. 31, 2020, at Feld Entertainment Center in Palmetto, Fla. (NBAE via Getty Images)

AB Hernandez has been dominating high school athletes all year long. Becky Pepper-Jackson won a girls' state championship in West Virginia in May.

You had volleyball player Blaire Fleming at SJSU. You had the Imane Khelif situation two summers ago in the Olympics. There was the high school trans pitcher in Minnesota who had a fastball that would make Nolan Ryan do a double-take.

Just this week, it came out that the brother of Olympian Alysa Liu is a transgender athlete in California, competing in track and field and girls’ varsity basketball.

But no, it's not a problem! Okeedokee, Gabby! Enjoy the sandbox.

OK, that's it for today — and this week. Good work, everyone. First week of August in the books. Let's stay hot this weekend.

Is it a problem? Email me at Zach.Dean@OutKick.com.

articles.body_text:
The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has released 15 prisoners and handed them over to rebels from ⁠the Congo River Alliance/March 23 movement (AFC/M23) in the east of the country.

The release was announced by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), which facilitated this first known transfer of prisoners under last year’s Qatar-mediated deal to end the fighting in the region.

The handover happened on Thursday and Friday after months of talks thrashing out the names of detainees to be freed.

An ICRC statement said the 15 prisoners agreed to be transferred before leaving the government-held eastern Congolese city of Beni in a convoy on Thursday evening.

The journey continued through Uganda before the convoy arrived in Rutshuru Territory in DRC’s North Kivu province, where the prisoners were ⁠⁠handed over to AFC/M23 on Friday, the statement added.

M23 seized the regional capitals in North and South Kivu from the Congolese government’s control in early 2025.

Stephanie Eller, head of ICRC operations in the capital ‌Kinshasa, said she hoped the transfer would pave the way for more releases.

“We hope that this ⁠operation will help bring relief ⁠to families who have been separated from their loved ones for a long time,” Eller said.

The release of detainees was one of the conditions in the Qatari-mediated agreement signed by the Congolese government and AFC/M23 in September.

“The release of the detained persons represents an important step towards enhancing confidence between the parties and creating favourable conditions for further progress towards reaching peaceful and sustainable solutions,” Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement.

It added that Qatar “expresses its hope that this step will serve as an impetus for further measures that enhance confidence-building between the parties and meet the aspirations of the Congolese people for peace, development and prosperity”.

DRC, the United Nations and Western powers have repeatedly accused neighbouring Rwanda of supporting the M23 with its ‌own ‌troops and weapons as the armed group has advanced in the east, a charge Rwanda denies.

articles.body_text:
Newly obtained 911 dispatch audio reveals a terrified friend hid in a closet as a 73-year-old neighbor gunned down a Missouri mom and her teenage daughter over a noise complaint. (Credit: Broadcastify)

FIRST ON FOX: A terrified teen hid in a closet and watched an elderly neighbor gun down her friend and the girl's mother in Missouri, dispatch audio obtained by Fox News Digital reveals.

Robert Winkelman, 73, walked down the street to his neighbor's House Springs, Missouri, home on July 25 at around 8:30 p.m. and confronted 38-year-old Jessica Lashly about what was going on at her house, the Jefferson County Sheriff's Office said.

When Lashly responded, Winkelman took out a gun and shot her in the head. As Lashly's 17-year-old daughter, Jersey Greer, rushed to help her mother, Winkelman shot the teen in the head as well, the sheriff's office said. He then chased a third person while still armed but did not fire, deputies said. Lashly and Greer died days later at a hospital.

MISSOURI NEIGHBOR ACCUSED OF KILLING MOTHER AND TEEN DAUGHTER AFTER CONFRONTING FAMILY OVER DISPUTE

Jessica Lashly, 38, and her 17-year-old daughter, Jersey Greer, were both fatally shot inside their House Springs, Missouri, home. (Midlawn Funeral Home & Memorial Gardens)

In new 911 dispatch audio obtained by Fox News Digital, a dispatcher can be heard saying that the slain 17-year old's friend was hiding in a closet.

"We do have a visual victim hiding in a closet, advising that her friend got shot. We do that law in route, but they are not on scene," the dispatcher said.

A dispatcher said two gunshots could be heard in the background of the call, which was placed by someone who reported a woman was struggling to breathe.

"Received a call, no longer receiving a response from anyone on the phone. We did hear shots in the background," the dispatcher said. "It sounds like possibly two gunshots went off."

TIKTOK INFLUENCER WHO ACCUSED ESTRANGED HUSBAND OF PEDOPHILIA FOUND DEAD IN POSSIBLE MURDER-SUICIDE

Robert Winkelman, 73, walked to his neighbor's home and opened fire, according to the Jefferson County Sheriff's Office. He later died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound. (Jefferson County Sheriff's Office)

"It's unclear what's going on at this time," he added.

When deputies arrived at Winkelman's home and moved to confront him a short time later, he turned the gun on himself.

He died at a hospital Aug. 2, according to investigators, who said he would have been charged with two counts of first-degree murder and two counts of armed criminal action.

Reports state that investigators said Winkleman initially went to Lashly's home to complain about noise. A spokesman for the sheriff's office described the horrifying incident to Fox News Digital as a "dispute between neighbors."

MISSOURI MOM OF 5 FATALLY SHOT WHILE BUYING SLUSHIES WITH CHILDREN; POLICE SEARCH FOR GUNMAN

Jersey Greer, 17, was fatally shot while trying to help her mother, according to the Jefferson County Sheriff's Office. (Ron & Lisa Rigdon | Cheap Seats Photography)

Investigators learned that Winkelman had "ongoing frustrations" with activities at Lashly's home.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Justice Greer, the teenage victim's twin sister, told KSDK, "She was literally just the funniest person ever."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

"She could make anybody laugh. She was really supportive about anything and everything. She could always tell when someone was sad or needed uplifting, and she was always the one to do it.

"Jersey's last moments, she was trying to save my mom. It just shows how brave she is, and I hope I can be half as brave as she is," she said.

Justice Greer said Lashly was a single mother who did all she could to provide for her twin daughters.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Relatives and a former coach remembered Jersey Greer as brave, funny and someone who could lift anyone's spirits. (Ron & Lisa Rigdon | Cheap Seats Photography)

"It was always just us three," Justice said. "It's going to be really hard because that's all I'm used to."

Abby Feldmann, who was Justice and Jersey Greer's coach in lacrosse, told KSDK Jersey was someone who could "change your whole perspective on life."

"There's not one person who would refuse to follow her," Feldmann said. "Everyone's behind her. She's really an amazing girl."

A young deaf migrant in Spain prepares for an emotional reunion with his family in Morocco after years apart.

Imade, a 23-year-old deaf migrant from Morocco, is forging a new life in Spain. He works as a kitchen porter in Barcelona and is learning Catalan sign language to overcome the communication challenges his deafness presents, navigating both social isolation and immigration bureaucracy. Imade left Morocco without his parents’ knowledge when he was 16. Unable to find work to support his large family, he worried that he would be just another mouth for them to feed. Now, for the first time since he left, he prepares for an emotional visit to Morocco to reunite with his family after six years of separation.
